Question 2014-10-18 Q1
Which of the following is the unit of power in the MKS system of units?

Unit question: build the power = work / time chain, starting from the unit of force.

Question 2014-10-18 Q1 · Solution
Setup

Power is work done per unit time: $P = W/t$. Work $W = F \cdot s$ is force $\times$ distance.

Model

The unit of force is $[F] = \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}/\text{s}^2$. Multiply by distance: $[W] = \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}^2$ (joule).

Derivation

$[P] = \dfrac{[W]}{[t]} = \dfrac{\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}^2}{\text{s}} = \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}^3$ (watt).

Correct answer: (e) $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}^3$

Trap

Option (a) is the joule (energy); anyone who forgets to divide by time falls for it.

Check

$P = F \cdot v$: $(\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}/\text{s}^2)(\text{m}/\text{s}) = \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}^3$ — both routes give the same unit.

The energy-power distinction is emphasized; the F·v route is used for the check.

Question 2014-10-18 Q2
Given $\vec{a} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - \hat{k}$ and $\vec{b} = \hat{i} + \hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$: if $\vec{c} = 2\vec{a} - 3\vec{b}$, what is $\vec{c} \cdot (\vec{a} \times \vec{b})$?

Scalar triple product: since c is a combination of a and b, the result can be anticipated.

Question 2014-10-18 Q2 · Solution
Setup

$\vec{c} = 2\vec{a} - 3\vec{b}$; the required $\vec{c} \cdot (\vec{a} \times \vec{b})$ is a scalar triple product.

Model

The vector $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}$ is perpendicular to the plane of $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$; $\vec{c}$ lies in the same plane.

Derivation

The dot product of an in-plane vector with a vector perpendicular to the plane is $0$. Direct calculation: $\vec{c} = (-1, 1, 4)$ and $\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = (-3, 1, -1)$, giving the product $3 + 1 - 4 = 0$.

Correct answer: (d) $0$

Trap

Diving blindly into component arithmetic wastes time; the geometric argument suffices.

Check

A triple product with a repeated component is always zero — two rows of the determinant are dependent.

First the geometry, then numerical verification.

Question 2014-10-18 Q3
If the nonzero vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ satisfy $|\vec{a} + \vec{b}| = |\vec{a} - \vec{b}|$, what is the angle between them?

Squaring technique: squaring both sides reveals the cross term.

Question 2014-10-18 Q3 · Solution
Setup

Square both sides: $|\vec{a}+\vec{b}|^2 = |\vec{a}-\vec{b}|^2$.

Model

$|\vec{a}+\vec{b}|^2 = a^2 + 2\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} + b^2$, $|\vec{a}-\vec{b}|^2 = a^2 - 2\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} + b^2$.

Derivation

Equating gives $4\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = 0$; for nonzero vectors this means perpendicularity.

Correct answer: (d) $90^\circ$

Trap

Equal diagonals mean the parallelogram is a rectangle; the $45^\circ$ intuition is wrong.

Check

Try perpendicular unit vectors: $|(1,1)| = |(1,-1)| = \sqrt{2}$ — the equality holds.

If the diagonals of a parallelogram are equal, the angle is a right angle.

Question 2014-10-18 Q4
Which is the unit vector $\hat{e}_d$ in the direction of the vector $\vec{d} = -2\hat{i} + \hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$?

Unit vector: first the magnitude, then divide each component by the magnitude.

Question 2014-10-18 Q4 · Solution
Setup

The unit vector is $\hat{e}_d = \vec{d}/|\vec{d}|$; first find the magnitude.

Model

$|\vec{d}| = \sqrt{(-2)^2 + 1^2 + (-2)^2} = \sqrt{9} = 3$.

Derivation

Each component is divided by $3$; signs are kept: $(-2/3, 1/3, -2/3)$.

Correct answer: (e) $-\frac{2}{3}\hat{i} + \frac{1}{3}\hat{j} - \frac{2}{3}\hat{k}$

Trap

Option (c) flips the last sign; check the signs one by one.

Check

Magnitude: $\sqrt{4/9+1/9+4/9} = 1$ — the unit-vector condition is satisfied.

Sign errors are the most common trap; a magnitude check is essential.

Question 2015-03-21 Q9
Given $\vec{A} = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - \hat{k}$ and $\vec{B} = a\hat{i} - \hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$: if $\vec{B}$ is perpendicular to the vector $\vec{A}$, what is $a$?

The perpendicularity condition is that the dot product is zero; it gives a single-unknown equation.

Question 2015-03-21 Q9 · Solution
Setup

Perpendicularity condition: $\vec{A} \cdot \vec{B} = 0$.

Model

Multiply the components and add: $(2)(a) + (3)(-1) + (-1)(-2)$.

Derivation

$2a - 3 + 2 = 2a - 1 = 0$, hence $a = 1/2$.

Correct answer: (a) $1/2$

Trap

Sign error: anyone writing the term $(-1)(-2) = +2$ with a minus gets a wrong result like $a = 5/2$.

Check

With $a = 1/2$: $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = 1 - 3 + 2 = 0$ — perpendicularity holds.

Watch the double-minus term; verify by substitution.

Question 2015-03-21 Q10
Which is the unit vector in the direction of the vector $\vec{A} = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - \hat{k}$?

Magnitude calculation is a sum of squares; watch numbers that do not come out of the root.

Question 2015-03-21 Q10 · Solution
Setup

The unit vector is $\vec{A}/|\vec{A}|$; first find $|\vec{A}|$.

Model

$|\vec{A}| = \sqrt{2^2 + 3^2 + (-1)^2} = \sqrt{4 + 9 + 1}$.

Derivation

$|\vec{A}| = \sqrt{14}$; the direction stays the same, signs do not change.

Correct answer: (a) $\frac{2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}-\hat{k}}{\sqrt{14}}$

Trap

Options (b) and (e) use $\sqrt{12}$; the sum of squares gives $14$, not $12$.

Check

$(4+9+1)/14 = 1$ — the unit-magnitude condition is satisfied.

Verify the radicand in the denominator by adding.

Question 2015-03-21 Q11
Given $\vec{A} = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - \hat{k}$ and $\vec{B} = a\hat{i} - \hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$ with $a = 1$, what is the magnitude of the projection of the vector $\vec{B}$ onto $\vec{A}$?

Projection magnitude formula: absolute value of the dot product divided by the axis length.

Question 2015-03-21 Q11 · Solution
Setup

Set $a = 1$: $\vec{B} = \hat{i} - \hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$. The projection magnitude is $|\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B}|/|\vec{A}|$.

Model

$\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = (2)(1) + (3)(-1) + (-1)(-2) = 2 - 3 + 2 = 1$.

Derivation

Since $|\vec{A}| = \sqrt{14}$, the projection is $1/\sqrt{14}$.

Correct answer: (b) $1/\sqrt{14}$

Trap

Do not fall for options that forget the division and say $1$, or that divide by $|\vec{B}|$.

Check

The projection must be smaller than $|\vec{B}|$: $1/\sqrt{14} \approx 0.27 < \sqrt{6}$ — consistent.

Which length you divide by is critical: divide by the length of the projection axis.

Question 2015-07-11 Q4
For the reference system shown (upward $\hat{j}$, rightward $\hat{k}$, out-of-page-downward $\hat{i}$), which one is incorrect?

First determine whether the system is right- or left-handed, then test the identities.

Question 2015-07-11 Q4 · Solution
Setup

The drawn axis arrangement is left-handed: $\hat{i} \times \hat{j} = -\hat{k}$ holds.

Model

In a left-handed system, $\hat{j} \times \hat{k} = -\hat{i}$ and $\hat{j} \times \hat{i} = +\hat{k}$ hold.

Derivation

With these rules, (a), (b), (d) and (e) come out true; $\hat{i} \times \hat{j} = \hat{k}$ in option (c) is incorrect (the correct form is $-\hat{k}$).

Correct answer: (c) $\hat{i} \times \hat{j} = \hat{k}$ (the incorrect one)

Trap

Anyone applying the right-hand rule from memory mistakes (c) as correct; the axis directions must be checked.

Check

$(\hat{j} \times \hat{i}) \cdot \hat{k} = (+\hat{k})\cdot\hat{k} = +1$ — consistent with (d); the system is left-handed.

The hand rule is set up from the diagram, not from memory.

Question 2015-07-11 Q11
Air pressure is given by the formula $P = \alpha h^x g^y d^z$ ($\alpha$ is dimensionless; $h$ is height, $g$ is acceleration, $d$ is density). What must $x$ be?

Dimensional analysis: the M, L, T exponents are equated separately.

Question 2015-07-11 Q11 · Solution
Setup

$[P] = ML^{-1}T^{-2}$; $[h]^x[g]^y[d]^z = L^x (LT^{-2})^y (ML^{-3})^z$.

Model

For M: $z = 1$; for T: $-2y = -2$, i.e. $y = 1$.

Derivation

For L: $x + y - 3z = -1$, i.e. $x + 1 - 3 = -1$, hence $x = 1$.

Correct answer: (d) $1$

Trap

Anyone mistaking the pressure dimension for $MLT^{-2}$ (force) finds the wrong exponent.

Check

The formula $P = \rho g h$ (hydrostatic) gives $x = y = z = 1$ — consistent.

The physical counterpart (liquid pressure) confirms the result.

Question 2015-07-11 Q12
Given $\vec{A} = 2\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$ and $\vec{B} = -3\hat{i} - 4\hat{j} + \hat{k}$: which is the unit vector in the direction of $\vec{B}$?

The sum 9+16+1 gives 26; divisors like 2 or 8 in the options are eliminated.

Question 2015-07-11 Q12 · Solution
Setup

The unit vector is $\vec{B}/|\vec{B}|$, where $|\vec{B}| = \sqrt{9 + 16 + 1}$.

Model

$|\vec{B}| = \sqrt{26}$; (a), (b) and (d) have the wrong divisor; (c) has no divisor.

Derivation

The direction is kept: $(-3\hat{i}-4\hat{j}+\hat{k})/\sqrt{26}$.

Correct answer: (e) $\frac{-3\hat{i}-4\hat{j}+\hat{k}}{\sqrt{26}}$

Trap

(d) points the opposite way; the direction requirement for a unit vector must not be forgotten.

Check

$(9+16+1)/26 = 1$ — unit magnitude is achieved.

First the denominator, then the direction is checked.

Question 2015-07-11 Q13
For $\vec{A} = 2\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$ and $\vec{B} = -3\hat{i} - 4\hat{j} + \hat{k}$, what is $\vec{A} \cdot \vec{B}$?

Straightforward component multiplication; write each term’s sign separately.

Question 2015-07-11 Q13 · Solution
Setup

Dot product: corresponding components are multiplied and added.

Model

$(2)(-3) + (-3)(-4) + (4)(1)$.

Derivation

$-6 + 12 + 4 = 10$.

Correct answer: (c) $10$

Trap

Writing the term $(-3)(-4) = +12$ with a minus gives $-14$ (option d).

Check

The result is positive: the angle must be acute, consistent with $\cos\theta > 0$ in Q16.

Sign tracking and consistency with the next question are checked.

Question 2015-07-11 Q14
For $\vec{A} = 2\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$ and $\vec{B} = -3\hat{i} - 4\hat{j} + \hat{k}$, what is $\vec{A} \times \vec{B}$?

Expand the determinant; the i component starts with plus, the j component with minus.

Question 2015-07-11 Q14 · Solution
Setup

Determinant: rows $\hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}$, $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$.

Model

$i[(-3)(1)-(4)(-4)] - j[(2)(1)-(4)(-3)] + k[(2)(-4)-(-3)(-3)]$.

Derivation

$i(-3+16) - j(2+12) + k(-8-9) = 13\hat{i} - 14\hat{j} - 17\hat{k}$.

Correct answer: (a) $13\hat{i} - 14\hat{j} - 17\hat{k}$

Trap

Forgetting the minus in the j component mixes $+14$ in place of $-13$ in option (d).

Check

Dotting the result with $\vec{A}$: $26 + 42 - 68 = 0$ — perpendicularity holds.

The perpendicularity test catches determinant errors.

Question 2015-07-11 Q15
What is the unit vector $\hat{c}$ perpendicular to the plane spanned by the vectors $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ (from Q12)?

The plane normal points along the cross product; both directions (±) are accepted.

Question 2015-07-11 Q15 · Solution
Setup

The direction perpendicular to the plane is $\vec{A}\times\vec{B}$ (result of Q14).

Model

$\hat{c} = \pm(\vec{A}\times\vec{B})/|\vec{A}\times\vec{B}|$.

Derivation

The numerator is $13\hat{i}-14\hat{j}-17\hat{k}$; the denominator is its magnitude.

Correct answer: (a) $\hat{c} = \pm\frac{13\hat{i}-14\hat{j}-17\hat{k}}{\sqrt{(13)^2+(-14)^2+(-17)^2}}$

Trap

(c) is not a unit vector; a denominator is required.

Check

Numerator and denominator come from the same vector; the magnitude is $1$.

The previous question’s result is used directly.

Question 2015-07-11 Q16
In which option is the cosine of the angle between $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ correctly given?

The cosine formula combines the previous two questions (dot product, magnitudes).

Question 2015-07-11 Q16 · Solution
Setup

$\cos\theta = (\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B})/(|\vec{A}||\vec{B}|)$.

Model

The numerator is $10$ from Q13; $|\vec{A}| = \sqrt{4+9+16} = \sqrt{29}$ and $|\vec{B}| = \sqrt{26}$.

Derivation

$\cos\theta = 10/(\sqrt{29}\sqrt{26})$ (positive, acute angle).

Correct answer: (b) $\frac{10}{\sqrt{29}\cdot\sqrt{26}}$

Trap

Options with negative numerators; the sign from Q13 is decisive.

Check

$10/(\sqrt{29}\sqrt{26}) \approx 0.36 < 1$ — within the cosine range.

The numerator’s sign tells in advance whether the angle is acute or obtuse.

Question 2015-11-07 Q1
Which of the following is NOT one of the base physical quantities in the SI system?

Base-derived distinction: force is derived from mass-length-time.

Question 2015-11-07 Q1 · Solution
Setup

SI base quantities: mass, length, time (plus electric current, temperature, amount of substance, luminous intensity).

Model

Force has dimension $[F] = MLT^{-2}$; it is derived, not base.

Derivation

Mass, length and time are base quantities; force is a combination of them.

Correct answer: (b) force

Trap

Option (c) says "all are base"; it must not be forgotten that force is derived.

Check

$F = ma$: its unit is $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}/\text{s}^2$ — the product of the three base units.

Newton’s second law shows that force is derived.

Question 2015-11-07 Q2
Given $\vec{a} = t\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + \hat{k}$ and $\vec{b} = \hat{i} - t\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$: at which instant $t$ is $\vec{a}$ perpendicular to the vector $\vec{b}$?

The dot product is a function of t; set it to zero and solve.

Question 2015-11-07 Q2 · Solution
Setup

Perpendicularity: $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = 0$.

Model

$(t)(1) + (2)(-t) + (1)(2) = t - 2t + 2$.

Derivation

$2 - t = 0$, hence $t = 2\ \text{s}$.

Correct answer: (c) $t = 2\ \text{s}$

Trap

Anyone equating components mistakes (equality of the same components) for perpendicularity; the condition is a sum of products.

Check

At $t = 2$: $\vec{a} = (2,2,1)$ and $\vec{b} = (1,-2,2)$; the product is $2-4+2 = 0$.

Verified by numerical substitution.

Question 2015-11-07 Q3
Which is the unit vector perpendicular to the plane spanned by the vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ from Q2 at the instant $t = 0$?

First write the t=0 vectors, then find the cross product and magnitude.

Question 2015-11-07 Q3 · Solution
Setup

At $t = 0$: $\vec{a} = 2\hat{j} + \hat{k}$ and $\vec{b} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{k}$.

Model

The normal direction is $\vec{a}\times\vec{b}$; expand the determinant.

Derivation

$\vec{a}\times\vec{b} = (4, 1, -2)$; the magnitude is $\sqrt{16+1+4} = \sqrt{21}$.

Correct answer: (d) $\frac{4\hat{i}+\hat{j}-2\hat{k}}{\sqrt{21}}$

Trap

Option (a) with denominator $\sqrt{24}$; the squared magnitude gives $21$.

Check

$(4,1,-2)\cdot(0,2,1) = 8 - 2 = 6$? Recalculating: $4\cdot 0 + 1\cdot 2 + (-2)(1) = 0$ — perpendicularity confirmed.

The cross product’s perpendicularity to both vectors is tested.

Question 2015-11-07 Q4
What is the distance between the two particles from Q2 at the instant $t = 3\ \text{s}$?

Distance is the magnitude of the position-difference vector.

Question 2015-11-07 Q4 · Solution
Setup

At $t = 3$: $\vec{a} = 3\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b} = \hat{i}-3\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$.

Model

Difference: $\vec{a}-\vec{b} = 2\hat{i}+5\hat{j}-\hat{k}$.

Derivation

Magnitude: $\sqrt{4+25+1} = \sqrt{30}\ \text{m}$.

Correct answer: (a) $\sqrt{30}\ \text{m}$

Trap

Do not fall for option (b), which forgets the square root and says $30$.

Check

$5 < \sqrt{30} < 6$; the largest component is $5$ — a reasonable range.

Check that the magnitude exceeds the largest component.

Question 2015-11-07 Q5
Which is the position vector of the first particle relative to the second at the instant $t = 3\ \text{s}$?

Relative position: subtract the second from the first; the order matters.

Question 2015-11-07 Q5 · Solution
Setup

Relative position is $\vec{a}-\vec{b}$; the values $t = 3$ are taken from Q4.

Model

$(3-1)\hat{i} + (2+3)\hat{j} + (1-2)\hat{k}$.

Derivation

$2\hat{i} + 5\hat{j} - \hat{k}$.

Correct answer: (e) $2\hat{i} + 5\hat{j} - \hat{k}$

Trap

Anyone mixing up the subtraction order gets a result with flipped signs.

Check

Its magnitude is $\sqrt{30}$ — the same as the Q4 distance; consistent.

Cross-checked against the previous question’s magnitude.

Question 2016-03-19 Q1
Given $\vec{A} = a\hat{i} - 2\hat{k}$ and $\vec{B} = b\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$ ($a, b > 0$), and $|\vec{A}| = 3$ with $|\vec{B}| = 4$, what is $|\vec{A}-\vec{B}|$?

First find a and b from the magnitudes, then write the difference vector.

Question 2016-03-19 Q1 · Solution
Setup

$|\vec{A}|^2 = a^2 + 4 = 9$, hence $a = \sqrt{5}$; $|\vec{B}|^2 = b^2 + 4 = 16$, hence $b = \sqrt{12}$.

Model

$\vec{A}-\vec{B} = \sqrt{5}\,\hat{i} - \sqrt{12}\,\hat{j}$ (the $k$ components cancel).

Derivation

Magnitude: $\sqrt{5 + 12} = \sqrt{17}$.

Correct answer: (b) $\sqrt{17}$

Trap

(c) and (d) are negative; a magnitude cannot be negative — eliminated immediately.

Check

$4 < \sqrt{17} < 5$; the triangle inequality ($|3-4| < $ result $< 7$) holds.

Options with negative magnitudes are eliminated without any calculation.

Question 2016-03-19 Q2
What is the angle between the vectors $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ from Q1?

The dot product comes only from the k components; the cosine is found from it.

Question 2016-03-19 Q2 · Solution
Setup

$\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = (a)(0) + (0)(b) + (-2)(-2) = 4$.

Model

$\cos\theta = 4/(|\vec{A}||\vec{B}|) = 4/12 = 1/3$.

Derivation

$\theta = \arccos(1/3)$.

Correct answer: (d) $\arccos 1/3$

Trap

(b) and (c) are memorized angles; the cosine $1/3$ gives no special angle.

Check

$0 < 1/3 < 1$ — acute angle, consistent with the positive product.

Products of non-shared components vanish; only the k contribution remains.

Question 2016-03-19 Q3
Which is the unit vector perpendicular to both of the vectors $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ from Q1?

Non-unit options (c) and (e) are eliminated by the denominator test.

Question 2016-03-19 Q3 · Solution
Setup

The perpendicular direction is $\vec{A}\times\vec{B}$; substitute $a = \sqrt{5}$ and $b = \sqrt{12}$.

Model

$\vec{A}\times\vec{B} = 2b\,\hat{i} + 2a\,\hat{j} + ab\,\hat{k}$; the magnitude is $|\vec{A}||\vec{B}|\sin\theta = 8\sqrt{2} = \sqrt{128}$.

Derivation

Normalizing gives $(\sqrt{12}\,\hat{i}+\sqrt{5}\,\hat{j}+\sqrt{15}\,\hat{k})/\sqrt{32}$.

Correct answer: (d) $(\sqrt{12}\,\hat{i} + \sqrt{5}\,\hat{j} + \sqrt{15}\,\hat{k})/\sqrt{32}$

Trap

(c) and (e) do not have unit magnitude; check $32$ inside the denominator: $12+5+15 = 32$.

Check

The sum of the squared numerator terms equals the denominator ($32$) — unit magnitude confirmed.

Numerator-denominator consistency is the fastest unit test.

Question 2016-07-23 Q1
If the vectors $\vec{A} = 2\hat{i} - 3\hat{j}$ and $\vec{B} = -\hat{i} + y\hat{j}$ are perpendicular, what is $y$?

Two-dimensional perpendicularity: a two-term sum is set to zero.

Question 2016-07-23 Q1 · Solution
Setup

Write down the condition $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = 0$.

Model

$(2)(-1) + (-3)(y) = -2 - 3y$.

Derivation

$-2 - 3y = 0$, hence $y = -2/3$.

Correct answer: (c) $-2/3$

Trap

(d) is a sign error; the sign of the term $(-3)(y)$ must be kept.

Check

$-2 - 3(-2/3) = -2 + 2 = 0$ — perpendicularity holds.

Quick verification by substitution.

Question 2016-07-23 Q2
Pressure is force applied per unit area. Which of the following is correct for the pascal (Pa)?

The joule-force conversion chain links pressure to energy density.

Question 2016-07-23 Q2 · Solution
Setup

Start with the definition $1\ \text{Pa} = 1\ \text{N}/\text{m}^2$.

Model

The newton in terms of joules: $1\ \text{N} = 1\ \text{J}/\text{m}$.

Derivation

$(1\ \text{J}/\text{m})/\text{m}^2 = 1\ \text{J}/\text{m}^3$.

Correct answer: (b) $1\ \text{Pa} = 1\ \text{J}/\text{m}^3$

Trap

Option (a) gives a force dimension; the number of divisions must not be mixed up.

Check

Dimension: $\text{J}/\text{m}^3 = ML^{-1}T^{-2}$ — the same as the pressure dimension.

Pressure is also an energy density.

Question 2016-11-05 Q1
For $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$, which of the following are true? i. If they are perpendicular, the cross-product magnitude is largest. ii. If they are parallel, the scalar product is largest. iii. The cross product is perpendicular to the plane.

The three statements are tested with the extreme values of sine-cosine and the cross-product definition.

Question 2016-11-05 Q1 · Solution
Setup

Write the formulas $|\vec{A}\times\vec{B}| = AB|\sin\theta|$ and $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = AB\cos\theta$.

Model

(i): $\sin\theta$ is largest at $90^\circ$. (ii): parallel means the same direction ($\theta = 0$), so $\cos 0 = 1$ is largest.

Derivation

(iii) is the definition of the cross product. All three are true.

Correct answer: (e) All of them

Trap

(ii) is not "larger when antiparallel"; parallel means the same direction, and the product is largest with $+AB$.

Check

At $\theta = 0$: cross $0$, dot $AB$; at $\theta = 90$: cross $AB$, dot $0$ — the extreme values check out.

The parallel-antiparallel distinction is clarified.

Question 2016-11-05 Q2
For $\vec{A}, \vec{B}, \vec{C}$, which of the following are always true? i. $\vec{A} \times (\vec{B} \times \vec{C}) = 0$ ii. $\vec{A} \times (\vec{B} \times \vec{A}) = 0$ iii. $\vec{A} \cdot (\vec{B} \times \vec{A}) = 0$

A scalar triple product containing a repeated vector is always zero; the others are refuted with a general example.

Question 2016-11-05 Q2 · Solution
Setup

(iii) $\vec{A}\cdot(\vec{B}\times\vec{A})$: $\vec{B}\times\vec{A}$ is perpendicular to the vector $\vec{A}$.

Model

The dot product of two perpendicular vectors is zero; (iii) is always true.

Derivation

Counterexample for (i) and (ii): $\vec{A}\times(\vec{B}\times\vec{A}) = \vec{B}A^2 - \vec{A}(\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B}) \neq 0$ in general.

Correct answer: (b) only iii

Trap

Confusing (ii) with (iii); cross-cross does not give zero.

Check

Try numerically: $\vec{A} = \hat{i}$ and $\vec{B} = \hat{j}$: (ii) gives $-\hat{j} \neq 0$, (iii) gives $0$.

Keep the unit-vector counterexample in mind.

Question 2017-03-25 Q1
Find the unit vector perpendicular to the vectors $\vec{A} = \hat{i} + \hat{j}$ and $\vec{B} = 2\hat{i} - 2\hat{k}$.

Find the cross-product numerator and magnitude; the numerator-denominator squares must match.

Question 2017-03-25 Q1 · Solution
Setup

The perpendicular direction is $\vec{A}\times\vec{B}$; expand the determinant.

Model

$i[(1)(0)-(0)(-2)] - j[(1)(0)-(0)(2)] + k[(1)(-2)-(1)(2)] = -2\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$.

Derivation

The magnitude is $\sqrt{4+4+4} = 2\sqrt{3}$; simplifying gives $(-\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k})/\sqrt{3}$.

Correct answer: (e) $\frac{-\hat{i} + \hat{j} - \hat{k}}{\sqrt{3}}$

Trap

(c) uses $\sqrt{6}$ with the same numerator; it must be $1+1+1 = 3$.

Check

The squared numerator terms $1+1+1 = 3$ equal the squared denominator; the result is perpendicular to $\vec{A}$: $-1+1+0 = 0$.

The canceling factor ($2$) shrinks numerator and denominator together.

Question 2017-07-22 Q1
For the position $x(t) = 3 + Bt^3 - Ct^2$ ($x$ in meters, $t$ in seconds), what is the SI unit of the constant $B$?

Every term in the sum carries the same unit; the constant is extracted from this.

Question 2017-07-22 Q1 · Solution
Setup

The term $Bt^3$ must be in meters: $[B]\cdot\text{s}^3 = \text{m}$.

Model

Since each term is added to a position, its dimension is length.

Derivation

$[B] = \text{m}/\text{s}^3$.

Correct answer: (e) $\text{m}/\text{s}^3$

Trap

Do not confuse the power with the unit power and select $\text{m}^2/\text{s}^3$ (d).

Check

It has the dimension of the third derivative of $B$ (jerk): differentiating $x$ three times with respect to $t$ gives $\text{m}/\text{s}^3$.

The derivative order matches the unit exponent.

Question 2017-07-22 Q8
For the force $\vec{F}(x) = (Cx - 3x^2)\hat{i}\ \text{N}$ ($x$ in meters), what is the dimension of the constant $C$?

The constant is extracted from the force term; the spring-constant dimension comes out.

Question 2017-07-22 Q8 · Solution
Setup

$Cx$ must be newtons: $[C]\cdot L = ML/T^2$.

Model

$[C] = (ML/T^2)/L = M/T^2$ (the spring-constant dimension).

Derivation

Select (e), which matches the options.

Correct answer: (e) $[M/T^2]$

Trap

(d) is the dimension of force itself; do not forget to divide by $x$.

Check

The spring constant $k$ has the same dimension $N/m = kg/s^2$ — same result.

The spring-constant analogy reinforces the result.

Question 2017-10-21 Q1
If $\vec{A} = 2\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + d\hat{k}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{B} = 4\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$, what is $d$?

The three-term dot product is set to zero; d is extracted from it.

Question 2017-10-21 Q1 · Solution
Setup

Write down the condition $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = 0$.

Model

$(2)(4) + (2)(4) + (d)(-2) = 8 + 8 - 2d$.

Derivation

$16 - 2d = 0$, hence $d = 8$.

Correct answer: (c) $8$

Trap

Anyone writing the term $(d)(-2)$ as $+2d$ gets an off-option result like $-8$.

Check

$8 + 8 - 16 = 0$ — perpendicularity holds.

Quick verification by substitution.

Question 2017-10-21 Q18
For the net force $\vec{F} = (Ax - 6x^2)\hat{i}$ ($x$ in meters, $F$ in newtons), what is the SI unit of the constant $A$?

Every term must be in units of force; A is extracted from this.

Question 2017-10-21 Q18 · Solution
Setup

$Ax$ must be newtons; $x$ is in meters.

Model

$[A] = \text{N}/\text{m}$.

Derivation

The second term $6x^2$ is also in newtons (the unit of $6$ is $\text{N}/\text{m}^2$) — consistent.

Correct answer: (c) $\text{N}/\text{m}$

Trap

(a) is the unit of the second term’s coefficient; $A$ belongs to the first term.

Check

$(\text{N}/\text{m})(\text{m}) = \text{N}$ — the term gives force.

Do not mix up which term it belongs to.

Question 2018-07-14 Q1
Which is the unit vector perpendicular to both of the vectors $\vec{A} = 2\hat{i} + \hat{j}$ and $\vec{B} = 3\hat{i} - 2\hat{k}$?

Find the cross-product numerator and magnitude; the numerator-denominator squares must match.

Question 2018-07-14 Q1 · Solution
Setup

With $\vec{A} = (2,1,0)$ and $\vec{B} = (3,0,-2)$, expand the determinant.

Model

$i[(1)(-2)-0] - j[(2)(-2)-0] + k[0-3] = -2\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} - 3\hat{k}$.

Derivation

The magnitude is $\sqrt{4+16+9} = \sqrt{29}$; the unit vector is numerator over magnitude.

Correct answer: (a) $\frac{-2\hat{i}+4\hat{j}-3\hat{k}}{\sqrt{29}}$

Trap

No sign-flipped vector is among the options; verify the numerator signs one by one.

Check

$4+16+9 = 29$ equals the squared denominator; perpendicularity with $\vec{A}$: $-4+4+0 = 0$.

In a determinant with a zero component, the j sign is critical.

Question 2018-07-14 Q17
The coefficient of kinetic friction is given by $\mu_k = bx$ ($x$ is position). What is the SI unit of the constant $b$?

The friction coefficient is dimensionless; the dimensionlessness of the product determines b.

Question 2018-07-14 Q17 · Solution
Setup

$\mu_k$ is dimensionless; $bx$ must also be dimensionless.

Model

$[b]\cdot\text{m} = 1$.

Derivation

$[b] = \text{m}^{-1}$.

Correct answer: (c) $\text{m}^{-1}$

Trap

Anyone inverting it and saying $\text{m}$ (a) has skipped the product rule.

Check

$(\text{m}^{-1})(\text{m}) = 1$ — dimensionlessness holds.

The dimensionlessness condition is the fastest unit test.

Question 2018-10-27 Q1
The unit of $\rho$ is $\text{kg}/\text{m}^3$, the unit of $P$ is $\text{N}/\text{m}^2$, and $c = \sqrt{5P/3\rho}$: what is the unit of $c$?

First simplify the ratio, then apply the square root’s effect on the unit.

Question 2018-10-27 Q1 · Solution
Setup

Write the unit of $P$ as $\text{N}/\text{m}^2 = \text{kg}/(\text{m}\cdot\text{s}^2)$.

Model

For the ratio $P/\rho$: $[\text{kg}/(\text{m}\cdot\text{s}^2)]/[\text{kg}/\text{m}^3] = \text{m}^2/\text{s}^2$.

Derivation

Taking the square root: $\text{m}/\text{s}$ (unit of velocity; numerical factors do not change the unit).

Correct answer: (c) $\text{m}/\text{s}$

Trap

Anyone forgetting the root and looking for $\text{m}^2/\text{s}^2$ is left without an option.

Check

The sound-speed formula has the same structure ($c = \sqrt{B/\rho}$) — velocity comes out.

The physical counterpart (sound speed) confirms the result.

Question 2018-10-27 Q3
Given $\vec{a} = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - 5\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b} = \hat{i} - 2\hat{j} - 3\hat{k}$. Which $\vec{c}$ is perpendicular to both of the vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$?

Three-component determinant; check each component’s sign separately.

Question 2018-10-27 Q3 · Solution
Setup

The perpendicular vector is along $\vec{a}\times\vec{b}$.

Model

$i[(3)(-3)-(-5)(-2)] - j[(2)(-3)-(-5)(1)] + k[(2)(-2)-(3)(1)]$.

Derivation

$i(-9-10) - j(-6+5) + k(-4-3) = -19\hat{i} + \hat{j} - 7\hat{k}$.

Correct answer: (d) $\vec{c} = -19\hat{i} + \hat{j} - 7\hat{k}$

Trap

(a) flips the last sign, (c) the middle sign; each component must be written separately.

Check

Dotting with $\vec{a}$: $-38 + 3 + 35 = 0$ — perpendicularity confirmed.

The perpendicularity test catches determinant errors.

Question 2018-10-27 Q4
If the angle between $\vec{A} = 4\hat{i} + a\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$ and $\vec{B} = -3\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + b\hat{k}$ is $90^\circ$, what is $a+b$?

a and b enter with the same coefficient; the sum is extracted directly.

Question 2018-10-27 Q4 · Solution
Setup

Diklik: $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = 0$.

Model

$(4)(-3) + 2a + 2b = -12 + 2(a+b)$.

Derivation

$-12 + 2(a+b) = 0$, hence $a+b = 6$.

Correct answer: (a) $6$

Trap

Trying to find a and b separately; a single equation does not give two unknowns, it gives the sum.

Check

$2(a+b) = 12$: the product is $-12+12 = 0$ — perpendicularity confirmed.

Factoring out the common factor reduces the question to a single step.

Question 2019-10-26 Q1
Given $\vec{A} = 2\hat{i} - a\hat{j} + \hat{k}$ and $\vec{B} = 3\hat{i} + \hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$ with $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = 3$, what is $a$?

The dot product is equated to the given value; the single unknown is solved.

Question 2019-10-26 Q1 · Solution
Setup

$\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = (2)(3) + (-a)(1) + (1)(-2) = 6 - a - 2$.

Model

Given value: $4 - a = 3$.

Derivation

Hence $a = 1$.

Correct answer: (e) $1$

Trap

Anyone writing the term $(-a)(1)$ as $+a$ finds $a = -1$ (c).

Check

$6 - 1 - 2 = 3$ — matches the given value.

Watch the minus-signed parameter term.

Question 2019-10-26 Q2
With $a = 1$ in Q1, what is the unit vector in the direction of $\vec{A}+\vec{B}$?

First write the sum vector (the j component cancels), then divide by the magnitude.

Question 2019-10-26 Q2 · Solution
Setup

With $a = 1$, $\vec{A} = 2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k}$; take the sum $\vec{A}+\vec{B}$.

Model

$(2+3)\hat{i} + (-1+1)\hat{j} + (1-2)\hat{k} = 5\hat{i} - \hat{k}$; the magnitude is $\sqrt{25+1} = \sqrt{26}$.

Derivation

The unit vector is $(5\hat{i}-\hat{k})/\sqrt{26}$.

Correct answer: (a) $(5\hat{i}-\hat{k})/\sqrt{26}$

Trap

(b) points the opposite way; the signs of the sum must be kept.

Check

$(25+1)/26 = 1$ — unit magnitude; the j component is zero, and no option contains j.

The canceling component is used to eliminate options.

H2 · Kinematics 1D/2D (1/2)

Kinematics: position, velocity, acceleration and projectiles

56 questions: the first half of the 2014–2016 midterms. One-dimensional integrals and graphs, vector derivations, relative motion, oblique/horizontal/vertical projectiles, average velocity and acceleration on circular paths.

Method: on each question first pick an option, then open the solution step by step: Setup → Model → Derivation → Result → Trap → Check.

Scope: position-velocity-acceleration relations · relative velocity · projectile formulas · average quantities.

H2a: a 56-question block of kinematics questions. The student makes a prediction on each question, then opens the solution steps.

H2 · Question 2014-10-18 5
An object has initial conditions $v(0) = 1\ \text{m/s}$ and $x(0) = 2\ \text{m}$ and acceleration $a(t) = 3t\ \text{m/s}^3 - 3\ \text{m/s}^2$. What is its position at $t = 1\ \text{s}$?

A double-integral question; have the constants written down first.

H2 · Question 2014-10-18 5 · Solution
Setup

Integrating the acceleration gives the velocity: $v(t) = v(0) + \int_0^t a(t')\,dt'$. The initial velocity is $v(0) = 1\ \text{m/s}$.

Model

Integrating the velocity gives the position: $x(t) = x(0) + \int_0^t v(t')\,dt'$, $x(0) = 2\ \text{m}$.

Derivation

This gives $v(t) = 1 + 1.5t^2 - 3t$ and $x(t) = 2 + t + 0.5t^3 - 1.5t^2$. At $t = 1\ \text{s}$, $x = 2 + 1 + 0.5 - 1.5 = 2\ \text{m}$.

Correct answer: (a) $2\ \text{m}$

Trap

Anyone forgetting the integration constants ($v(0)$, $x(0)$) gets a wrong result; integrating twice requires two initial conditions.

Check

Check back by differentiating: $dx/dt = 1 + 1.5t^2 - 3t = v(t)$ and $dv/dt = 3t - 3 = a(t)$ hold.

Integration constants are stressed; verified by differentiating.

H2 · Question 2014-10-18 6
Which step of the derivation of the time-independent relation for constant-acceleration motion contains an invalid operation? I. $\vec{s} = \vec{v}t$; II. $\vec{s} = \left[\frac{\vec{v}+\vec{v}_0}{2}\right] \cdot \left[\frac{\vec{v}-\vec{v}_0}{\vec{a}}\right]$; III. $2\vec{a} \cdot \vec{s} = (\vec{v} + \vec{v}_0) \cdot (\vec{v} - \vec{v}_0)$; IV. $2\vec{a} \cdot \vec{s} = \vec{v} \cdot \vec{v} - \vec{v}_0 \cdot \vec{v}_0$; V. $2\vec{a} \cdot \vec{s} = v^2 - v_0^2$.

A concept question stressing that division by a vector is undefined.

H2 · Question 2014-10-18 6 · Solution
Setup

For constant acceleration the correct relations are: $\vec{s} = \vec{v}_{ort}\,t$ and $\vec{v} = \vec{v}_0 + \vec{a}\,t$ ($t$ is a scalar).

Model

Step I is valid if $\vec{v}$ is read as the average velocity: $\vec{s} = \vec{v}_{ort}\,t$.

Derivation

In step II, $t = (\vec{v}-\vec{v}_0)/\vec{a}$ is written; dividing a vector by a vector is undefined. Moreover, the scalar product of the two bracketed quantities gives a scalar, whereas the left side holds the vector $\vec{s}$.

Correct answer: (c) II

Trap

Do not be fooled by the scalar result $v^2 - v_0^2$ in step V into thinking the derivation is correct; the error is much earlier, in the division.

Check

In a correct derivation $t$ is eliminated as a scalar and $2\vec{a}\cdot\vec{s} = v^2 - v_0^2$ is obtained; both sides are dimensionally scalars.

The faulty step is found by dimensional analysis.

H2 · Question 2014-10-18 7
A cargo ship moves south through the water at $20.0\ \text{km/h}$ while a passenger walks east across the deck at $5.0\ \text{km/h}$. What is the passenger's velocity relative to the ground?

Have the perpendicular components drawn for relative velocity.

H2 · Question 2014-10-18 7 · Solution
Setup

The velocity relative to the ground is the vector sum of the ship's velocity and the passenger's velocity relative to the ship: $\vec{v} = \vec{v}_{gemi} + \vec{v}_{yolcu}$.

Model

The two velocities are perpendicular (south-east): the magnitude follows from Pythagoras.

Derivation

$|\vec{v}| = \sqrt{20^2 + 5^2} = \sqrt{425} \approx 20.6\ \text{km/h}$. Since the south component dominates, the direction is slightly east of south.

Correct answer: (c) $20.6\ \text{km/h}$, slightly east of south

Trap

Options (a) and (e) add the speeds as scalars ($20+5$); perpendicular vectors add by Pythagoras.

Check

The ratio of the east component $5$ to the south component $20$ confirms the direction; the angle is close to due south.

Checked with Pythagoras and the direction ratio.

H2 · Question 2014-10-18 11
A rabbit's position is given by $x(t) = (5.0\ \text{m/s})t + (6.0\ \text{m/s}^2)t^2$ and $y(t) = (7.0\ \text{m}) - (3.0\ \text{m/s}^3)t^3$ ($x, y$ in metres, $t$ in seconds). What is the velocity vector at $t = 3.0\ \text{s}$? ($v_x = dx/dt$, $v_y = dy/dt$.)

Have derivatives taken component by component.

H2 · Question 2014-10-18 11 · Solution
Setup

Differentiating position with respect to time gives velocity: $v_x = dx/dt$, $v_y = dy/dt$.

Model

$v_x = 5 + 12t$ and $v_y = -9t^2$ (in units of $\text{m/s}$).

Derivation

At $t = 3$, $v_x = 5 + 36 = 41$, $v_y = -81$. That is, $\vec{v} = 41\hat{\imath} - 81\hat{\jmath}\ \text{m/s}$.

Correct answer: (e) $41\hat{\imath} - 81\hat{\jmath}\ \text{m/s}$

Trap

Anyone substituting the coefficients directly (like $5$ or $6$) forgets to differentiate; in a polynomial the exponent comes down as a factor.

Check

The $y$ component is negative because $y(t)$ is decreasing; the sign is consistent with the physical situation.

The physical meaning of the sign is checked.

H2 · Question 2014-10-18 12
For the same rabbit ($x(t)$, $y(t)$ as above), what is the acceleration vector at $t = 3.0\ \text{s}$? ($a_x = dv_x/dt$, $a_y = dv_y/dt$.)

Stressed that this is a second derivative.

H2 · Question 2014-10-18 12 · Solution
Setup

Acceleration is the derivative of velocity: $a_x = dv_x/dt$, $a_y = dv_y/dt$.

Model

Since $v_x = 5 + 12t$ and $v_y = -9t^2$, $a_x = 12$ and $a_y = -18t$.

Derivation

At $t = 3$, $\vec{a} = 12\hat{\imath} - 54\hat{\jmath}\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Correct answer: (a) $12\hat{\imath} - 54\hat{\jmath}\ \text{m/s}^2$

Trap

Anyone mistaking the position coefficients for acceleration (like $54$) forgets to differentiate twice.

Check

$a_x$ is constant ($x$ is quadratic) while $a_y$ grows with time ($y$ is cubic); the structure is consistent.

The polynomial degree is matched to the acceleration structure.

H2 · Question 2014-10-18 13
For the same rabbit, what is the position vector at $t = 3.0\ \text{s}$?

A direct-substitution question.

H2 · Question 2014-10-18 13 · Solution
Setup

The position vector is $\vec{r} = x(t)\hat{\imath} + y(t)\hat{\jmath}$; the given $t$ is substituted directly.

Model

$x(3) = 15 + 54 = 69$; $y(3) = 7 - 3\cdot 27 = 7 - 81 = -74$.

Derivation

Substitution gives: $\vec{r} = 69\hat{\imath} - 74\hat{\jmath}\ \text{m}$.

Correct answer: (b) $69\hat{\imath} - 74\hat{\jmath}\ \text{m}$

Trap

Anyone skipping the $3\cdot 27 = 81$ multiplication in the $y(3)$ calculation ends up with results like $7 - 27$.

Check

$y$ is negative; the rabbit has crossed to the other side of the starting line, so the sign is consistent.

The arithmetic is verified step by step.

H2 · Question 2014-10-18 14
A golf ball is struck with initial speed $v_0$ at an angle $\theta$ above the horizontal (no air resistance, no spin). Which expression gives the maximum height the ball reaches?

The vertical component is used for the height.

H2 · Question 2014-10-18 14 · Solution
Setup

The vertical component is $v_{0y} = v_0\sin\theta$; at the peak the vertical velocity is zero.

Model

The time-independent equation in the vertical direction: $0 - v_{0y}^2 = -2gH$.

Derivation

This gives $H = v_{0y}^2/2g = (v_0\sin\theta)^2/2g$.

Correct answer: (d) $\frac{(v_0\sin\theta)^2}{2g}$

Trap

Options (b)–(c), which use the horizontal component ($v_0\cos\theta$), confuse height with range.

Check

Dimensionally $[L]^2/[L/T^2] = [L]$; for $\theta = 90$ it gives $v_0^2/2g$, which is correct.

Checked with limits and dimensions.

H2 · Question 2014-10-18 15
How far away does the same golf ball land at ground level (range)?

The identity step is written out explicitly.

H2 · Question 2014-10-18 15 · Solution
Setup

The horizontal speed is constant: $v_{0x} = v_0\cos\theta$. The flight time is $T = 2v_0\sin\theta/g$.

Model

The range is computed from the model $R = v_{0x}T$.

Derivation

$R = v_0\cos\theta \cdot 2v_0\sin\theta/g = v_0^2\sin 2\theta/g$.

Correct answer: (b) $\frac{v_0^2\sin 2\theta}{g}$

Trap

Option (c) catches anyone forgetting the factor of $2$; the identity $\sin 2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta$ is needed.

Check

At $\theta = 45$, $R = v_0^2/g$ is maximal; consistent with the known result.

Checked against the maximum-range angle.

H2 · Question 2014-10-18 20
A mass $m$ is dropped from a height $h$ above a cart $M$ (frictionless system). If the mass's vertical acceleration component is $a_{my}$, which expression gives the time to fall onto $M$?

Axis independence is stressed.

H2 · Question 2014-10-18 20 · Solution
Setup

Vertically there is uniformly accelerated motion with no initial velocity: $h = \frac{1}{2}a_{my}t^2$.

Model

The horizontal acceleration $a_{mx}$ does not enter the fall time; vertical motion is independent.

Derivation

This gives $t = \sqrt{2h/a_{my}}$.

Correct answer: (d) $\sqrt{2h/a_{my}}$

Trap

Options (a)–(e) containing $a_{mx}$ catch anyone missing horizontal-vertical independence; options with a factor of $g$ are dimensionally wrong.

Check

Dimensionally, the square root of $[L]/[L/T^2]$ gives $[T]$; larger $h$ means larger $t$.

Verified by dimensional analysis.

H2 · Question 2015-03-21 2
A stone is thrown upward at an angle to the horizontal (no air resistance). What does the stone's speed-versus-time graph look like while it is in the air? Graphs: (I) decreasing straight line, (II) concave decreasing curve, (III) U-shaped curve, (IV) curve dipping then rising, (V) humped curve.

Students distinguish speed from a velocity component.

H2 · Question 2015-03-21 2 · Solution
Setup

Speed is $|\vec{v}| = \sqrt{v_x^2 + v_y^2}$; $v_x$ is constant while $v_y$ passes linearly through zero.

Model

At the peak the vertical component is zero but the horizontal component remains; the speed takes its smallest (nonzero) value.

Derivation

The speed first decreases, reaches a minimum at the peak, then increases: the U-shaped (III) graph.

Correct answer: (b) III

Trap

Anyone confusing this with the graph of the velocity component $v_y$ picks the decreasing line (I); the question asks for the speed ($|\vec{v}|$).

Check

At the peak the speed equals $v_x$; the bottom of the U curve lies above zero.

Stressed that the bottom of the U is not zero.

H2 · Question 2015-03-21 8
In a strobe photograph taken at equal time intervals, the spacings between successive images of an insect flying in the $+x$ direction grow from left to right. Which graph best represents the motion? (I) constant $v_x$, (II) decreasing $a_x$, (III) decreasing $x$, (IV) linearly increasing $v_x$, (V) decreasing $v_x$.

Students practise reading a strobe photograph.

H2 · Question 2015-03-21 8 · Solution
Setup

The dot spacings give the distance covered in equal times; since the spacing grows, the insect is accelerating in the $+x$ direction.

Model

Under constant-acceleration speed-up, $v_x$ grows linearly with time.

Derivation

The linearly increasing $v_x$ graph (IV) is the correct choice.

Correct answer: (a) IV

Trap

Anyone confusing spacings with times picks a decreasing graph; a spacing is a position difference, which grows as the speed grows.

Check

Under speed-up the successive spacing differences are constant; the photograph is consistent with this pattern.

The spacing-velocity-acceleration link is built.

H2 · Question 2015-03-21 12
While a balloon rises at a constant $20\ \text{m/s}$, an object is thrown horizontally out of it at $20\ \text{m/s}$ when the balloon is $160\ \text{m}$ above the ground ($g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$). What is the horizontal distance between the balloon and the object's landing point?

The sign of the initial vertical velocity is stressed.

H2 · Question 2015-03-21 12 · Solution
Setup

The object's initial vertical velocity equals the balloon's: $+20\ \text{m/s}$ (upward). The vertical equation: $160 + 20t - 5t^2 = 0$.

Model

There is no horizontal acceleration: $x = v_{0x}t = 20t$. The balloon has no horizontal motion.

Derivation

From $t^2 - 4t - 32 = 0$, $t = 8\ \text{s}$; the horizontal distance is $x = 20\cdot 8 = 160\ \text{m}$.

Correct answer: (c) $160\ \text{m}$

Trap

Anyone treating the object as dropped with no initial vertical velocity finds a short time via $160 = 5t^2$; the initial upward velocity lengthens the flight.

Check

$t = 8\ \text{s}$ satisfies the equation: $160 + 160 - 320 = 0$.

Verified by substitution into the equation.

H2 · Question 2015-03-21 13
When the same object hits the ground, what are its speed components $(|V_x|, |V_y|)$?

The component order is read carefully.

H2 · Question 2015-03-21 13 · Solution
Setup

The horizontal component is constant: $V_x = 20\ \text{m/s}$. Vertically, $V_y = 20 - 10t$.

Model

The flight time $t = 8\ \text{s}$ (previous question) is used.

Derivation

$V_y = 20 - 80 = -60\ \text{m/s}$, magnitude $60\ \text{m/s}$. The answer is $(20, 60)\ \text{m/s}$.

Correct answer: (e) $(20\,\frac{m}{s}, 60\,\frac{m}{s})$

Trap

Anyone mixing up the component order picks option (d); the first component is the horizontal one.

Check

$V_y^2 = 20^2 + 2\cdot 10\cdot 160 = 3600$ also gives $60\ \text{m/s}$ via the time-independent equation.

Found a second way via the time-independent equation.

H2 · Question 2015-03-21 14
When the object hits the ground, how high above the ground is the balloon? (The balloon keeps rising at $20\ \text{m/s}$.)

The balloon's independent motion is stressed.

H2 · Question 2015-03-21 14 · Solution
Setup

The balloon rises at constant velocity: $y_b = 160 + 20t$.

Model

The flight time $t = 8\ \text{s}$ is used.

Derivation

$y_b = 160 + 160 = 320\ \text{m}$.

Correct answer: (b) $320\ \text{m}$

Trap

Anyone thinking the balloon stops finds $160\ \text{m}$; the balloon is unaffected since its mass is large.

Check

The object first climbs to a peak of $180\ \text{m}$ (next question); the balloon being above it is consistent.

Compared with the peak height.

H2 · Question 2015-03-21 15
What is the maximum height the object reaches above the ground?

The peak condition is written down.

H2 · Question 2015-03-21 15 · Solution
Setup

The peak is reached when the vertical velocity vanishes: $20 - 10t = 0$, $t = 2\ \text{s}$.

Model

The peak height is found from $y = 160 + 20t - 5t^2$.

Derivation

$y_{max} = 160 + 40 - 20 = 180\ \text{m}$.

Correct answer: (d) $180\ \text{m}$

Trap

Anyone forgetting the extra rise $v^2/2g = 20\ \text{m}$ picks $160\ \text{m}$.

Check

The time-independent equation $180 - 160 = 20^2/(2\cdot 10) = 20\ \text{m}$ confirms it.

Verified with the time-independent equation.

H2 · Question 2015-03-21 16
Find a time after the object is thrown at which the displacements of the object and the balloon are equal in magnitude.

A magnitude equality is set up.

H2 · Question 2015-03-21 16 · Solution
Setup

Measured from the release point, the balloon's displacement is $(0, 20t)$ and the object's is $(20t, 20t - 5t^2)$.

Model

The displacement magnitudes are equated: $(20t)^2 + (20t-5t^2)^2 = (20t)^2$.

Derivation

From $20t - 5t^2 = 0$ (with $t > 0$), $t = 4\ \text{s}$.

Correct answer: (c) $4\ \text{s}$

Trap

Some equate the positions; what are equated are the magnitudes, not the vectors.

Check

$t = 4\ \text{s}$ is shorter than the flight time ($8\ \text{s}$); the object is still airborne, which is consistent.

Checked that the time falls within the flight interval.

H2 · Question 2015-03-21 17
A runner runs clockwise at a constant speed of $6.0\ \text{m/s}$ on a circular track of diameter $200\ \text{m}$ ($\pi = 3$). What is the average velocity over one full lap?

Students practise the velocity-speed distinction.

H2 · Question 2015-03-21 17 · Solution
Setup

Average velocity is $\vec{v}_{ort} = \Delta\vec{r}/\Delta t$; over a full lap the net displacement is zero.

Model

Speed versus velocity distinction: the average speed would be $6\ \text{m/s}$, but the question asks for velocity.

Derivation

Since $\Delta\vec{r} = 0$, the average velocity is $0\ \text{m/s}$.

Correct answer: (a) $0\,\frac{m}{s}$

Trap

Anyone confusing speed with velocity picks option (d); velocity is a vector.

Check

Over any closed path the full-lap average is zero; the general rule confirms it.

Generalised with the closed-orbit rule.

H2 · Question 2015-03-21 18
What are the $x$ and $y$ components of the same runner's average velocity between points A and B (a quarter lap)? (A is on the left, B is at the top; radius $100\ \text{m}$.)

The displacement vector is drawn.

H2 · Question 2015-03-21 18 · Solution
Setup

Going clockwise from A to B over a quarter lap, the displacement is $(100, 100)\ \text{m}$.

Model

The quarter circumference is $(2\cdot 3\cdot 100)/4 = 150\ \text{m}$; the time is $150/6 = 25\ \text{s}$.

Derivation

The average velocity is $(100/25, 100/25) = (4, 4)\ \text{m/s}$.

Correct answer: (e) $(4\,\frac{m}{s}, 4\,\frac{m}{s})$

Trap

Anyone mistaking the instantaneous speed for a component falls for option (a); the average comes from the total displacement.

Check

The unit-vector directions agree with the motion in the figure (up at A, right at B).

Signs are checked against the direction of motion.

H2 · Question 2015-03-21 19
What are the components $(a_x, a_y)_{ort}$ of the same runner's average acceleration between points A and B?

The velocity-difference vector is constructed.

H2 · Question 2015-03-21 19 · Solution
Setup

Average acceleration is $\vec{a}_{ort} = \Delta\vec{v}/\Delta t$. Clockwise, $\vec{v}_A = (0, 6)$, $\vec{v}_B = (6, 0)$ ($\text{m/s}$).

Model

$\Delta\vec{v} = (6, -6)\ \text{m/s}$, $\Delta t = 25\ \text{s}$ (previous question).

Derivation

$\vec{a}_{ort} = (6/25, -6/25)\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Correct answer: (b) $(\frac{6}{25}\,\frac{m}{s^2}, -\frac{6}{25}\,\frac{m}{s^2})$

Trap

Anyone confusing this with the centripetal acceleration magnitude ($v^2/r$) goes for the large-valued options; average acceleration comes from the velocity difference.

Check

$\Delta\vec{v}$ points down-right, not up-left; the signs are consistent with the motion.

Direction and magnitude are checked separately.

H2 · Question 2015-07-11 1
A toy locomotive moving along the $x$ axis has position $x(t) = t^3 - 6t^2 + 9t$ (metres, seconds). At what time does the distance covered reach its maximum?

The turning-point concept is built.

H2 · Question 2015-07-11 1 · Solution
Setup

The velocity is $v = dx/dt = 3t^2 - 12t + 9 = 3(t-1)(t-3)$; it vanishes at $t = 1$ and $t = 3$.

Model

The position reaches a local maximum ($x = 4\ \text{m}$) at $t = 1$, then turns back.

Derivation

The distance covered takes its largest value at the first turning point: $t = 1\ \text{s}$.

Correct answer: (c) $1\ \text{s}$

Trap

Anyone picking $t = 3$, where the velocity vanishes a second time, misses that the turn-back happens earlier.

Check

$x(1) = 1 - 6 + 9 = 4\ \text{m}$, $x(0) = 0$; the position indeed first increases and then decreases.

Verified by substituting values.

H2 · Question 2015-07-11 2
An object moves along a curved path with velocities $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ that have the same magnitude but different directions. Which vector best represents the average acceleration from time $t_A$ to time $t_B$?

The difference vector is drawn.

H2 · Question 2015-07-11 2 · Solution
Setup

The average acceleration points along $\Delta\vec{v} = \vec{B} - \vec{A}$.

Model

Subtracting the right-leaning vector from the other vector of equal length leaves a difference pointing up-left.

Derivation

The correct direction is $\nwarrow$.

Correct answer: (d) $\nwarrow$

Trap

Anyone mistaking the velocity direction for acceleration goes for $\longrightarrow$; acceleration points along the velocity difference.

Check

The vector-subtraction rule ($\vec{B} + (-\vec{A})$) gives the same direction.

Found a second way with the addition rule.

H2 · Question 2015-07-11 10
An object is thrown horizontally at $v_0 = 10\ \text{m/s}$ from a height $H$, and its range is also $H$. What is the time of flight? ($g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$.)

Both axis equations are written together.

H2 · Question 2015-07-11 10 · Solution
Setup

The range is $H = v_0 t = 10t$; vertically, $H = \frac{1}{2}gt^2 = 5t^2$.

Model

The two expressions are equated (range equals height).

Derivation

From $10t = 5t^2$, $t = 2\ \text{s}$.

Correct answer: (a) $2\ \text{s}$

Trap

Anyone assuming a free-fall time assigns numbers without knowing $H$; the two equations must be solved together.

Check

This gives $H = 20\ \text{m}$, which satisfies both equations.

The $H$ found is tested in both equations.

H2 · Question 2015-07-11 20
A vehicle of length $L = 6\ \text{m}$ accelerates from rest at $A = 9\ \text{m/s}^2$. A block $m$ on the front wall slides to the rear wall (relative acceleration magnitude $3\ \text{m/s}^2$). How long does this take?

The relative frame is chosen.

H2 · Question 2015-07-11 20 · Solution
Setup

In motion relative to the vehicle, the relative distance to cover is $6\ \text{m}$ and the relative acceleration has magnitude $3\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Model

Uniformly accelerated motion from rest: $6 = \frac{1}{2}\cdot 3t^2$.

Derivation

From $t^2 = 4$, $t = 2\ \text{s}$.

Correct answer: (d) $2\ \text{s}$

Trap

Anyone using the ground-frame acceleration finds the wrong time; distance and acceleration must be in the same frame.

Check

After $t = 2\ \text{s}$ the vehicle has gone $18\ \text{m}$ and the block $12\ \text{m}$; the difference is $6\ \text{m}$, as required.

Consistency with ground-frame positions is checked.

H2 · Question 2015-07-11 21
In the same situation ($A = 9\ \text{m/s}^2$), what is the block's velocity vector relative to the ground when it reaches the rear wall?

A frame transformation is practised.

H2 · Question 2015-07-11 21 · Solution
Setup

Relative to the ground the block's acceleration is forward: $A - 3 = 6\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Model

The time is $t = 2\ \text{s}$ (previous question); the initial velocity is zero.

Derivation

$v = 6\cdot 2 = 12\hat{\imath}\ \text{m/s}$.

Correct answer: (b) $12\hat{\imath}\ \text{m/s}$

Trap

Anyone mistaking the relative velocity for the ground-frame one goes for the backward options; a frame transformation is needed.

Check

The block moves slower than the vehicle but still forward; the ordering $0 < 12 < 18\ \text{m/s}$ is consistent.

Physical consistency is checked via the speed ordering.

H2 · Question 2015-11-07 6
A ball is thrown vertically upward, reaches its highest point, and falls back. Which of the following is correct?

Students practise separating velocity from acceleration.

H2 · Question 2015-11-07 6 · Solution
Setup

With no air resistance the only acceleration is gravity: $\vec{a} = -g\hat{\jmath}$ (always downward).

Model

At the peak the velocity is zero but the acceleration remains $g$.

Derivation

The acceleration points downward at every instant.

Correct answer: (e) The acceleration is always downward.

Trap

Anyone thinking everything vanishes at the peak (mixing up velocity and acceleration) is wrong.

Check

On the way up the velocity is up and the acceleration down (slowing), on the way down both are down (speeding up); the model is consistent.

Consistency with the rising-falling phases is checked.

H2 · Question 2015-11-07 7
A child in an elevator at a building entrance holds a ball $1\ \text{m}$ above the floor. The elevator starts accelerating in the $+y$ direction at $2\ \text{m/s}^2$. What is the elevator's velocity $10\ \text{s}$ later?

The correct kinematic equation is selected.

H2 · Question 2015-11-07 7 · Solution
Setup

There is uniformly accelerated motion from rest: $v = v_0 + at$, $v_0 = 0$.

Model

Substitute $a = 2\ \text{m/s}^2$ and $t = 10\ \text{s}$.

Derivation

$v = 2\cdot 10 = 20\ \text{m/s}$.

Correct answer: (b) $20\ \text{m/s.}$

Trap

Anyone using the position formula ends up with values like $100\ \text{m}$; the question asks for velocity.

Check

The average velocity is $10\ \text{m/s}$ over $10\ \text{s}$; consistent with a position of $100\ \text{m}$.

Cross-checked with the position question.

H2 · Question 2015-11-07 8
How high above the ground is the same elevator $10\ \text{s}$ later?

The average-velocity method is recalled.

H2 · Question 2015-11-07 8 · Solution
Setup

For uniformly accelerated motion from rest, $y = \frac{1}{2}at^2$.

Model

Substitute $a = 2\ \text{m/s}^2$ and $t = 10\ \text{s}$.

Derivation

$y = \frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot 100 = 100\ \text{m}$.

Correct answer: (d) $100\ \text{m.}$

Trap

Anyone using $v\cdot t = 200\ \text{m}$ forgets that the velocity is not constant.

Check

Multiplying by the average velocity ($10\ \text{m/s}$) gives $100\ \text{m}$; the two routes agree.

Verified with two independent products.

H2 · Question 2015-11-07 9
At the 10th second the child drops the ball from $1\ \text{m}$ up; the elevator keeps rising at $2\ \text{m/s}^2$. What is the ball's acceleration relative to the elevator? ($+y$ is up, $g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$.)

The relative-acceleration definition is built.

H2 · Question 2015-11-07 9 · Solution
Setup

Relative to the ground the ball's acceleration is $-g = -10\ \text{m/s}^2$ and the elevator's is $+2\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Model

Relative acceleration is the difference: $a_{rel} = a_{top} - a_{asansor}$.

Derivation

$a_{rel} = -10 - 2 = -12\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Correct answer: (e) $-12\ \text{m/s}^2$

Trap

Anyone marking the ground-frame acceleration ($-10$) forgets the frame difference.

Check

To someone in the elevator the ball appears to fall faster ($12 > 10$); consistent with physical expectation.

The magnitude is compared with expectation.

H2 · Question 2015-11-07 10
How long after its release does the ball reach the elevator floor? (Relative acceleration magnitude $12\ \text{m/s}^2$, initial relative speed zero, relative distance $1\ \text{m}$; take $6^{-1/2} = 0.4$.)

The relative-motion equation is constructed.

H2 · Question 2015-11-07 10 · Solution
Setup

In relative motion the initial velocity is zero: $1 = \frac{1}{2}\cdot 12\cdot t^2$.

Model

Since the elevator accelerates upward, the ball falls with a larger acceleration relative to it.

Derivation

From $t^2 = 1/6$, $t = 1/\sqrt{6} \approx 0.4\ \text{s}$.

Correct answer: (a) $0.4\ \text{s}$

Trap

Anyone assuming the ground-frame free-fall time finds a longer time; the frame's acceleration must be added.

Check

The given value $6^{-1/2} = 0.4$ confirms the result.

Verified with the given numerical value.

H2 · Question 2015-11-07 11
When the ball reaches the elevator floor, how high above the ground is the elevator? (Contact happens at $t = 10.4\ \text{s}$.)

The total time is stressed.

H2 · Question 2015-11-07 11 · Solution
Setup

The elevator's position is found from $y = \frac{1}{2}at^2$, with $a = 2\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Model

The total time $10 + 0.4 = 10.4\ \text{s}$ is used.

Derivation

$y = (10.4)^2 = 108.16 \approx 108\ \text{m}$.

Correct answer: (d) $108\ \text{m.}$

Trap

Anyone marking the $100\ \text{m}$ value at $10\ \text{s}$ forgets the extra $0.4\ \text{s}$.

Check

The extra distance is $\approx 20\cdot 0.4 = 8\ \text{m}$; consistent with $100 + 8 = 108\ \text{m}$.

Approximately verified with the average velocity.

H2 · Question 2015-11-07 12
Harry runs across a bridge $h = 5\ \text{m}$ high at $v_P = 3\ \text{m/s}$ and drops a stone. Which trajectory best describes the stone? (a: vertical, b/c: forward parabolas, d/e: backward ones.)

Conservation of the initial velocity is stressed.

H2 · Question 2015-11-07 12 · Solution
Setup

The stone keeps its initial horizontal velocity ($3\ \text{m/s}$ forward) and falls freely in the vertical.

Model

A forward parabola is expected; the vertical drop (a) ignores the initial velocity.

Derivation

The forward-opening parabola is path $c$.

Correct answer: (e) path c

Trap

Anyone picking the vertical line forgets that horizontal velocity is conserved.

Check

The $3\ \text{m}$ range (next question) is consistent with the forward parabola.

Cross-checked with the range calculation.

H2 · Question 2015-11-07 13
What horizontal distance does the stone cover from point P until it hits the river? ($h = 5\ \text{m}$, $g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$.)

The fall time is found first.

H2 · Question 2015-11-07 13 · Solution
Setup

The fall time is found from $5 = \frac{1}{2}\cdot 10t^2$ to be $t = 1\ \text{s}$.

Model

The horizontal distance is $x = v_P t = 3t$.

Derivation

$x = 3\cdot 1 = 3\ \text{m}$.

Correct answer: (e) $3\ \text{m}$

Trap

Anyone applying the vertical formula horizontally ends up with values like $5\ \text{m}$.

Check

$t = 1\ \text{s}$ satisfies the equation exactly; horizontal-vertical independence holds.

Verified by substitution into the equation.

H2 · Question 2015-11-07 14
What is the stone's speed when it hits the river? ($v_x = 3\ \text{m/s}$, $t = 1\ \text{s}$.)

The resultant magnitude is constructed.

H2 · Question 2015-11-07 14 · Solution
Setup

$v_x = 3\ \text{m/s}$ is constant; $v_y = 10\cdot 1 = 10\ \text{m/s}$.

Model

The speed is found from $|\vec{v}| = \sqrt{v_x^2 + v_y^2}$.

Derivation

$|\vec{v}| = \sqrt{9 + 100} = \sqrt{109}\ \text{m/s}$.

Correct answer: (e) $\sqrt{109}\ \text{m/s}$

Trap

Anyone adding the components ($13$) forgets Pythagoras.

Check

$\sqrt{109} \approx 10.4 > 10$; the vertical component dominates, as expected.

Expectation is checked with the approximate value.

H2 · Question 2015-11-07 15
Sally runs in the opposite direction to Harry at $v_Q = 2\ \text{m/s}$ and drops a stone from Q, $2\ \text{m}$ to the right of P (at the same instant). What is the distance between the landing points of the two stones?

Each stone's position is written separately.

H2 · Question 2015-11-07 15 · Solution
Setup

The fall time is $t = 1\ \text{s}$ for both.

Model

Harry's stone lands at $x_P + 3$, Sally's at $x_Q - 2 = x_P + 2 - 2 = x_P$.

Derivation

The distance is found to be $3\ \text{m}$.

Correct answer: (e) $3\ \text{m}$

Trap

Anyone taking the $2\ \text{m}$ gap between release points as the answer forgets the horizontal drift.

Check

Sally's stone lands exactly level with P; the symmetry check confirms it.

Verified with the symmetry special case.

H2 · Question 2015-11-07 24
The blocks are given an initial speed of $1.0\ \text{m/s}$ (hanging block down, $2.0\ \text{kg}$ block up). How far do the blocks travel before stopping? [ambiguous]

The inconsistency of the options is discussed openly.

H2 · Question 2015-11-07 24 · Solution
Setup

While there is motion, kinetic friction ($f_k = 8\ \text{N}$) acts down the slope; in the B-down direction the net force gives $-10 = 3a$.

Model

With deceleration magnitude $|a| = 10/3\ \text{m/s}^2$, the stopping distance is $d = v_0^2/(2|a|) = 3/20 = 0.15\ \text{m}$.

Derivation

This value is not among the options; the closest option corresponding to the assumption $|a| = 13/3$ is (c) $3/26\ \text{m}$. [ambiguous]

Correct answer: (c) $3/26\ \text{m}$ [ambiguous — the correct value $3/20\ \text{m}$ is not among the options; closest option corresponding to an acceleration of $13/3$]

Trap

Do not take the option at face value; this question's options are inconsistent with the correct physics.

Check

After stopping the blocks stay put (the required $2\ \text{N}$ is less than $\mu_s N = 9.6\ \text{N}$); (b) is wrong too.

The equilibrium after stopping is checked separately.

H2 · Question 2016-03-19 4
An object is launched with initial speed $V_0 = 10\ \text{m/s}$ at $\theta_0 = 30^{\circ}$ to the vertical ($g \approx 10\ \text{m/s}^2$, no air resistance). What is its acceleration at maximum height?

Students practise separating velocity from acceleration.

H2 · Question 2016-03-19 4 · Solution
Setup

In projectile motion the acceleration is gravity at every instant (peak included).

Model

Zero velocity does not zero the acceleration; acceleration comes from force.

Derivation

This gives $\vec{a} = -g\hat{\jmath}$.

Correct answer: (b) $\vec{a} = -g\hat{\jmath}$

Trap

Anyone thinking acceleration is zero because velocity is zero at the peak falls for option (d).

Check

The acceleration is the same on the way up and down; continuity requires it.

Verified with the continuity principle.

H2 · Question 2016-03-19 5
In the same launch ($v_{0x} = 5\ \text{m/s}$, $v_{0y} = 5\sqrt{3}\ \text{m/s}$), what maximum height can be reached?

The angle reference is read.

H2 · Question 2016-03-19 5 · Solution
Setup

The vertical component is $v_{0y} = V_0\cos\theta_0 = 5\sqrt{3}\ \text{m/s}$.

Model

The peak height is found from $H = v_{0y}^2/(2g)$.

Derivation

$H = 75/20 = 15/4\ \text{m}$.

Correct answer: (e) $15/4\,\mathrm{m}$

Trap

Anyone thinking the angle is measured from the horizontal uses the horizontal component; the angle is from the vertical.

Check

$H < v_0^2/2g = 5\ \text{m}$ ($15/4 = 3.75$); less than for a straight-up launch, which is consistent.

Compared with the upper bound.

H2 · Question 2016-03-19 6
In the same launch, how long does it take to reach maximum height?

The peak condition is written down.

H2 · Question 2016-03-19 6 · Solution
Setup

On the way to the peak the vertical velocity vanishes: $t = v_{0y}/g$.

Model

Substitute $v_{0y} = 5\sqrt{3}\ \text{m/s}$.

Derivation

$t = 5\sqrt{3}/10 = \sqrt{3}/2\ \text{s}$.

Correct answer: (b) $\sqrt{3}/2\,\mathrm{s}$

Trap

Anyone marking the total flight time picks double the value.

Check

The total time is $\sqrt{3}\ \text{s}$ (next question); being half of it is consistent.

The ratio to the total time is checked.

H2 · Question 2016-03-19 7
In the same launch, what is the horizontal distance covered (range)?

The full flight time is used.

H2 · Question 2016-03-19 7 · Solution
Setup

The flight time is $T = 2v_{0y}/g = \sqrt{3}\ \text{s}$; the horizontal speed $v_{0x} = 5\ \text{m/s}$ is constant.

Model

The range is found from $R = v_{0x}T$.

Derivation

$R = 5\sqrt{3}\ \text{m}$.

Correct answer: (e) $5\sqrt{3}\,\mathrm{m}$

Trap

Anyone multiplying by the rise time finds half the range; the full flight time must be used.

Check

$R/T = 5\ \text{m/s} = v_{0x}$ checks back; internal consistency holds.

Checked back by division.

H2 · Question 2016-03-19 8
The object passes through the point $(x = \sqrt{3}\,\mathrm{m},\, y)$. What is the value of $y$?

Parametric elimination is practised.

H2 · Question 2016-03-19 8 · Solution
Setup

To eliminate time, $t = x/v_{0x} = \sqrt{3}/5\ \text{s}$.

Model

On the trajectory, write $y = v_{0y}t - gt^2/2$.

Derivation

$y = 3 - 5(3/25) = 3 - 3/5 = 12/5\ \text{m}$.

Correct answer: (e) $12/5\,\mathrm{m}$

Trap

Anyone setting up a linear proportion (thinking $y/x$ is constant) misses the parabola's curvature.

Check

$12/5 = 2.4 < H = 3.75$; the point lies below the peak, which is consistent.

Compared with the peak height.

H2 · Question 2016-03-19 9
What is the object's velocity when it hits the ground? ($v_x = 5\ \text{m/s}$, $T = \sqrt{3}\ \text{s}$.)

The sign at impact is checked.

H2 · Question 2016-03-19 9 · Solution
Setup

The horizontal component is a constant $5\ \text{m/s}$; vertically, $v_y = v_{0y} - gT$ becomes.

Model

This gives $v_y = 5\sqrt{3} - 10\sqrt{3} = -5\sqrt{3}\ \text{m/s}$.

Derivation

The impact velocity is $5\hat{\imath} - 5\sqrt{3}\,\hat{\jmath}\ \text{m/s}$.

Correct answer: (a) $5\hat{\imath} - 5\sqrt{3}\,\hat{\jmath}\ \text{m/s}$

Trap

Option (e), which keeps the vertical sign positive, forgets that the motion points downward at impact.

Check

The speed is $10\ \text{m/s} = V_0$; consistent with energy conservation.

The magnitude is verified with energy.

H2 · Question 2016-07-23 4
Which of the following is true of instantaneous velocity?

The limit direction is read correctly.

H2 · Question 2016-07-23 4 · Solution
Setup

Instantaneous velocity is $\vec{v} = d\vec{r}/dt$; since displacement lies along the trajectory, the derivative points tangentially.

Model

Average velocity equals instantaneous velocity only as $\Delta t \to 0$.

Derivation

Instantaneous velocity is tangent to the path.

Correct answer: (b) The instantaneous velocity is tangent to the path followed.

Trap

The phrase “as it goes to infinity” in option (d) is backwards; it is correct as it goes to zero.

Check

In uniform circular motion the velocity being perpendicular to the radius is consistent with tangency.

Consistency with the special motion is checked.

H2 · Question 2016-07-23 5
Which of the following is true of accelerated motion?

Sign independence is stressed.

H2 · Question 2016-07-23 5 · Solution
Setup

Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity; its sign does not fix the sign of velocity.

Model

A nonzero constant acceleration changes the velocity continuously.

Derivation

An object with constant acceleration cannot remain at rest.

Correct answer: (e) An object with constant acceleration cannot remain at rest.

Trap

Options (b)–(d), which match velocity and acceleration signs, reflect a misconception.

Check

The peak of a vertical toss: velocity zero but acceleration $g$; confirms the rule.

Reinforced with the peak example.

H2 · Question 2016-07-23 12
A ball is thrown with initial velocity $\vec{v}_0$ at an angle $\theta$. At $5\ \text{m}$ above the ground its velocity is $\vec{v} = (10\hat{\imath} - \sqrt{44}\,\hat{\jmath})\ \text{m/s}$ ($g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$). What is the initial velocity vector?

Backward reasoning with energy is practised.

H2 · Question 2016-07-23 12 · Solution
Setup

The horizontal component is conserved: $v_{0x} = 10\ \text{m/s}$. Vertically, energy gives $v_{0y}^2 = 44 + 2\cdot 10\cdot 5 = 144$.

Model

This gives $v_{0y} = 12\ \text{m/s}$ (positive, launch direction).

Derivation

The result is $\vec{v}_0 = 10\hat{\imath} + 12\hat{\jmath}\ \text{m/s}$.

Correct answer: (e) $10\hat{\imath} + 12\hat{\jmath}\ \text{m/s}$

Trap

Anyone mixing up the component order falls for option (d); the first component is the horizontal one.

Check

$|\vec{v}_0| = \sqrt{244} \approx 15.6$ is larger than $|\vec{v}| = 12$; no energy loss, consistent.

Checked via the magnitude ordering.

H2 · Question 2016-07-23 13
When the same ball reaches its highest point, what is its position vector? ($v_{0x} = 10$, $v_{0y} = 12$, in metres/second.)

The peak conditions are written separately.

H2 · Question 2016-07-23 13 · Solution
Setup

The peak height is $H = 144/20 = 7.2\ \text{m}$; the rise time is $t = 12/10 = 1.2\ \text{s}$.

Model

The horizontal position is $x = 10\cdot 1.2 = 12\ \text{m}$.

Derivation

The position is $12\hat{\imath} + 7.2\hat{\jmath}\ \text{m}$.

Correct answer: (b) $12\hat{\imath} + 7.2\hat{\jmath}\ \text{m}$

Trap

Option (a), which uses the total flight time, confuses the peak with the range.

Check

$7.2 > 5$ (measurement height); the ball has risen above the measurement point, consistent.

Compared with the measurement height.

H2 · Question 2016-07-23 14
Which is the trajectory equation of the same ball?

The template coefficients are computed separately.

H2 · Question 2016-07-23 14 · Solution
Setup

The trajectory is written with the template $y = (v_{0y}/v_{0x})x - gx^2/(2v_{0x}^2)$.

Model

$v_{0y}/v_{0x} = 1.2$ and $g/(2v_{0x}^2) = 10/200 = 1/20$.

Derivation

$y = 1.2x - x^2/20$ is obtained.

Correct answer: (d) $y = 1.2x - x^2/20$

Trap

Options mixing up the coefficients get the slope ($1.2$) and the curvature ($1/20$) wrong separately.

Check

Substituting $x = 12$ gives $y = 14.4 - 7.2 = 7.2\ \text{m}$; matches the peak point.

Verified by substituting the peak point.

H2 · Question 2016-07-23 15
How many seconds does it take the ball to reach a height of $63/20\ \text{m}$?

The physical meaning of the two roots is given.

H2 · Question 2016-07-23 15 · Solution
Setup

The vertical equation is written as $12t - 5t^2 = 3.15$.

Model

The quadratic $5t^2 - 12t + 3.15 = 0$ is solved.

Derivation

$t = (12\pm 9)/10 = 0.3,\ 2.1\ \text{s}$ (rising and falling).

Correct answer: (e) $0.3$ and $2.1\ \text{s}$

Trap

Anyone finding a single root misses one of the rising or falling instants.

Check

The roots sum to $2.4 = 2\cdot 1.2\ \text{s}$; symmetric about the peak instant, consistent.

Verified with root symmetry.

H2 · Question 2016-07-23 16
When the ball is at $x = 3\ \text{m}$ and $y = 63/20\ \text{m}$, what is its average velocity vector measured from the launch instant? ($\text{m/s}$.)

The average definition is applied.

H2 · Question 2016-07-23 16 · Solution
Setup

At $x = 3\ \text{m}$, $t = 0.3\ \text{s}$ (previous question).

Model

Average velocity is found from $\vec{v}_{ort} = \vec{r}/t$.

Derivation

$(3\hat{\imath} + 3.15\hat{\jmath})/0.3 = 10\hat{\imath} + 10.5\hat{\jmath}\ \text{m/s}$.

Correct answer: (c) $10\hat{\imath} + 10.5\hat{\jmath}\ \text{m/s}$

Trap

Anyone marking the instantaneous velocity forgets the average definition.

Check

The $x$ component equals $v_{0x} = 10$; horizontally average and instantaneous coincide, consistent.

Cross-checked with the horizontal component.

H2 · Question 2016-11-05 3
A mouse has position vector $\vec{r}_{fare} = At^2\,\hat{\imath} + Bt\,\hat{\jmath}$ ($A = 1\ \text{m/s}^2$, $B = 2\ \text{m/s}$). What is the mouse's velocity at $t = 2.\ \text{s}$? ($\text{m/s}$.)

Derivatives are taken component by component.

H2 · Question 2016-11-05 3 · Solution
Setup

Velocity is the derivative of position: $\vec{v} = 2At\,\hat{\imath} + B\,\hat{\jmath}$.

Model

Substitute $A = 1$, $B = 2$, $t = 2$.

Derivation

$\vec{v} = 4\hat{\imath} + 2\hat{\jmath}\ \text{m/s}$.

Correct answer: (a) $4\,\hat{\imath} + 2\,\hat{\jmath}\ \text{m/s}$

Trap

Anyone substituting without differentiating goes for option (c).

Check

The $x$ component grows with time ($At^2$) while the $y$ component is steady ($Bt$); consistent with the structure.

Consistency with the polynomial structure is checked.

H2 · Question 2016-11-05 4
A cat has acceleration $\vec{a}_{kedi} = C\,\hat{\imath} + Dt\,\hat{\jmath}$ ($C = 2/3\ \text{m/s}^2$, $D = 2\ \text{m/s}^3$) and is initially at rest. What is the mouse's velocity relative to the cat at $t = 2.\ \text{s}$? ($\text{m/s}$.)

Each velocity is found separately first.

H2 · Question 2016-11-05 4 · Solution
Setup

The cat's velocity from the integral: $\vec{v}_{kedi} = Ct\,\hat{\imath} + Dt^2/2\,\hat{\jmath}$; at $t = 2$, $(4/3)\hat{\imath} + 4\hat{\jmath}$. The mouse's velocity is $4\hat{\imath} + 2\hat{\jmath}$.

Model

Relative velocity is the difference: $\vec{v}_{fare} - \vec{v}_{kedi}$.

Derivation

$(4 - 4/3)\hat{\imath} + (2-4)\hat{\jmath} = (8/3)\hat{\imath} - 2\hat{\jmath}\ \text{m/s}$.

Correct answer: (c) $8/3\,\hat{\imath} - 2\,\hat{\jmath}\ \text{m/s}$

Trap

Anyone mistaking acceleration for velocity, or reversing the subtraction order, falls for those options.

Check

The cat is faster in $y$ ($4 > 2$); the difference's $y$ component is negative, consistent.

The sign is checked by comparing components.

H2 · Question 2016-11-05 5
The cat catches the mouse at $\vec{r} = 9\,(\text{m})\,\hat{\imath} + 6\,(\text{m})\,\hat{\jmath}$. What was the cat's initial position? (metres.)

The catch time is found first.

H2 · Question 2016-11-05 5 · Solution
Setup

From the mouse's equations $t^2 = 9$, $2t = 6$, it is caught at $t = 3\ \text{s}$.

Model

The cat's position is $\vec{r}(t) = \vec{r}_0 + (Ct^2/2)\hat{\imath} + (Dt^3/6)\hat{\jmath}$; at $t = 3$ the gain is $3\hat{\imath} + 9\hat{\jmath}$.

Derivation

$\vec{r}_0 = (9-3)\hat{\imath} + (6-9)\hat{\jmath} = 6\hat{\imath} - 3\hat{\jmath}\ \text{m}$.

Correct answer: (d) $6\,\hat{\imath} - 3\,\hat{\jmath}\ \text{m}$

Trap

Anyone forgetting the integration constant ($\vec{r}_0$) mistakes the gain vector for the answer.

Check

$t = 3\ \text{s}$ satisfies both mouse equations; the time is consistent.

The time is verified in both equations.

H2 · Question 2016-11-05 6
A ball is thrown vertically upward with speed $20\ \text{m/s}$ (no air resistance, $g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$). What maximum height can it reach?

The time-independent equation is written down.

H2 · Question 2016-11-05 6 · Solution
Setup

The peak condition is $v = 0$; the time-independent equation $0 - v_0^2 = -2gH$ is written.

Model

The template $H = v_0^2/(2g)$ is used.

Derivation

$H = 400/20 = 20\ \text{m}$.

Correct answer: (a) $20\ \text{m}$

Trap

Anyone using $v_0^2/g$ forgets the factor of $2$ and ends up near $40\ \text{m}$.

Check

The rise time is $2\ \text{s}$, the average speed $10\ \text{m/s}$; their product confirms $20\ \text{m}$.

Found a second way with the average velocity.

H2 · Question 2016-11-05 7
When the same ball has risen to $5\ \text{m}$, what is its speed?

The root of the equation is taken.

H2 · Question 2016-11-05 7 · Solution
Setup

The time-independent equation $v^2 = v_0^2 - 2gy$ is written.

Model

This gives $v^2 = 400 - 2\cdot 10\cdot 5 = 300$.

Derivation

$v = 10\sqrt{3}\ \text{m/s}$.

Correct answer: (e) $10\sqrt{3}\ \text{m/s}$

Trap

Anyone forgetting the square root picks (d) $300\ \text{m/s}$; even the units fail.

Check

$10\sqrt{3} \approx 17.3 < 20$; the speed has decreased, as expected.

Checked via the magnitude ordering.

H2 · Question 2016-11-05 8
While moving upward, how long does the ball take to reach $5\ \text{m}$ above the launch point?

The root is chosen on physical grounds.

H2 · Question 2016-11-05 8 · Solution
Setup

The vertical equation is $5 = 20t - 5t^2$, i.e. $t^2 - 4t + 1 = 0$.

Model

The roots are $t = 2\pm\sqrt{3}$; on the way up the small root is taken.

Derivation

$t = 2 - \sqrt{3}\ \text{s}$.

Correct answer: (d) $(2 - \sqrt{3})\ \text{s}$

Trap

Taking the large root finds the way-down instant; when the way up is asked, the small root is chosen.

Check

$2 - \sqrt{3} \approx 0.27\ \text{s}$; the distance from the average velocity is $\approx 5\ \text{m}$, consistent.

Consistency is checked with the approximate value.

H2 · Question 2016-11-05 9
While moving downward, how much time has passed when the ball is $5\ \text{m}$ above the launch point?

Students practise the down-up distinction.

H2 · Question 2016-11-05 9 · Solution
Setup

This time the large root of the same equation ($t^2 - 4t + 1 = 0$) is taken.

Model

The elapsed time on the way down is longer than on the way up.

Derivation

$t = 2 + \sqrt{3}\ \text{s}$.

Correct answer: (d) $(\sqrt{3} + 2)\ \text{s}$

Trap

Anyone re-marking the way-up root has not read the stem carefully.

Check

The two roots sum to $4\ \text{s}$, the total flight time; symmetry confirms it.

Verified with the root-sum rule.

H2 · Question 2016-11-05 10
What is the ball's speed just before it hits the ground?

Energy conservation is applied.

H2 · Question 2016-11-05 10 · Solution
Setup

With no air resistance, mechanical energy is conserved.

Model

The return speed equals the launch speed.

Derivation

The impact speed is $20\ \text{m/s}$.

Correct answer: (e) $20\ \text{m/s}$

Trap

Large-valued options that add acceleration to velocity miss energy conservation.

Check

Symmetry: the rise time ($2\ \text{s}$) equals the fall time; the speeds are equal too.

Reinforced with time symmetry.

H2 · 1D/2B Kinematics · second half

Kinematics (2/2): derivatives–integrals, pursuit, projectile motion, relative motion

57 questions, 2 slides each (question + solution). Topics: position–velocity–acceleration relations, constant-acceleration motion, pursuit, projectile/horizontal launch, average/magnitude, relative velocity–position, tube + range optimization.

Exams: 2017-03-25, 2017-07-22, 2017-10-21, 2018-03-17, 2018-07-14, 2018-10-27, 2019-03-16, 2019-07-13, 2019-10-26. Click a choice, → for the solution.

H2b week header: 57 questions, 114 question/solution slides. One question carries an [ambiguous] misprint note (17-07-22 S4).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 17-03-25 S2
The position of a particle varies with time as $\vec{x} = 3t^2\,\hat{\imath}\ \text{(m)}$. What is the particle's acceleration at $3\ \text{s}$?

Acceleration by differentiation; decide whether or not the acceleration is constant. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 17-03-25 S2 · Solution
Setup

Position $x(t) = 3t^2\ \text{m}$, one dimension. Velocity and acceleration are found by time differentiation.

Model

$\vec{v} = d\vec{x}/dt$, $\vec{a} = d\vec{v}/dt$. Differentiate the constant-coefficient polynomial.

Derivation

$\vec{v} = 6t\,\hat{\imath}$, $\vec{a} = 6\,\hat{\imath}\ \text{m/s}^2$. Since the acceleration is constant, it is the same at $t = 3\ \text{s}$.

Correct answer: (c) $6\ \text{m/s}^2$

Trap

(e) $18\ \text{m/s}^2$ is a trap: that is $x(3) = 27$, not the acceleration — position must not be confused with acceleration; differentiate twice.

Check

Dimension check: $[x]/[t]^2 = \text{m/s}^2$ ✓ — the acceleration unit works out.

Acceleration by differentiation; decide whether or not the acceleration is constant. Source: Opus_Format/2017-03-25.md S2 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 17-03-25 S4
A rocket moves in one dimension for $20\ \text{s}$ with initial speed $5\ \text{m/s}$ and acceleration $a_t = 1 + 2t + 3t^2\ (\text{m/s}^2)$. What is its speed at the end of $20\ \text{s}$?
