Velocity by integration; add the initial condition. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 17-03-25 S4 · Solution
Setup

$v_0 = 5\ \text{m/s}$, $a(t) = 1 + 2t + 3t^2$, $\Delta t = 20\ \text{s}$. The change in velocity is the integral of the acceleration.

Model

$v = v_0 + \int_0^{20} a(t)\,dt = v_0 + [t + t^2 + t^3]_0^{20}$.

Derivation

$[t + t^2 + t^3]_0^{20} = 20 + 400 + 8000 = 8420$. $v = 5 + 8420 = 8425\ \text{m/s}$.

Correct answer: (d) $8425\ \text{m/s}$

Trap

(e) $8420$ is a trap: the integral is correct, but the initial $5\ \text{m/s}$ is left out.

Check

The dominant term is $t^3 = 8000$; the total is of order $10^4$ ✓.

Velocity by integration; add the initial condition. Source: Opus_Format/2017-03-25.md S4 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 17-03-25 S22

A motorcyclist at constant $36\ \text{m/s}$ passes a parked officer; the officer chases with constant acceleration $4\ \text{m/s}^2$.

How long does it take the officer to catch the motorcyclist?

Pursuit: equate the positions, not the velocities. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 17-03-25 S22 · Solution
Setup

$x_m = 36t$, $x_p = 2t^2$ (starting from rest with $a = 4\ \text{m/s}^2$). Capture means equal positions.

Model

Solve the equation $36t = 2t^2$ ($t > 0$).

Derivation

If $36 = 2t$ then $t = 18\ \text{s}$.

Correct answer: (a) $18\ \text{s}$

Trap

(b) $9\ \text{s}$ is a trap: that is the instant the velocities match ($4t = 36$), not the positions.

Check

$x = 36 \cdot 18 = 648\ \text{m}$; police distance $2 \cdot 18^2 = 648\ \text{m}$ ✓.

Pursuit: equate the positions, not the velocities. Source: Opus_Format/2017-03-25.md S22 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 17-03-25 S23

A motorcyclist at constant $36\ \text{m/s}$ passes a parked officer; the officer chases with constant acceleration $4\ \text{m/s}^2$ ($t = 18\ \text{s}$).

When the motorcyclist is caught, what is the speed of the police car?

At capture the speed is twice the target speed. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 17-03-25 S23 · Solution
Setup

Police car: $v_0 = 0$, $a = 4\ \text{m/s}^2$, $t = 18\ \text{s}$.

Model

$v = v_0 + at$.

Derivation

$v = 4 \cdot 18 = 72\ \text{m/s}$.

Correct answer: (c) $72\ \text{m/s}$

Trap

(e) $36\ \text{m/s}$ is a trap: at capture the speeds are not equal; the police car is faster.

Check

Since the average police speed is $36\ \text{m/s}$, the distance is $36 \cdot 18 = 648\ \text{m}$ ✓.

At capture the speed is twice the target speed. Source: Opus_Format/2017-03-25.md S23 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 17-03-25 S24

A motorcyclist at constant $36\ \text{m/s}$ passes a parked officer; the officer chases with constant acceleration $4\ \text{m/s}^2$ ($t = 18\ \text{s}$).

When the motorcyclist is caught, how far has the police car traveled from its initial position?

Verify the position both ways. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 17-03-25 S24 · Solution
Setup

Capture time $t = 18\ \text{s}$; the motorcyclist travels at $36\ \text{m/s}$.

Model

$x = v_m t$ (or $x = at^2/2$).

Derivation

$x = 36 \cdot 18 = 648\ \text{m}$.

Correct answer: (d) $648\ \text{m}$

Trap

(e) $324\ \text{m}$ is a trap: it drops the one-half factor, as if $at^2/2$ were $at^2$.

Check

Police distance $2 \cdot 18^2 = 648\ \text{m}$ — both calculations agree ✓.

Verify the position both ways. Source: Opus_Format/2017-03-25.md S24 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 17-03-25 S25

A goose flying north at $15\ \text{m/s}$ from height $h_g = 46\ \text{m}$ drops an egg onto the windshield ($h_c = 1{,}0\ \text{m}$) of a car heading south at $97{,}2\ \text{km/h} = 27\ \text{m/s}$; horizontal separation $d = 126\ \text{m}$.

What is the velocity of the egg relative to the car at the instant it hits the windshield? ($g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$)

First relative to the ground, then relative velocity. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 17-03-25 S25 · Solution
Setup

Drop height $45\ \text{m}$; horizontal closing speed $15 + 27 = 42\ \text{m/s}$.

Model

$t = \sqrt{2h/g}$; relative to the ground $\vec{v} = 15\hat{\imath} - gt\,\hat{\jmath}$; relative to the car $\vec{V} = \vec{v} - \vec{v}_c$.

Derivation

$t = \sqrt{90/10} = 3\ \text{s}$ (closing distance $42 \cdot 3 = 126\ \text{m}$ ✓). $\vec{V} = (15 + 27)\hat{\imath} - 30\hat{\jmath} = 42\hat{\imath} - 30\hat{\jmath}$.

Correct answer: (d) $\vec{V} = 42\hat{\imath} - 30\hat{\jmath}\ \text{m/s}$

Trap

(a) is the ground-frame velocity; for the relative velocity, the car's $-27\hat{\imath}$ velocity must be subtracted.

Check

Distance consistency $(15+27)\cdot 3 = 126\ \text{m}$ confirms the fall time ✓.

First relative to the ground, then relative velocity. Source: Opus_Format/2017-03-25.md S25 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 17-07-22 S2

A particle moving along the $x$-axis: $x(t) = 3 + Bt^3 - Ct^2$ ($x$ in meters, $t$ in seconds).

If the particle is at $x = 24\ \text{m}$ at $t = 3\ \text{s}$ with zero velocity, what are $B$ and $C$?

Two conditions, two unknowns. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 17-07-22 S2 · Solution
Setup

$v(t) = 3Bt^2 - 2Ct$; the conditions $x(3) = 24$, $v(3) = 0$ give two equations.

Model

$3 + 27B - 9C = 24$ and $27B - 6C = 0$.

Derivation

From the second, $9B = 2C$; in the first, $27B - 9C = 21$. Solution: $C = -7$, $B = -14/9$.

Correct answer: (a) $-14/9$ and $-7$

Trap

Plugging numbers into the position equation without differentiating is a common mistake; write $v(t)$ first.

Check

$v(3) = 27(-14/9) - 6(-7) = -42 + 42 = 0$ ✓.

Two conditions, two unknowns. Source: Opus_Format/2017-07-22.md S2 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 17-07-22 S3

$x(t) = 3 + Bt^3 - Ct^2$, $B = -14/9$, $C = -7$.

When is the particle's acceleration zero?

Zero acceleration is not zero velocity. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 17-07-22 S3 · Solution
Setup

$a(t) = dv/dt = 6Bt - 2C$.

Model

$a(t) = 6(-14/9)t + 14 = -28t/3 + 14 = 0$.

Derivation

If $28t/3 = 14$ then $t = 1{,}5\ \text{s}$.

Correct answer: (c) $1{,}5\ \text{s}$

Trap

The $v = 0$ instant ($t = 3\ \text{s}$) must not be confused with the $a = 0$ instant.

Check

At $t = 1{,}5$: $a = -14 + 14 = 0$ ✓.

Zero acceleration is not zero velocity. Source: Opus_Format/2017-07-22.md S3 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 17-07-22 S4

$x(t) = 3 + Bt^3 - Ct^2$, $B = -14/9$, $C = -7$; $v(t) = -14t^2/3 + 14t$.

Which is the average acceleration vector $\vec{a}_{av}$ of the particle between $t = 1\ \text{s}$ and $t = 3\ \text{s}$?

[ambiguous]: the calculation matches none of the options. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 17-07-22 S4 · Solution
Setup

Average acceleration $\vec{a}_{av} = [\vec{v}(3) - \vec{v}(1)]/(3 - 1)$.

Model

$v(3) = 0$, $v(1) = -14/3 + 14 = 28/3$.

Derivation

$\vec{a}_{av} = (0 - 28/3)/2\ \hat{\imath} = -14/3\ \hat{\imath}\ \text{m/s}^2 \approx -4{,}67\hat{\imath}$. This value appears in none of the options (closest option (c) $-24/5 = -4{,}8$).

Correct answer: [ambiguous] (calculation gives $-14/3\ \hat{\imath}\ \text{m/s}^2$; matches none of the options — probable misprint)

Trap

Average acceleration is not the mean of the endpoint values of $a(t)$; the definition is $\Delta \vec{v}/\Delta t$.

Check

$-14/3 \approx -4{,}67 \ne -4{,}8$; no match ✓ (confirmed by independent review of Opus 5.5).

[ambiguous]: the calculation matches none of the options. Source: Opus_Format/2017-07-22.md S4 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 17-07-22 S5

A body with constant $\vec{a} = (4\hat{\imath} + 2\hat{\jmath})\ \text{m/s}^2$ passes through the origin at $t = 0$ with $\vec{v}_0 = -8\hat{\jmath}\ \text{m/s}$.

Which is the velocity vector of the particle as a function of time?

Add component by component. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 17-07-22 S5 · Solution
Setup

At constant acceleration, $\vec{v} = \vec{v}_0 + \vec{a}t$.

Model

$\vec{v} = -8\hat{\jmath} + (4\hat{\imath} + 2\hat{\jmath})t$.

Derivation

$\vec{v}(t) = 4t\,\hat{\imath} + (2t - 8)\,\hat{\jmath}\ \text{m/s}$.

Correct answer: (b) $\vec{v}(t) = [(4t)\hat{\imath} + (2t - 8)\hat{\jmath}]\ \text{m/s}$

Trap

(a) is the trap that swaps the components: the coefficient $4$ belongs to the $x$ component.

Check

At $t = 0$, $\vec{v} = -8\hat{\jmath} = \vec{v}_0$ ✓.

Add component by component. Source: Opus_Format/2017-07-22.md S5 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 17-07-22 S6

Constant $\vec{a} = (4\hat{\imath} + 2\hat{\jmath})\ \text{m/s}^2$, $\vec{v}_0 = -8\hat{\jmath}\ \text{m/s}$; $v_y = 2t - 8$.

When does the particle reach its minimum $y$-coordinate?

At an extremum the relevant velocity component is zero. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 17-07-22 S6 · Solution
Setup

The $y$ extremum occurs at the $v_y = 0$ instant (crossing from below to above).

Model

$v_y = 2t - 8 = 0$.

Derivation

$t = 4\ \text{s}$.

Correct answer: (d) $t = 4\ \text{s}$

Trap

Looking for the $v_x = 0$ instant means looking at the wrong axis; $v_x = 4t$ never vanishes ($t > 0$).

Check

Since $a_y = 2 > 0$, this instant is a minimum ✓.

At an extremum the relevant velocity component is zero. Source: Opus_Format/2017-07-22.md S6 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 17-07-22 S7

First particle: $\vec{v}_1(t) = 4t\,\hat{\imath} + (2t - 8)\,\hat{\jmath}$; second: $\vec{v}_2 = 2\hat{\imath} + 3\hat{\jmath}\ \text{m/s}$.

At $t = 2\ \text{s}$, what is the velocity vector of the first particle relative to the second?

In relative velocity the subtraction order matters. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 17-07-22 S7 · Solution
Setup

Relative velocity $\vec{v}_{1/2} = \vec{v}_1 - \vec{v}_2$; at $t = 2$, $\vec{v}_1 = 8\hat{\imath} - 4\hat{\jmath}$.

Model

$(8\hat{\imath} - 4\hat{\jmath}) - (2\hat{\imath} + 3\hat{\jmath})$.

Derivation

$\vec{v}_{1/2} = 6\hat{\imath} - 7\hat{\jmath}\ \text{m/s}$.

Correct answer: (d) $6\hat{\imath} - 7\hat{\jmath}\ \text{m/s}$

Trap

(c) is the option for those who reverse the subtraction order ($\vec{v}_2 - \vec{v}_1$).

Check

At $t = 2$, $\vec{v}_1 = 8\hat{\imath} - 4\hat{\jmath}$ by direct substitution ✓.

In relative velocity the subtraction order matters. Source: Opus_Format/2017-07-22.md S7 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 17-10-21 S2

A particle is launched from height $y_0 = h$ with speed $V_0$ at angle $\theta$ to the horizontal; the origin is on the ground.

What is the maximum height the particle can reach relative to the chosen origin? (gravity $g$)

Peak plus base height. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 17-10-21 S2 · Solution
Setup

Vertical launch component $V_0\sin\theta$; peak condition $v_y = 0$.

Model

Extra climb: $(V_0\sin\theta)^2/(2g)$. Relative to the origin the total is $h + \dots$.

Derivation

$h_{max} = h + V_0^2\sin^2\theta/(2g)$.

Correct answer: (e) $h+V_0^2\sin^2\theta/(2g)$

Trap

(b) is the option for those who forget the base $h$; (c) confuses it with the $\sin(2\theta)$ range formula.

Check

At $\theta = 90^\circ$: $h + V_0^2/(2g)$ — vertical launch ✓.

Peak plus base height. Source: Opus_Format/2017-10-21.md S2 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 17-10-21 S3

A body starts with $\vec{r}_0 = 10\hat{\imath} - 4{,}0\hat{\jmath}\ (\text{m})$, $\vec{V}_0 = 4{,}0\hat{\imath} + 1{,}0\hat{\jmath}\ (\text{m/s})$; after $20\ \text{s}$, $\vec{V} = 20\hat{\imath} - 5{,}0\hat{\jmath}\ (\text{m/s})$. Constant acceleration.

What is the magnitude of the body's acceleration (in $\text{m/s}^2$ units)?

First the vector, then the magnitude. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 17-10-21 S3 · Solution
Setup

$\vec{a} = (\vec{V} - \vec{V}_0)/\Delta t$, $\Delta t = 20\ \text{s}$.

Model

$\vec{a} = (16\hat{\imath} - 6\hat{\jmath})/20 = 0{,}8\hat{\imath} - 0{,}3\hat{\jmath}$.

Derivation

$|\vec{a}| = \sqrt{0{,}64 + 0{,}09} = \sqrt{0{,}73} = \sqrt{73}/10$.

Correct answer: (c) $\sqrt{73}/10$

Trap

(a) is only the $x$ component; the magnitude is computed with both components.

Check

$0{,}73 \cdot 100 = 73$ ✓.

First the vector, then the magnitude. Source: Opus_Format/2017-10-21.md S3 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 17-10-21 S4

$\vec{r}_0 = 10\hat{\imath} - 4{,}0\hat{\jmath}\ (\text{m})$, $\vec{V}_0 = 4{,}0\hat{\imath} + 1{,}0\hat{\jmath}$, $\vec{a} = 0{,}8\hat{\imath} - 0{,}3\hat{\jmath}$.

What is the position vector $2\ \text{s}$ after the start of the motion?

Write all three terms. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 17-10-21 S4 · Solution
Setup

$\vec{r} = \vec{r}_0 + \vec{V}_0 t + \vec{a}t^2/2$, $t = 2\ \text{s}$.

Model

$x: 10 + 8 + 0{,}8 \cdot 2 = 19{,}6$; $y: -4 + 2 - 0{,}3 \cdot 2 = -2{,}6$.

Derivation

$\vec{r} = 19{,}6\hat{\imath} - 2{,}6\hat{\jmath}\ \text{m}$.

Correct answer: (e) $19{,}6\hat{\imath} - 2{,}6\hat{\jmath}$

Trap

(d) is for those who drop the $y$ component; $\vec{r}_0$ must not be forgotten.

Check

At $t = 0$ the formula gives $\vec{r}_0$ ✓.

Write all three terms. Source: Opus_Format/2017-10-21.md S4 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 17-10-21 S5

$\vec{V}_0 = 4{,}0\hat{\imath} + 1{,}0\hat{\jmath}$, $\vec{a} = 0{,}8\hat{\imath} - 0{,}3\hat{\jmath}$.

What is the velocity vector $2\ \text{s}$ after the start of the motion?

There is no $t^2$ term in the velocity. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 17-10-21 S5 · Solution
Setup

$\vec{V} = \vec{V}_0 + \vec{a}t$, $t = 2\ \text{s}$.

Model

$\vec{V} = 4\hat{\imath} + 1\hat{\jmath} + 2(0{,}8\hat{\imath} - 0{,}3\hat{\jmath})$.

Derivation

$\vec{V} = 5{,}6\hat{\imath} + 0{,}4\hat{\jmath}\ \text{m/s}$.

Correct answer: (e) $5{,}6\hat{\imath} + 0{,}4\hat{\jmath}$

Trap

(a) is only the $\vec{a}t$ term; $\vec{V}_0$ must be added.

Check

At $t = 0$: $\vec{V}_0$ ✓.

There is no $t^2$ term in the velocity. Source: Opus_Format/2017-10-21.md S5 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 17-10-21 S6

$x(t) = 10 + 4t + 0{,}4t^2$ (all coefficients positive, $t \ge 0$).

At what time $t$ does the $x$ coordinate of the body's position vanish?

Question the sign of the root. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 17-10-21 S6 · Solution
Setup

Look for the $t > 0$ root of $x(t) = 10 + 4t + 0{,}4t^2 = 0$.

Model

All terms are positive for $t > 0$; the only root is $t = -5\ \text{s}$ (the past).

Derivation

In the future $x$ stays positive; it never vanishes.

Correct answer: (b) never

Trap

Solving the equation mechanically picks the negative root; physical time is $t \ge 0$.

Check

$x(0) = 10 > 0$ and $dx/dt > 0$; zero is impossible ✓.

Question the sign of the root. Source: Opus_Format/2017-10-21.md S6 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 18-03-17 S1

A body is launched from point $A$ ($h = 1\ \text{m}$) with $v_0 = 10\ \text{m/s}$ at $\theta = 53^\circ$; point $D$ is at $H = 7/4\ \text{m}$. ($\sin53 = 4/5$, $g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$)

Which is the $y(t)$ position function of the body, in meters?

Separate the components. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 18-03-17 S1 · Solution
Setup

$y_0 = 1$, $v_{0y} = 10\sin53 = 8$, $a_y = -10$.

Model

$y = y_0 + v_{0y}t + a_y t^2/2$.

Derivation

$y(t) = 1 + 8t - 5t^2$.

Correct answer: (a) $1 + 8t - 5t^2$

Trap

(c) is for those who use the horizontal component ($6$) in the vertical direction.

Check

$y(0) = 1 = h$ ✓.

Separate the components. Source: Opus_Format/2018-03-17.md S1 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 18-03-17 S2

$y(t) = 1 + 8t - 5t^2$; point $D$ is at $H = 7/4\ \text{m}$.

In how many seconds does the body reach point $D$?

Pick the physical one of the two roots. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 18-03-17 S2 · Solution
Setup

Solve $1 + 8t - 5t^2 = 7/4$.

Model

$20t^2 - 32t + 3 = 0$; $t = (32 \pm 28)/40$.

Derivation

The roots are $0{,}1$ and $1{,}5$; the descending branch is $t = 3/2\ \text{s}$.

Correct answer: (b) $3/2$

Trap

$t = 0{,}1$ is the rising branch; arrival at $D$ is on the descending branch.

Check

$y(1{,}5) = 1 + 12 - 11{,}25 = 1{,}75 = 7/4$ ✓.

Pick the physical one of the two roots. Source: Opus_Format/2018-03-17.md S2 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 18-03-17 S3

$v_x = 10\cos53 = 6\ \text{m/s}$; peak $C$, total horizontal distance $d$ ($t = 1{,}5\ \text{s}$).

If point $C$ is the highest point of the trajectory, what is the ratio $R/d$? ($R$: peak range)

Horizontal velocity is constant. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 18-03-17 S3 · Solution
Setup

Peak time $t_C = v_{0y}/g = 0{,}8\ \text{s}$.

Model

$R = 6 \cdot 0{,}8 = 4{,}8$; $d = 6 \cdot 1{,}5 = 9$.

Derivation

$R/d = 4{,}8/9 = 8/15$.

Correct answer: (c) $8/15$

Trap

Taking the peak for half the total time is a mistake (this is not a ground-to-ground launch).

Check

$8/15 \approx 0{,}53 < 1$; the peak is less than half of the total ✓.

Horizontal velocity is constant. Source: Opus_Format/2018-03-17.md S3 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 18-03-17 S4

$B$ and $D$ are at the same height ($7/4\ \text{m}$); the $y = 7/4$ instants are $t = 0{,}1$ and $1{,}5\ \text{s}$.

What does the length $x_B$ equal?

The small root belongs to $B$. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 18-03-17 S4 · Solution
Setup

$B$ is on the rising branch: $t_B = 0{,}1\ \text{s}$; $x = v_x t$.

Model

$x_B = 6 \cdot 0{,}1 = 0{,}6$.

Derivation

$x_B = 3/5\ \text{m}$.

Correct answer: (a) $3/5$

Trap

Using $t = 1{,}5$ finds point $D$, not $B$.

Check

$0{,}6 < 4{,}8 = R$; $B$ is to the left of the peak ✓.

The small root belongs to $B$. Source: Opus_Format/2018-03-17.md S4 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 18-03-17 S5

At point $B$, $t = 0{,}1\ \text{s}$; $v_x = 6$, $v_{0y} = 8$, $g = 10$.

What is the velocity vector $\vec{v}_B$ ($\text{m/s}$) of the body at point $B$?

On the way up $v_y$ is positive. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 18-03-17 S5 · Solution
Setup

$v_x$ is constantly $6$; $v_y = 8 - 10t$.

Model

At $t = 0{,}1$: $v_y = 8 - 1 = 7$.

Derivation

$\vec{v}_B = 6\hat{\imath} + 7\hat{\jmath}\ \text{m/s}$.

Correct answer: (e) $6\hat{\imath} + 7\hat{\jmath}$

Trap

(a) is the descending-branch velocity; $B$ is on the way up ($v_y > 0$).

Check

$|\vec{v}_B| = \sqrt{85} < 10 = v_0$ ✓.

On the way up $v_y$ is positive. Source: Opus_Format/2018-03-17.md S5 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 18-03-17 S6

A constant-acceleration particle in the $xy$-plane: $\vec{r}_0 = 2\hat{\imath} - 3\hat{\jmath}\ (\text{m})$; $\vec{v}(0) = 10\hat{\imath}$, $\vec{v}(3) = 4\hat{\imath} + 3\hat{\jmath}\ (\text{m/s})$.

What is the acceleration of the particle?

Divide the velocity difference by the time. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 18-03-17 S6 · Solution
Setup

$\vec{a} = [\vec{v}(3) - \vec{v}(0)]/3$.

Model

$[(-6\hat{\imath} + 3\hat{\jmath})]/3$.

Derivation

$\vec{a} = -2\hat{\imath} + 1\hat{\jmath}\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Correct answer: (e) $(-2\ \text{m/s}^2)\hat{\imath} + (1\ \text{m/s}^2)\hat{\jmath}$

Trap

(b) is for those who forget to divide by $3$.

Check

$\vec{v}(0) + 3\vec{a} = 10\hat{\imath} - 6\hat{\imath} + 3\hat{\jmath} = \vec{v}(3)$ ✓.

Divide the velocity difference by the time. Source: Opus_Format/2018-03-17.md S6 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 18-03-17 S7

$\vec{r}_0 = 2\hat{\imath} - 3\hat{\jmath}$, $\vec{v}_0 = 10\hat{\imath}$, $\vec{a} = -2\hat{\imath} + 1\hat{\jmath}$.

At $t = 3\ \text{s}$, what is the position vector of the particle?

Write all three terms. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 18-03-17 S7 · Solution
Setup

$\vec{r} = \vec{r}_0 + \vec{v}_0 t + \vec{a}t^2/2$, $t = 3$.

Model

$x: 2 + 30 - 9 = 23$; $y: -3 + 0 + 4{,}5 = 3/2$.

Derivation

$\vec{r} = 23\hat{\imath} + (3/2)\hat{\jmath}\ \text{m}$.

Correct answer: (d) $(23\ \text{m})\hat{\imath} + (3/2\ \text{m})\hat{\jmath}$

Trap

Options like (e) drop $\vec{r}_0$.

Check

$[\vec{r}(3) - \vec{r}_0]/3 = 7\hat{\imath} + 1{,}5\hat{\jmath} = \vec{v}_{av}$ (Question 8) ✓.

Write all three terms. Source: Opus_Format/2018-03-17.md S7 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 18-03-17 S8

$\vec{r}(3) = 23\hat{\imath} + (3/2)\hat{\jmath}$, $\vec{r}_0 = 2\hat{\imath} - 3\hat{\jmath}$; $\Delta t = 3\ \text{s}$.

Over the interval $t_i = 0$ to $t_f = 3\ \text{s}$, what is the average velocity vector of the particle?

Same result both ways. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 18-03-17 S8 · Solution
Setup

$\vec{v}_{av} = [\vec{r}(3) - \vec{r}_0]/3$.

Model

$(21\hat{\imath} + 4{,}5\hat{\jmath})/3$.

Derivation

$\vec{v}_{av} = 7\hat{\imath} + 1{,}5\hat{\jmath}\ \text{m/s}$ (in the options the unit is written as $\text{m}$).

Correct answer: (e) $(7\ \text{m})\hat{\imath} + (3/2\ \text{m})\hat{\jmath}$

Trap

Instantaneous velocity must not be confused with average velocity.

Check

At constant acceleration, $\vec{v}_{av} = [\vec{v}(0) + \vec{v}(3)]/2 = 7\hat{\imath} + 1{,}5\hat{\jmath}$ ✓.

Same result both ways. Source: Opus_Format/2018-03-17.md S8 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 18-07-14 S2

$m_1$ is launched vertically with $v_1 = 5\ \text{m/s}$ while $m_2$ is launched at angle $\theta = 53^\circ$ with $v_2 = 5\ \text{m/s}$, both at the same time. ($g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$)

What is the acceleration vector of $m_1$ relative to $m_2$?

Same acceleration, zero relative acceleration. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 18-07-14 S2 · Solution
Setup

Both bodies accelerate only under gravity: $\vec{a}_1 = \vec{a}_2 = -g\hat{\jmath}$.

Model

Relative acceleration $\vec{a}_{1/2} = \vec{a}_1 - \vec{a}_2$.

Derivation

$\vec{a}_{1/2} = 0$.

Correct answer: (e) $0$

Trap

One might think different velocities imply different accelerations; the acceleration is the same.

Check

That the relative velocity stays constant (Question 4) confirms this ✓.

Same acceleration, zero relative acceleration. Source: Opus_Format/2018-07-14.md S2 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 18-07-14 S3

$m_1$ is launched vertically with $v_1 = 5\ \text{m/s}$ while $m_2$ is launched at angle $\theta = 53^\circ$ with $v_2 = 5\ \text{m/s}$. ($v_{2x} = 3\ \text{m/s}$, $v_{2y0} = 4\ \text{m/s}$)

When $m_2$ reaches the highest point of its trajectory, what is the velocity vector ($\text{m/s}$) of $m_1$ relative to $m_2$?

Relative velocity is constant. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 18-07-14 S3 · Solution
Setup

Peak time $t = 4/10 = 0{,}4\ \text{s}$; at that instant $\vec{v}_2 = 3\hat{\imath}$, $\vec{v}_1 = (5 - 4)\hat{\jmath} = 1\hat{\jmath}$.

Model

$\vec{v}_{1/2} = \vec{v}_1 - \vec{v}_2$.

Derivation

$\vec{v}_{1/2} = -3\hat{\imath} + 1\hat{\jmath}\ \text{m/s}$.

Correct answer: (a) $-3\hat{\imath} + \hat{\jmath}$

Trap

Reversing the subtraction order flips the signs.

Check

The relative velocity is the same at every instant ($\vec{a}_{1/2} = 0$); at $t = 0$ it is $-3\hat{\imath} + \hat{\jmath}$ too ✓.

Relative velocity is constant. Source: Opus_Format/2018-07-14.md S3 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 18-07-14 S4

Relative velocity is constant: $\vec{v}_{1/2} = -3\hat{\imath} + 1\hat{\jmath}\ \text{m/s}$; the bodies start from the same point.

At $t = 0{,}5\ \text{s}$, what is the distance between $m_1$ and $m_2$?

Like a single body in the relative frame. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 18-07-14 S4 · Solution
Setup

Relative displacement $\Delta\vec{r} = \vec{v}_{1/2}\,t$.

Model

$\Delta\vec{r} = (-3\hat{\imath} + \hat{\jmath}) \cdot 0{,}5 = -1{,}5\hat{\imath} + 0{,}5\hat{\jmath}$.

Derivation

$d = \sqrt{2{,}25 + 0{,}25} = \sqrt{10}/2\ \text{m}$.

Correct answer: (b) $\sqrt{10}/2\ \text{m}$

Trap

Adding the components but forgetting the square root lands on a wrong option.

Check

$d/t = \sqrt{10}/1 = |\vec{v}_{1/2}| = \sqrt{10}$ ✓.

Like a single body in the relative frame. Source: Opus_Format/2018-07-14.md S4 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 18-07-14 S11

A small car moves at constant speed $v = 6\ \text{m/s}$ on a vertical circle of radius $R = 1{,}5\ \text{m}$; at $t = 0$ it is at point $A$ ($R,0$). Period $\pi/2\ \text{s}$.

Between $t = 0$ and $t = \pi/4\ \text{s}$, what is the average velocity vector ($\text{m/s}$) of the car?

Over half a turn the displacement is the diameter. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 18-07-14 S11 · Solution
Setup

$\Delta t = \pi/4$ is half a period; the car travels from $A(R,0)$ to $C(-R,0)$: $\Delta\vec{r} = -3\hat{\imath}$.

Model

$\vec{v}_{av} = \Delta\vec{r}/\Delta t = -3\hat{\imath}/(\pi/4)$.

Derivation

$\vec{v}_{av} = -12\hat{\imath}/\pi\ \text{m/s}$.

Correct answer: (b) $-\frac{12}{\pi}\hat{\imath}$

Trap

A direction error is the (c) trap; the displacement points to the left.

Check

Magnitude $12/\pi \approx 3{,}8 < 6 = v$ ✓ (the chord is shorter than the arc).

Over half a turn the displacement is the diameter. Source: Opus_Format/2018-07-14.md S11 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 18-07-14 S12

The same car: at $A$, $\vec{v} = +6\hat{\jmath}$; at $C$, $\vec{v} = -6\hat{\jmath}$; $\Delta t = \pi/4\ \text{s}$.

Between $t = 0$ and $t = \pi/4\ \text{s}$, what is the average acceleration vector ($\text{m/s}^2$) of the car?

Average acceleration comes from the velocity difference. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 18-07-14 S12 · Solution
Setup

$\vec{a}_{av} = \Delta\vec{v}/\Delta t = (-6\hat{\jmath} - 6\hat{\jmath})/(\pi/4)$.

Model

$\Delta\vec{v} = -12\hat{\jmath}$.

Derivation

$\vec{a}_{av} = -48\hat{\jmath}/\pi\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Correct answer: (d) $-\frac{48}{\pi}\hat{\jmath}$

Trap

Using the position change instead of the velocity change mixes up the axes.

Check

Centripetal acceleration $v^2/R = 24$; the average $|a| = 48/\pi \approx 15{,}3$ is consistent in magnitude ✓.

Average acceleration comes from the velocity difference. Source: Opus_Format/2018-07-14.md S12 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 18-10-27 S6

A driver going at $40\ \text{m/s}$ sees a police car $50\ \text{m}$ ahead going at a constant $30\ \text{m/s}$ and slows down with deceleration $1{,}0\ \text{m/s}^2$.

How long after braking do you catch up with the police car?

Perfect square: a single (tangent) meeting. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 18-10-27 S6 · Solution
Setup

$x_{siz} = 40t - 0{,}5t^2$, $x_{polis} = 50 + 30t$.

Model

$40t - 0{,}5t^2 = 50 + 30t$, i.e. $t^2 - 20t + 100 = 0$.

Derivation

$(t - 10)^2 = 0$; $t = 10\ \text{s}$ (tangent meeting).

Correct answer: (b) $10\ \text{s}$

Trap

Dividing the initial relative speed $10$ by the deceleration to get $20\ \text{s}$ ignores the $50\ \text{m}$ gap.

Check

At $t = 10$ your speed is $30\ \text{m/s}$: exactly the police speed — tangent ✓.

Perfect square: a single (tangent) meeting. Source: Opus_Format/2018-10-27.md S6 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 18-10-27 S7

Same scenario: they meet at $t = 10\ \text{s}$.

After braking, how far do you drive to catch up with the police car?

Verify the distance from both sides. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 18-10-27 S7 · Solution
Setup

$x = 40t - 0{,}5t^2$, $t = 10\ \text{s}$.

Model

$x = 400 - 50$.

Derivation

$x = 350\ \text{m}$.

Correct answer: (b) $350\ \text{m}$

Trap

Multiplying at a constant $40\ \text{m/s}$ gives $400\ \text{m}$; the slowing-down must be taken into account.

Check

Police distance $50 + 300 = 350\ \text{m}$ ✓.

Verify the distance from both sides. Source: Opus_Format/2018-10-27.md S7 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 18-10-27 S8

A particle moves from the origin at $t = 0$ with $\vec{v}_0 = 4{,}0\hat{\jmath}\ \text{m/s}$ under constant $\vec{a} = (2{,}0\hat{\imath} - 3{,}0\hat{\jmath})\ \text{m/s}^2$.

After $t = 2{,}0\ \text{s}$, how far from the origin has the particle gone?

First the vector, then the distance. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 18-10-27 S8 · Solution
Setup

$\vec{r} = \vec{v}_0 t + \vec{a}t^2/2$, $t = 2$.

Model

$\vec{r} = 8\hat{\jmath} + (2\hat{\imath} - 3\hat{\jmath}) \cdot 2 = 4\hat{\imath} + 2\hat{\jmath}$.

Derivation

$|\vec{r}| = \sqrt{16 + 4} = \sqrt{20} = 2\sqrt{5}\ \text{m}$.

Correct answer: (d) $2\sqrt{5}\ \text{m}$

Trap

Dropping one of the components and getting $4\ \text{m}$ is an incomplete calculation.

Check

$|\vec{r}| \approx 4{,}47$; larger than the components, smaller than their sum ✓.

First the vector, then the distance. Source: Opus_Format/2018-10-27.md S8 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 18-10-27 S9

The same particle: $\vec{v}_0 = 4{,}0\hat{\jmath}$, $\vec{a} = 2{,}0\hat{\imath} - 3{,}0\hat{\jmath}$.

Find the velocity vector ($\text{m/s}$) of the particle after $t = 2{,}0\ \text{s}$.

Add component by component. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 18-10-27 S9 · Solution
Setup

$\vec{v} = \vec{v}_0 + \vec{a}t$, $t = 2$.

Model

$\vec{v} = 4\hat{\jmath} + (2\hat{\imath} - 3\hat{\jmath}) \cdot 2$.

Derivation

$\vec{v} = 4\hat{\imath} - 2\hat{\jmath}\ \text{m/s}$.

Correct answer: (d) $4{,}0\hat{\imath} - 2{,}0\hat{\jmath}$

Trap

A sign error is the (e) trap; $4 - 6 = -2$ is negative.

Check

At $t = 0$ the formula gives $\vec{v}_0$ ✓.

Add component by component. Source: Opus_Format/2018-10-27.md S9 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 18-10-27 S10

The first body has $\vec{v}_1 = 4\hat{\imath} - 2\hat{\jmath}$ at $t = 2$; the second body has $\vec{v}_2 = -2\hat{\imath} + \hat{\jmath}\ (\text{m/s})$.

What is the relative velocity vector ($\text{m/s}$) of the second body with respect to the first?

Order matters in relative velocity. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 18-10-27 S10 · Solution
Setup

$\vec{v}_{2/1} = \vec{v}_2 - \vec{v}_1$.

Model

$(-2\hat{\imath} + \hat{\jmath}) - (4\hat{\imath} - 2\hat{\jmath})$.

Derivation

$\vec{v}_{2/1} = -6\hat{\imath} + 3\hat{\jmath}\ \text{m/s}$.

Correct answer: (e) $-6{,}0\hat{\imath} + 3{,}0\hat{\jmath}$

Trap

(c) is for those who reverse the order ($\vec{v}_1 - \vec{v}_2$).

Check

$\vec{v}_{2/1} = -\vec{v}_{1/2}$; magnitude $\sqrt{45} = 3\sqrt{5}$ ✓.

Order matters in relative velocity. Source: Opus_Format/2018-10-27.md S10 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 19-03-16 S3

A and B are launched from the same point with initial speeds of equal magnitude at angles $\alpha_A$ and $\alpha_B$; both land at the same point.

Which of the following is always true?

Complementary angles give the same range. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 19-03-16 S3 · Solution
Setup

Range $R = v_0^2\sin(2\alpha)/g$; same $v_0$ and same $R$.

Model

$\sin(2\alpha_A) = \sin(2\alpha_B)$; for distinct angles, $2\alpha_A + 2\alpha_B = \pi$.

Derivation

$\alpha_A + \alpha_B = \pi/2$ (complementary angles).

Correct answer: (d) $\alpha_A+\alpha_B = \pi/2$

Trap

(b) is for those who forget the doubling of the angles; the equality of the sines is at the $2\alpha$ level.

Check

The special case $\alpha = 45^\circ$: $2\alpha = 90^\circ$, maximum range ✓.

Complementary angles give the same range. Source: Opus_Format/2019-03-16.md S3 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 19-03-16 S4

The weight of a $10\ \text{kg}$ body is $50\ \text{N}$; initial speed $50\ \text{m/s}$; no air resistance.

What is the greatest range of this body?

First find $g$. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 19-03-16 S4 · Solution
Setup

From the weight, $g = 50/10 = 5\ \text{m/s}^2$. The greatest range is at $45^\circ$.

Model

$R_{max} = v_0^2/g$.

Derivation

$R_{max} = 2500/5 = 500\ \text{m}$.

Correct answer: (d) $500\ \text{m}$

Trap

(a) is for those who take $g = 10$ ($2500/10$, not $2500/2{,}5$); $g$ is found in the question.

Check

Units: $(\text{m/s})^2/(\text{m/s}^2) = \text{m}$ ✓.

First find $g$. Source: Opus_Format/2019-03-16.md S4 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 19-03-16 S5

$1\ \text{kg}$ particle: $\vec{r}(t) = t/2\,\hat{\imath} - t^3\,\hat{\jmath}\ (\text{m})$. (No $\vec{F}(t)$ information is needed in this question.)

What is the average velocity vector of the particle between $t = 1$ and $t = 3\ \text{s}$?

Divide the position difference by the time. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 19-03-16 S5 · Solution
Setup

$\vec{v}_{av} = [\vec{r}(3) - \vec{r}(1)]/2$.

Model

$\vec{r}(3) = 1{,}5\hat{\imath} - 27\hat{\jmath}$; $\vec{r}(1) = 0{,}5\hat{\imath} - \hat{\jmath}$.

Derivation

$[(1{,}0)\hat{\imath} - 26\hat{\jmath}]/2 = 0{,}5\hat{\imath} - 13\hat{\jmath}\ \text{m/s}$.

Correct answer: (b) $1/2\,\hat{\imath} - 13\,\hat{\jmath}$

Trap

(e) is a division mistake ($-26/2 = -13$, not $-14$).

Check

The $x$ component moves at constant speed: $0{,}5$ ✓.

Divide the position difference by the time. Source: Opus_Format/2019-03-16.md S5 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 19-03-16 S7

On a straight road, $v(t) = -t^2/2 + 3t + 3/2$ ($v$: $\text{m/s}$, $t$: $\text{s}$).

Calculate the acceleration of the particle at $t = 2\ \text{s}$.

Acceleration is the derivative of velocity. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 19-03-16 S7 · Solution
Setup

$a = dv/dt$.

Model

$a(t) = -t + 3$.

Derivation

$a(2) = 1\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Correct answer: (e) $1\ \text{m/s}^2$

Trap

Marking the velocity itself ($v(2) = 11/2$) is the (c) trap.

Check

The unit is $\text{m/s}^2$ ✓.

Acceleration is the derivative of velocity. Source: Opus_Format/2019-03-16.md S7 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 19-03-16 S8

Same motion: $a(t) = -t + 3$; the force points along the acceleration via $F = ma$.

Calculate the instant at which the force acting on the particle changes direction.

Zero force means zero acceleration. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 19-03-16 S8 · Solution
Setup

The direction change happens at $F = 0$, i.e. at $a = 0$.

Model

$-t + 3 = 0$.

Derivation

$t = 3\ \text{s}$.

Correct answer: (d) $3\ \text{s}$

Trap

It must not be confused with the instant at which the velocity vanishes.

Check

Before $t = 3$, $a > 0$; after it, $a < 0$ ✓.

Zero force means zero acceleration. Source: Opus_Format/2019-03-16.md S8 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 19-03-16 S9

Same motion: $v(t) = -t^2/2 + 3t + 3/2$, $r(0) = 0$; the force changes direction at $t = 3\ \text{s}$.

Calculate the position at the instant the force changes direction.

Position is the integral of velocity. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 19-03-16 S9 · Solution
Setup

$r(3) = \int_0^3 v\,dt$.

Model

$[-t^3/6 + 3t^2/2 + 3t/2]_0^3 = -27/6 + 27/2 + 9/2$.

Derivation

$r(3) = -4{,}5 + 13{,}5 + 4{,}5 = 13{,}5 = 27/2\ \text{m}$.

Correct answer: (b) $27/2\ \text{m}$

Trap

Forgetting $+C$ in the indefinite integral misses the $r(0) = 0$ condition.

Check

Differentiating back gives $v(3) = -9/2 + 9 + 3/2 = 6$ ✓.

Position is the integral of velocity. Source: Opus_Format/2019-03-16.md S9 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 19-03-16 S10

$\vec{r}_{A/E} = (3t^2+104)\hat{\imath} + 2t\,\hat{\jmath} + \hat{k}$; $\vec{r}_{B/A} = (-t^2+2t-100)\hat{\imath} + (-2t+5)\hat{\jmath} - \hat{k}$.

Find the position vector $\vec{r}_{B/E}$ of B relative to the ground.

Add the relative position to the base (Earth-frame) position. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 19-03-16 S10 · Solution
Setup

$\vec{r}_{B/E} = \vec{r}_{A/E} + \vec{r}_{B/A}$ (vector addition).

Model

$x: 3t^2 + 104 - t^2 + 2t - 100 = 2t^2 + 2t + 4$; $y: 5$; $z: 0$.

Derivation

$\vec{r}_{B/E} = (2t^2+2t+4)\hat{\imath} + 5\hat{\jmath}$.

Correct answer: (e) $(2t^2+2t+4)\,\hat{\imath} + 5\,\hat{\jmath}$

Trap

(b) is for those who leave $2\hat{k}$ in $z$; $\hat{k} - \hat{k} = 0$.

Check

At $t = 0$: $\vec{r}_{A/E} + \vec{r}_{B/A} = 4\hat{\imath} + 5\hat{\jmath}$ ✓.

Add the relative position to the base (Earth-frame) position. Source: Opus_Format/2019-03-16.md S10 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 19-03-16 S11

$\vec{r}_{B/E} = (2t^2+2t+4)\hat{\imath} + 5\hat{\jmath}$.

Find the velocity vector $\vec{v}_{B/E}$ of B relative to the ground.

The derivative of a constant term is zero. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 19-03-16 S11 · Solution
Setup

$\vec{v}_{B/E} = d\vec{r}_{B/E}/dt$.

Model

Derivative: $(4t + 2)\hat{\imath} + 0\hat{\jmath}$.

Derivation

$\vec{v}_{B/E} = (4t+2)\hat{\imath}\ \text{m/s}$.

Correct answer: (e) $(4t+2)\,\hat{\imath}$

Trap

Those who think the derivative of the constant $5\hat{\jmath}$ is nonzero pick a wrong option.

Check

At $t = 0$, $\vec{v}_B = 2\hat{\imath}$ (consistent with Question 13) ✓.

The derivative of a constant term is zero. Source: Opus_Format/2019-03-16.md S11 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 19-03-16 S12

B has velocity $\vec{v}_B = (4t+2)\hat{\imath}$; $m_B = 5\ \text{kg}$.

Find the magnitude of the total force acting on B.

Force comes from acceleration. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 19-03-16 S12 · Solution
Setup

$\vec{a}_B = d\vec{v}_B/dt = 4\hat{\imath}$; $|\vec{F}| = m_B|\vec{a}_B|$.

Model

$|\vec{F}| = 5 \cdot 4$.

Derivation

$|\vec{F}| = 20\ \text{N}$.

Correct answer: (e) $20\ \text{N}$

Trap

(a) is for those who multiply the mass by the velocity instead of the acceleration ($m\,v$ is momentum).

Check

A magnitude cannot be negative; (d) is ruled out ✓.

Force comes from acceleration. Source: Opus_Format/2019-03-16.md S12 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 19-03-16 S13

$\vec{v}_A = 6t\,\hat{\imath} + 2\,\hat{\jmath}$; $\vec{v}_B = (4t+2)\,\hat{\imath}$; $t = 0$.

At $t = 0$, find the magnitude of the velocity of A relative to B.

First the vector difference, then the magnitude. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 19-03-16 S13 · Solution
Setup

At $t = 0$: $\vec{v}_A = 2\hat{\jmath}$, $\vec{v}_B = 2\hat{\imath}$.

Model

$\vec{v}_{A/B} = \vec{v}_A - \vec{v}_B = -2\hat{\imath} + 2\hat{\jmath}$.

Derivation

$|\vec{v}_{A/B}| = \sqrt{4 + 4} = 2\sqrt{2}\ \text{m/s}$.

Correct answer: (c) $2\sqrt{2}\ \text{m/s}$

Trap

Taking the component difference ($2$) for the magnitude is the (a) trap.

Check

$2\sqrt{2} \approx 2{,}83$; two perpendicular components of $2$ ✓.

First the vector difference, then the magnitude. Source: Opus_Format/2019-03-16.md S13 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 19-03-16 S14

$\vec{r}_{B/A} = (-t^2+2t-100)\hat{\imath} + (-2t+5)\hat{\jmath} - \hat{k}$; A and B are pointlike.

When do A and B meet?

All three components must vanish. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 19-03-16 S14 · Solution
Setup

Meeting requires $\vec{r}_{B/A} = 0$ (all three components zero).

Model

The $z$ component is persistently $-\hat{k} \ne 0$; the $x$ equation $-t^2 + 2t - 100 = 0$ has no real roots.

Derivation

They never meet.

Correct answer: (b) Never

Trap

Zeroing a single component to get (d) $5/2$ skips checking $z$.

Check

The discriminant of the $x$ equation is $4 - 400 < 0$ ✓.

All three components must vanish. Source: Opus_Format/2019-03-16.md S14 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 19-07-13 S2

$m_1$ is launched horizontally to the left with $v_{01} = 20\ \text{m/s}$, $m_2$ to the right with $v_{02} = 50\ \text{m/s}$. ($g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$)

In which option are the velocities of the masses at $t = 3\ \text{s}$ given correctly?

Horizontal velocity does not change. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 19-07-13 S2 · Solution
Setup

Horizontal speeds stay constant; vertical speed $v_y = -gt$.

Model

At $t = 3$, $v_y = -30\ \text{m/s}$ for both.

Derivation

$\vec{v}_1 = -20\hat{\imath} - 30\hat{\jmath}$, $\vec{v}_2 = 50\hat{\imath} - 30\hat{\jmath}\ \text{m/s}$.

Correct answer: (a) $\vec{v}_1 = -20\,\hat{\imath} - 30\,\hat{\jmath}$; $\vec{v}_2 = 50\,\hat{\imath} - 30\,\hat{\jmath}$

Trap

Options that change the horizontal speed too are ruled out; there is no horizontal acceleration.

Check

At $t = 0$ the vertical component is zero ✓.

Horizontal velocity does not change. Source: Opus_Format/2019-07-13.md S2 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 19-07-13 S3

Same launch: horizontal separation speed $20 + 50 = 70\ \text{m/s}$; vertical positions are the same.

At $t = 3\ \text{s}$, how many meters apart are the masses?

The vertical difference is zero. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 19-07-13 S3 · Solution
Setup

Since the vertical positions are equal, the separation is the horizontal distance.

Model

$\Delta x = (20 + 50) \cdot t$.

Derivation

$\Delta x = 70 \cdot 3 = 210\ \text{m}$.

Correct answer: (c) $210$

Trap

Trying to add the vertical drop as well misses the fact that the difference is zero.

Check

Relative speed $70\ \text{m/s}$; $70 \cdot 3 = 210$ ✓.

The vertical difference is zero. Source: Opus_Format/2019-07-13.md S3 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 19-07-13 S4

$\vec{v}_1 = -20\hat{\imath} - 30\hat{\jmath}$, $\vec{v}_2 = 50\hat{\imath} - 30\hat{\jmath}$ ($t = 3\ \text{s}$).

At $t = 3\ \text{s}$, what is the velocity vector of mass $m_1$ relative to $m_2$?

The vertical parts cancel. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 19-07-13 S4 · Solution
Setup

$\vec{v}_{1/2} = \vec{v}_1 - \vec{v}_2$; the vertical components are equal and cancel.

Model

$(-20 - 50)\hat{\imath} + (-30 + 30)\hat{\jmath}$.

Derivation

$\vec{v}_{1/2} = -70\hat{\imath}\ \text{m/s}$.

Correct answer: (e) $-70\,\hat{\imath}\,\text{m/s}$

Trap

Reversing the subtraction order gives the positive sign.

Check

$|\vec{v}_{1/2}| = 70$; consistent with the distance growth rate in Question 3 ✓.

The vertical parts cancel. Source: Opus_Format/2019-07-13.md S4 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 19-07-13 S5

$\vec{v}_1 = -20\hat{\imath} - 10t\,\hat{\jmath}$, $\vec{v}_2 = 50\hat{\imath} - 10t\,\hat{\jmath}$.

At what time $t$ do the velocity vectors of the masses become perpendicular to each other?

For perpendicularity the dot product is zero. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 19-07-13 S5 · Solution
Setup

Perpendicularity condition: $\vec{v}_1 \cdot \vec{v}_2 = 0$.

Model

$(-20)(50) + (-10t)(-10t) = -1000 + 100t^2 = 0$.

Derivation

$t^2 = 10$; $t = \sqrt{10}\ \text{s}$.

Correct answer: (d) $\sqrt{10}\,\text{s}$

Trap

It must not be confused with the instant that makes the position vectors perpendicular.

Check

$t = \sqrt{10} \approx 3{,}16$; at $t = 3$ the product is $-100 < 0$ (still an obtuse angle) ✓.

For perpendicularity the dot product is zero. Source: Opus_Format/2019-07-13.md S5 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 19-10-26 S3

A $0{,}5\ \text{kg}$ body: $a(t) = 3t^2 - 1$ ($\text{m/s}^2$); $v(0) = 3\ \text{m/s}$.

What is the displacement of the body during the first $2$ seconds?

Two integrals for the displacement. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 19-10-26 S3 · Solution
Setup

Double integral: $v(t) = 3 + t^3 - t$; $x(t) = 3t + t^4/4 - t^2/2$.

Model

At $t = 2$: $x = 6 + 4 - 2$.

Derivation

$x = 8\ \text{m}$.

Correct answer: (e) $8\ \text{m}$

Trap

Stopping after a single integral and marking $v(2) = 9$ is the (b) trap.

Check

Average speed $4\ \text{m/s}$; $4 \cdot 2 = 8$ ✓.

Two integrals for the displacement. Source: Opus_Format/2019-10-26.md S3 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 19-10-26 S4

The same body: $v(t) = 3 + t^3 - t$; $v(0) = 3$, $v(2) = 9\ \text{m/s}$; $m = 0{,}5\ \text{kg}$.

Between $0$ and $2\ \text{s}$, what is the magnitude of the average force acting on the body?

For the average force, first the average acceleration. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 19-10-26 S4 · Solution
Setup

Average acceleration $\vec{a}_{avg} = \Delta \vec{v}/\Delta t$; average force $m\vec{a}_{avg}$.

Model

$\vec{a}_{avg} = [(3 + 8 - 2) - 3]/2 = 3\ \text{m/s}^2$; $F = 0{,}5 \cdot 3$.

Derivation

$F_{av} = 1{,}5\ \text{N}$.

Correct answer: (a) $1{,}5\,\text{N}$

Trap

Forgetting to multiply by the mass gives (b) $3\ \text{N}$ (that is the acceleration).

Check

Units: $\text{kg} \cdot \text{m/s}^2 = \text{N}$ ✓.

For the average force, first the average acceleration. Source: Opus_Format/2019-10-26.md S4 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 19-10-26 S5

$v(t) = 3 + t^3 - t$; $a(t) = 3t^2 - 1$.

What is the acceleration at the instant the body's speed is $9\ \text{m/s}$?

First find the time, then the acceleration. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 19-10-26 S5 · Solution
Setup

First find the instant from $3 + t^3 - t = 9$.

Model

The ($t > 0$) root of $t^3 - t - 6 = 0$ is $t = 2\ \text{s}$.

Derivation

$a(2) = 3 \cdot 4 - 1 = 11\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Correct answer: (b) $11\,\text{m/s}^2$

Trap

No number can be put into the $a$ formula before the instant is found.

Check

$v(2) = 9$ is satisfied ✓.

First find the time, then the acceleration. Source: Opus_Format/2019-10-26.md S5 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 19-10-26 S9

A particle is launched with $v_0$ from the edge of a wall of height $h$; it slows with deceleration $-a$ along a tube of length $x$, then undergoes a horizontal launch from height $h$.

What is the total horizontal distance $l$ from the edge of the wall to the landing point?

Combine the two stages. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 19-10-26 S9 · Solution
Setup

Tube exit speed: $v_1^2 = v_0^2 - 2ax$; fall time $t = \sqrt{2h/g}$.

Model

$l = x + v_1 t$.

Derivation

$l = x + \sqrt{v_0^2-2ax}\sqrt{2h/g}$.

Correct answer: (e) $x + \sqrt{v_0^2-2ax}\sqrt{2h/g}$

Trap

Options (b)/(d) drop the factor $2$; the $v^2$ formula contains $2a\Delta x$.

Check

At $x = 0$: $l = v_0\sqrt{2h/g}$ — plain horizontal launch ✓.

Combine the two stages. Source: Opus_Format/2019-10-26.md S9 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 19-10-26 S10

$l(x) = x + \sqrt{v_0^2-2ax}\sqrt{2h/g}$.

For the maximum value of $l$, what should the tube length $x$ be?

Set the derivative to zero. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 19-10-26 S10 · Solution
Setup

Optimization: $dl/dx = 0$.

Model

$dl/dx = 1 - a\sqrt{2h/g}/\sqrt{v_0^2-2ax} = 0$; hence $\sqrt{v_0^2-2ax} = a\sqrt{2h/g}$.

Derivation

$v_0^2 - 2ax = 2a^2h/g$; $x = v_0^2/(2a) - ah/g$.

Correct answer: (a) $\dfrac{v_0^2}{2a} - \dfrac{ah}{g}$

Trap

Looking for an extremum without setting the derivative to zero is a mistake.

Check

At $h = 0$: $x = v_0^2/(2a)$ — full stop inside the tube ✓.

Set the derivative to zero. Source: Opus_Format/2019-10-26.md S10 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 19-10-26 S11

Tube exit speed $v_1 = \sqrt{v_0^2-2ax}$; in a horizontal launch the horizontal speed is unchanged.

What is the magnitude of the horizontal component of the particle's velocity at the instant it hits the ground?

Horizontal velocity is conserved. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 19-10-26 S11 · Solution
Setup

In a horizontal launch the horizontal speed equals the tube exit speed.

Model

$|v_x| = v_1 = \sqrt{v_0^2-2ax}$.

Derivation

It is directly the $v_1$ value.

Correct answer: (e) $\sqrt{v_0^2-2ax}$

Trap

(a) is the trap that confuses $h$ with $x$; the horizontal speed does not depend on $h$.

Check

At $x = 0$: $|v_x| = v_0$ ✓.

Horizontal velocity is conserved. Source: Opus_Format/2019-10-26.md S11 (Opus 5.5).

H2 · Kinematics (2/2) · Question 19-10-26 S12

The vertical motion is free fall starting from rest (height $h$).

What is the magnitude of the vertical component of the particle's velocity at the instant it hits the ground?

Vertical velocity depends only on $h$. The student first picks an option; then continues to the solution with →.

H2 · Question 19-10-26 S12 · Solution
Setup

$v_y^2 = 0 + 2gh$ (free fall from rest).

Model

$|v_y| = \sqrt{2gh}$ (direction downward: $-\sqrt{2gh}$).

Derivation

Correct answer (b) $-\sqrt{2gh}$ (magnitude $\sqrt{2gh}$).

Correct answer: (b) $-\sqrt{2gh}$

Trap

Options confusing $x$ with $h$ are ruled out; the vertical speed is independent of the tube.

Check

Energy: $mgh = mv_y^2/2$ ✓.

Vertical velocity depends only on $h$. Source: Opus_Format/2019-10-26.md S12 (Opus 5.5).

H3 · Question 14-10 16
A mass $m$ is released from height $h$ on a cart of mass $M$. Friction and pulley weights are neglected. What is the relation between the $x$ component $a_{mx}$ of the acceleration of mass $m$ and the $x$ component $a_{Mx}$ of mass $M$?

Have the student think about the horizontal constraint first. Source: 2014-10-18 Question 16.

H3 · Question 14-10 16 · Solution
Setup

Mass $m$ hangs at height $h$ on cart $M$; the rope runs from the cart through a moving pulley and two fixed pulleys on the right.

Model

Horizontally $m$ leans against the tower and shares the cart's horizontal motion; there is no independent horizontal degree of freedom.

Derivation

The horizontal constraint gives a single equation: $x_m - X_M = \text{sabit}$; differentiating gives $a_{mx} = a_{Mx}$.

Result

Correct answer: (A) $a_{mx} = a_{Mx}$

Trap

Options (b) and (c) try to apply the rope constraint to the horizontal arm; but the factor of 2 is only in the vertical arm.

Check

In the limit $M \to \infty$ the cart stays fixed and $m$ stays fixed horizontally; the equality is consistent with this limit.

The horizontal equality sets up the factor of 2 in the vertical. Source: 2014-10-18 Question 16.

H3 · Question 14-10 17
In the same setup, what is the relation between the $y$ component $a_{my}$ of the acceleration of mass $m$ and the $x$ component $a_{Mx}$ of mass $M$?

Make them write the rope constraint. Source: 2014-10-18 Question 17.

H3 · Question 14-10 17 · Solution
Setup

Rope length: the vertical arm $y_m$ plus two horizontal arms $2X$ is constant in total; the number of pulleys sets the factor of two.

Model

Write the total length $L = y_m + 2X + \text{sabit}$ and differentiate twice.

Derivation

$0 = a_{my} + 2a_{Mx}$, so in magnitude $|a_{my}| = 2|a_{Mx}|$; as the cart moves right, $m$ descends twice as fast.

Result

Correct answer: (C) $a_{my} = 2a_{Mx}$

Trap

Option (e) gives the inverse ratio; anyone mixing up which arm of the rope folds falls here.

Check

If the change in $X$ is $\Delta$, the two arms of the rope release $2\Delta$; the vertical drop is doubled.

The two arms give the factor of 2. Source: 2014-10-18 Question 17.

H3 · Question 14-10 18
In the same setup, calculate the $y$ component $a_{my}$ of mass $m$ in terms of $m$, $M$ and $g$.

Three equations, three unknowns. Source: 2014-10-18 Question 18.

H3 · Question 14-10 18 · Solution
Setup

Vertically $mg - T = ma_{my}$; horizontally, cart plus contact force, $2T = (M+m)a_{Mx}$; constraint $a_{my} = 2a_{Mx}$.

Model

The $ma_{Mx}$ term in the horizontal equation is the tower's reaction on $m$; the system is pushed horizontally by $2T$.

Derivation

Writing $mg = 2ma_{Mx} + (M+m)a_{Mx}/2$ gives $a_{Mx} = 2mg/(5m+M)$, and twice that is $a_{my} = 4mg/(5m+M)$.

Result

Correct answer: (E) $a_{my} = 4mg/(5m+M)$

Trap

Option (a) misses a coefficient in the denominator; anyone forgetting the horizontal inertia of $m$ falls here.

Check

For large $M$, $a_{my} \to 0$; for $M=0$, $4g/5 < g$ remains, so the rope still carries load.

Do the limit check. Source: 2014-10-18 Question 18.

H3 · Question 14-10 19
In the same setup, calculate the rope tension $T$ in terms of $m$, $M$ and $g$.

Extract T from the horizontal. Source: 2014-10-18 Question 19.

H3 · Question 14-10 19 · Solution
Setup

Use the acceleration solution of the previous question: $a_{Mx} = 2mg/(5m+M)$ and the horizontal equation $2T = (M+m)a_{Mx}$.

Model

Tension sets the scale of the horizontal balance; it can be cross-checked with the vertical equation.

Derivation

This gives $T = (M+m)a_{Mx}/2 = (M+m)mg/(5m+M)$.

Result

Correct answer: (C) $T = mg(m+M)/(5m+M)$

Trap

The extra factor of 2 in (d) comes from mistaking $2T$ for a single $T$; anyone miscounting the forces falls here.

Check

Substituting into $mg - T = ma_{my}$ satisfies the equality.

Verify with the vertical equation. Source: 2014-10-18 Question 19.

H3 · Question 14-10 20
Express the time for mass $m$ to fall onto cart $M$ in terms of $m$, $h$ and $g$.

Which axis brings it down? Source: 2014-10-18 Question 20.

H3 · Question 14-10 20 · Solution
Setup

Uniform acceleration from rest in the vertical: distance $h$, acceleration $a_{my}$; the horizontal acceleration does not affect the fall.

Model

Choose the kinematic model $h = \frac{1}{2}a_{my}t^2$; there is no tilt.

Derivation

$t^2 = 2h/a_{my}$, hence $t = \sqrt{2h/a_{my}}$.

Result

Correct answer: (D) $t = \sqrt{2h/a_{my}}$

Trap

Options (a) and (e) mix the horizontal acceleration into the fall; anyone not separating the axes falls here.

Check

Dimensional check: the ratio $h/a$ gives $\text{s}^2$, whose root is $\text{s}$.

Do dimensional analysis. Source: 2014-10-18 Question 20.

H3 · Question 15-03 6
A ball is in free fall and feels air resistance as it falls. Which graph best represents how the ball's acceleration varies with time?

Recall the terminal speed. Source: 2015-03-21 Question 6.

H3 · Question 15-03 6 · Solution
Setup

The ball is released from rest; $mg$ acts downward and a speed-growing air resistance $f$ acts upward.

Model

Newton: $ma = mg - f_{\text{hava}}$; $f$ grows with speed, so the net force shrinks.

Derivation

Initially $a = g$; as the speed grows the acceleration decays exponentially toward zero, vanishing at the terminal speed.

Result

Correct answer: (E) curve (IV): a decreasing curve with a zero asymptote.

Trap

(I) is fall without air; (II) reverses the direction of change; (V) goes to the wrong limit.

Check

As $t \to \infty$, $a \to 0$ and $v \to v_{\text{limit}}$ must hold.

Ask about the asymptote. Source: 2015-03-21 Question 6.

H3 · Question 15-03 20
A body of mass $m_1 = 2.00\ \text{kg}$ is placed in front of a mass $m_2 = 7.00\ \text{kg}$. A force $F = 360\ \text{N}$ pushes the system. There is no friction between the large mass and the table. What is the magnitude of the acceleration of the small mass?

Take the system first. Source: 2015-03-21 Question 20.

H3 · Question 15-03 20 · Solution
Setup

The small block leans on the left face of the large one; $F$ pushes from the left; grip is assumed.

Model

The system moves as a whole: set up the model $a = F/(m_1+m_2)$.

Derivation

Compute $a = 360/9 = 40\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Result

Correct answer: (B) $40\ \text{m/s}^2$

Trap

Option (a) divides $F$ by the small mass alone; anyone splitting the system falls here.

Check

Compare with the maximum static $\mu N$ and check whether the grip is consistent.

Grip condition comes later. Source: 2015-03-21 Question 20.

H3 · Question 15-03 21
In the same setup, what is the magnitude of the normal force between the masses?

Focus on the small mass. Source: 2015-03-21 Question 21.

H3 · Question 15-03 21 · Solution
Setup

The only horizontal force accelerating the small mass is the normal force between the two blocks.

Model

Write the model $N = m_1 a$ using $a = 40\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Derivation

This gives $N = 2 \cdot 40 = 80\ \text{N}$.

Result

Correct answer: (B) $80\ \text{N}$

Trap

Option (c) confuses it with the weight; here the normal force depends on the acceleration, not the weight.

Check

$N/m_1 = 40$ should give the system acceleration; it does.

Ratio check. Source: 2015-03-21 Question 21.

H3 · Question 15-03 22
In the same setup, what is the magnitude of the friction force between the masses? ($g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$)

Write the vertical equilibrium. Source: 2015-03-21 Question 22.

H3 · Question 15-03 22 · Solution
Setup

Vertically the small mass is in equilibrium; friction carries its weight.

Model

Write the equilibrium condition $f = m_1 g$ and compare with the maximum $\mu N = 40\ \text{N}$.

Derivation

Since $f = 20\ \text{N} < 40\ \text{N}$, it grips, and the value is $20\ \text{N}$.

Result

Correct answer: (E) $20\ \text{N}$

Trap

Option (a) mistakes the maximum value for the actual value; anyone confusing need with capacity falls here.

Check

The condition $f \le \mu N$ holds, so the regime stays static.

Compare the capacity. Source: 2015-03-21 Question 22.

H3 · Question 15-03 23
In the same setup, what is the magnitude of the normal force between the large mass and the table?

What does the table carry? Source: 2015-03-21 Question 23.

H3 · Question 15-03 23 · Solution
Setup

The table carries both masses; vertically the total weight is balanced.

Model

Set up the model $N = (m_1+m_2)g$.

Derivation

This gives $N = 9 \cdot 10 = 90\ \text{N}$.

Result

Correct answer: (D) $90\ \text{N}$

Trap

Option (b) mixes the horizontal $F$ into the vertical; anyone not separating axes falls here.

Check

Summing the individual block normals gives the same result.

Total weight. Source: 2015-03-21 Question 23.

H3 · Question 15-07 3
Which of the following is true for normal forces?

Start from the definition. Source: 2015-07-11 Question 3.

H3 · Question 15-07 3 · Solution
Setup

The normal force is the contact surface's reaction; by definition it is perpendicular to the surface.

Model

Its magnitude depends on the situation: consider the inclined-plane example $N = mg\cos\theta$.

Derivation

By definition its direction is always perpendicular to the surface; the other options are special cases, not rules.

Result

Correct answer: (B) (b) is always perpendicular to the surface.

Trap

Option (c) is only the horizontal-plane special case; anyone generalizing it falls here.

Check

Inclined-plane example: for $\theta > 0$, $N < mg$, which also eliminates (d).

Do not generalize the special case. Source: 2015-07-11 Question 3.

H3 · Question 15-07 5
Which of the graphs below is correct for static friction $F_s$ and kinetic friction $F_k$? (Horizontal axis is the applied force.)

Separate the two regimes. Source: 2015-07-11 Question 5.

H3 · Question 15-07 5 · Solution
Setup

In the static region $a = 0$, so $F_s$ grows equal to the applied force; once sliding starts the kinetic regime begins.

Model

Model: while $F_{\text{uyg}} < f_{\text{max}}$, $F_s = F_{\text{uyg}}$; afterwards $F_k = \mu_k N$, constant and lower.

Derivation

The graph that rises linearly, jumps down at breakaway, then continues as a low horizontal line is (c).

Result

Correct answer: (C) (c) graph.

Trap

Option (d) swaps the kinetic and static magnitudes; anyone mixing up the observation falls here.

The note that acceleration starts growing at breakaway confirms the graph.

Mark the breakaway point. Source: 2015-07-11 Question 5.

H3 · Question 15-07 17
A cart of length $L = 6\ \text{m}$, at rest at $t = 0$, starts with constant acceleration $A$. A block $m = 2\ \text{kg}$ stands at the front wall. $\mu_s = 0.8$, $\mu_k = 0.6$, $g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$. What is the minimum $A$ for the block to start sliding?

Draw the fictitious force. Source: 2015-07-11 Question 17.

H3 · Question 15-07 17 · Solution
Setup

In the cart frame the fictitious force $mA$ points backward; grip is limited by $\mu_s mg$.

Model

Write the grip condition $mA \le \mu_s mg$.

Derivation

This gives $A \le 8\ \text{m/s}^2$; sliding starts at $A > 8$, so the threshold is $8$.

Result

Correct answer: (C) $8\ \text{m/s}^2$

Trap

Option (b) uses the kinetic coefficient at the threshold; anyone using kinetic instead of static falls here.

Check

The product $\mu_s g$ directly gives the threshold: $0.8 \cdot 10 = 8$.

Write the threshold condition. Source: 2015-07-11 Question 17.

H3 · Question 15-07 18
If $A = 9\ \text{m/s}^2$, what is the acceleration vector of mass $m$ relative to the cart?

Which regime? Source: 2015-07-11 Question 18.

H3 · Question 15-07 18 · Solution
Setup

There is sliding: kinetic friction $f_k = \mu_k mg = 12\ \text{N}$ acts forward.

Model

Net relative to the cart: $-mA + f_k = -18 + 12 = -6\ \text{N}$.

Derivation

This gives $a_{\text{rel}} = -6/2 = -3\hat{i}\ \text{m/s}^2$, pointing backward.

Result

Correct answer: (D) $-3\hat{i}\ \text{m/s}^2$

Trap

Option (a) flips the sign; anyone mixing up the relative direction falls here.

Check

The shortcut $|a_{\text{rel}}| = A - \mu_k g = 3$ gives the same.

Check the sign. Source: 2015-07-11 Question 18.

H3 · Question 15-07 19
If $A = 6\ \text{m/s}^2$, what is the friction force acting on the block?

Check first whether it slides. Source: 2015-07-11 Question 19.

H3 · Question 15-07 19 · Solution
Setup

Since $6 < 8$, the block does not slide; the static regime holds.

Model

Static friction balances the fictitious force: set up $f = mA$.

Derivation

This gives $f = 2 \cdot 6 = 12\ \text{N}$.

Result

Correct answer: (E) $12\ \text{N}$

Trap

Option (d) mistakes the maximum ($16\ \text{N}$) for the actual value; anyone missing the need-versus-capacity distinction falls here.

Check

Since $12 < 16$, the static regime stays consistent.

Compare with the capacity. Source: 2015-07-11 Question 19.

H3 · Question 15-07 20
If $A = 9\ \text{m/s}^2$, how long does the block take to slide to the rear wall? ($L = 6\ \text{m}$)

Take the relative distance. Source: 2015-07-11 Question 20.

H3 · Question 15-07 20 · Solution
Setup

The relative acceleration has magnitude $3\ \text{m/s}^2$, and the relative distance to cover is $6\ \text{m}$.

Model

Write the relative kinematics $6 = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 3 t^2$.

Derivation

So $t^2 = 4$, hence $t = 2\ \text{s}$.

Result

Correct answer: (D) $2\ \text{s}$

Trap

Option (b) forgets the $1/2$ factor; anyone writing the kinematic template incompletely falls here.

Check

Cross-check with the final speed $v_{\text{rel}} = 6\ \text{m/s}$.

Do not forget the coefficient. Source: 2015-07-11 Question 20.

H3 · Question 15-07 21
If $A = 9\ \text{m/s}^2$, what is the ground-frame velocity vector of the block when it reaches the rear wall?

Transform back to the ground frame. Source: 2015-07-11 Question 21.

H3 · Question 15-07 21 · Solution
Setup

The ground-frame block acceleration is $A - 3 = 6\ \text{m/s}^2$ forward; time $t = 2\ \text{s}$.

Model

Set up the model $v = a_{\text{yer}} t$.

Derivation

This gives $v = 6 \cdot 2 = 12\hat{i}\ \text{m/s}$.

Result

Correct answer: (B) $12\hat{i}\ \text{m/s}$

Trap

Option (e) mistakes the relative speed for the ground speed; anyone skipping the frame transformation falls here.

Setup

The first law defines the inertial frame; an accelerating frame needs a fictitious force.

I, III and IV are accelerating, so they are eliminated; only II remains.

Only inertial frames obey the law.

Result

Correct answer: (C) (c) only II.

H3 · Question 15-11 17
A $5\ \text{kg}$ body is attached by a spring scale to the wall of a $10\ \text{kg}$ cart on a frictionless plane. While the cart accelerates the scale reads $20\ \text{N}$, and at rest it reads $0\ \text{N}$. What is the acceleration of the cart?

Focus on the block. Source: 2015-11-07 Question 17.

H3 · Question 15-11 17 · Solution
Setup

On the frictionless floor, only the scale tension acts horizontally on the $5\ \text{kg}$ block.

Model

Write $T = ma$: $20 = 5a$, hence $a = 4\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Derivation

Since the block travels with the cart, the cart's acceleration is also $4\hat{i}$ in the $+x$ direction.

Result

Correct answer: (D) $4\hat{i}\ \text{m/s}^2$

Trap

Option (a) flips the sign; anyone thinking the acceleration opposes the tension falls here.

Check

The ratio $a = T/m$ passes the unit check.

Use the joint motion. Source: 2015-11-07 Question 17.

H3 · Question 15-11 18
In the same setup, if the cart moves at constant velocity, what does the scale read?

What if acceleration is zero? Source: 2015-11-07 Question 18.

H3 · Question 15-11 18 · Solution
Setup

At constant velocity the acceleration is zero; no net force on the block is needed.

Model

Set up $F_{\text{net}} = 0$ in the inertial frame.

Derivation

The spring does not stretch; the reading is $0\ \text{N}$.

Result

Correct answer: (E) $0\ \text{N}$

Trap

Option (a) thinks it reads part of the weight; anyone mixing horizontal with vertical falls here.

Check

By the first law, tension vanishes in the unaccelerated frame.

Connect to the first law. Source: 2015-11-07 Question 18.

H3 · Question 15-11 19
A toy horse of mass $m$ hangs on a rope tied to the tops of two vertical posts. The height drops are $h_1$ on the left and $h_2$ on the right, each at horizontal distance $d$. What is the relation between the left ($T_1$) and right ($T_2$) rope tensions?

Equate the horizontal components. Source: 2015-11-07 Question 19.

H3 · Question 15-11 19 · Solution
Setup

Horizontal equilibrium: $T_1\cos\theta_1 = T_2\cos\theta_2$; from geometry $\cos\theta_1 = d/\sqrt{h_1^2+d^2}$.

Model

The ratio of cosines is tied to the ratio of tensions.

Derivation

This gives $T_1/T_2 = \sqrt{h_1^2+d^2}/\sqrt{h_2^2+d^2}$.

Result

Correct answer: (D) option (d).

Trap

Option (e) assumes symmetry; anyone expecting equality with different posts falls here.

Check

In the special case $h_1 = h_2$, $T_1 = T_2$, consistently.

Check the symmetric limit. Source: 2015-11-07 Question 19.

H3 · Question 15-11 20
In the same setup, what is $T_1$?

Write the vertical equilibrium. Source: 2015-11-07 Question 20.

H3 · Question 15-11 20 · Solution
Setup

Combine vertical equilibrium $T_1\sin\theta_1 + T_2\sin\theta_2 = mg$ with $T_2 = T_1\cos\theta_1/\cos\theta_2$.

Model

Write the sines with $h_1, h_2$ and take a common denominator.

Derivation

Then $T_1(h_1+h_2)/\sqrt{h_1^2+d^2} = mg$ gives the result.

Result

Correct answer: (B) $T_1 = mg\sqrt{h_1^2+d^2}/(h_1+h_2)$

Trap

Option (c) adds a factor of 2; anyone counting two sides twice falls here.

Check

Option (d) is dimensionless, so it cannot be a tension; eliminate it by dimensions.

Dimensional check. Source: 2015-11-07 Question 20.

H3 · Question 15-11 21
Block A ($2\ \text{kg}$) is on an incline with $\theta = 37^{\circ}$ and connected over a massless pulley to block B ($1\ \text{kg}$). $\mu_s = 0.6$, $\mu_k = 0.5$, $g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$. Assuming statics, what is the static friction on A? ($\sin37^{\circ} = 0.6$, $\cos37^{\circ} = 0.8$)

Write the components first. Source: 2015-11-07 Question 21.

H3 · Question 15-11 21 · Solution
Setup

The downslope component pulling A is $2 \cdot 10 \cdot 0.6 = 12\ \text{N}$; the weight of B, $10\ \text{N}$, pulls the other way.

Model

Equilibrium model: friction closes the difference.

Derivation

This gives $12 - 10 = 2\ \text{N}$ uphill.

Result

Correct answer: (A) $2\ \text{N}$ uphill.

Trap

Option (c) mistakes the maximum capacity for the actual value; anyone confusing need with capacity falls here.

Check

The regime is confirmed in the next question via $2 < 9.6$.

Mark the direction. Source: 2015-11-07 Question 21.

H3 · Question 15-11 22
In the same setup, is the static-friction assumption valid, and why?

Need versus capacity. Source: 2015-11-07 Question 22.

H3 · Question 15-11 22 · Solution
Setup

Required friction is $2\ \text{N}$; the maximum is $\mu_s N = 0.6 \cdot 2 \cdot 10 \cdot 0.8 = 9.6\ \text{N}$.

Model

Set up the comparison model $f_{\text{gerek}} < f_{\text{max}}$.

Derivation

Since $2 < 9.6$, the static regime holds.

Result

Correct answer: (C) (c) Yes, $f_s < \mu_s N$.

Trap

Option (e) assumes equality always holds; anyone taking the limiting value as the actual one falls here.

Check

Units and dimensions are force on both sides.

Set up the inequality. Source: 2015-11-07 Question 22.

H3 · Question 15-11 23
If the blocks are given an initial speed of $1.0\ \text{m/s}$ (B down, A up), what is the acceleration of the hanging block?

Switch to kinetics. Source: 2015-11-07 Question 23.

H3 · Question 15-11 23 · Solution
Setup

While moving, kinetic friction $f_k = \mu_k N = 0.5 \cdot 16 = 8\ \text{N}$ opposes the motion, acting downhill.

Model

Net in the B-down direction: $10 - 12 - 8 = -10 = 3a$.

Derivation

$a = -10/3$; the speed decreases, acceleration opposes the motion, i.e. upward for B.

Result

Correct answer: (B) $10/3$ upward.

Trap

Option (e) flips the friction direction; anyone forgetting that kinetic friction opposes velocity falls here.

Check

With $|a| = 10/3$ the stopping time is $0.3\ \text{s}$; the sign is consistent.

Take the direction from the velocity. Source: 2015-11-07 Question 23.

H3 · Question 15-11 24
How far do the blocks move until they stop (metres)? [ambiguous]

The options are inconsistent. Source: 2015-11-07 Question 24.

H3 · Question 15-11 24 · Solution
Setup

With deceleration $|a| = 10/3$, the stopping distance is $d = v_0^2/(2|a|) = 1/(20/3) = 3/20 = 0.15\ \text{m}$; this value is not among the options.

Model

Option $(c)$, $3/26$, corresponds to assuming $|a| = 13/3$; it is the closest option.

Derivation

Opus 5.5 note: the correct physics gives $3/20\ \text{m}$; the options are inconsistent, so the marked (c) carries an [ambiguous] flag.

Result

Correct answer: (C) option (c) [ambiguous]: $3/20\ \text{m}$ is not among the options; the closest option, corresponding to an acceleration of $13/3$.

Trap

Option (b) is wrong: after stopping, the required $2\ \text{N}$ stays below $\mu_s N = 9.6\ \text{N}$, so the blocks remain at rest.

Handle the ambiguous flag. Source: 2015-11-07 Question 24.

H3 · Question 15-11 25
On a horizontal plane, block A sits on block B; B is pulled to the right by $F$. All surfaces have kinetic coefficient $\mu_k$. A rope connects A and B over a fixed pulley on the left. What is the acceleration of the system?

Write the constraint. Source: 2015-11-07 Question 25.

H3 · Question 15-11 25 · Solution
Setup

Rope constraint $a_A = -a_B$; for A, $-T + \mu_k m_A g = -m_A a$; for B, $F - T - \mu_k m_A g - \mu_k(m_A+m_B)g = m_B a$.

Model

Three friction contributions: $m_A$ twice at the A-B interface, plus $m_A+m_B$ at the floor.

Derivation

Then $(m_A+m_B)a = F - \mu_k(3m_A+m_B)g$ gives the result.

Result

Correct answer: (B) option (b).

Trap

Option (c) counts $F$ twice; anyone miscounting the tension falls here.

Check

For large $F$, $a$ grows; as $\mu_k \to 0$, $F/(m_A+m_B)$ remains.

Friction count is 3. Source: 2015-11-07 Question 25.
