H3 · Question 16-03 16
In the same setup, if $m_1$ slides, what is the acceleration of $m_2$?

What pushes m2? Source: 2016-03-19 Question 16.

H3 · Question 16-03 16 · Solution
Setup

The only force pushing $m_2$ horizontally is the reaction friction from $m_1$.

Model

Write $m_2 a_2 = \mu_k m_1 g$.

Derivation

This gives $a_2 = \mu_k g m_1/m_2$.

Result

Correct answer: (D) $\mu_k g m_1/m_2$.

Trap

Option (a) puts $m_2$ in the numerator too; anyone mixing up the carrier mass falls here.

Check

As $m_1$ grows, $a_2$ grows, consistently.

Ratio intuition. Source: 2016-03-19 Question 16.

H3 · Question 16-03 17
In the same setup, if $m_1$ slides, what is the acceleration of $m_3$?

Sum the connected pair. Source: 2016-03-19 Question 17.

H3 · Question 16-03 17 · Solution
Setup

For $m_1$: $T - \mu_k m_1 g = m_1 a$; for $m_3$: $m_3 g - T = m_3 a$.

Model

$m_2$ does not enter this pair; add side by side.

Derivation

This gives $a = (m_3 - \mu_k m_1)g/(m_1 + m_3)$.

Result

Correct answer: (B) option (b).

Trap

Option (c) puts $m_2$ in the acceleration denominator; anyone adding the unconnected mass falls here.

Check

For $\mu_k = 0$ the Atwood result comes out.

Atwood limit. Source: 2016-03-19 Question 17.

H3 · Question 16-03 18
In the same setup, if $m_1$ slides, what is the rope tension?

Extract T. Source: 2016-03-19 Question 18.

H3 · Question 16-03 18 · Solution
Setup

Combine $T = m_1(a + \mu_k g)$ with the value of $a$.

Model

Equalize the denominators and simplify.

Derivation

This gives $T = m_1 m_3 g(1+\mu_k)/(m_1+m_3)$.

Result

Correct answer: (A) option (a).

Trap

Option (c) writes the static coefficient in place of the kinetic one; anyone mixing up regimes falls here.

Check

For $\mu_k = 0$ the familiar Atwood tension comes out.

Atwood limit. Source: 2016-03-19 Question 18.

H3 · Question 16-03 19
Suppose $m_1$ and $m_2$ move without slipping. What condition must $m_3$ satisfy?

No-slip inequality. Source: 2016-03-19 Question 19.

H3 · Question 16-03 19 · Solution
Setup

Joint acceleration $a = m_3 g/(m_1+m_2+m_3)$; the friction accelerating $m_2$ must satisfy $m_2 a \le \mu_s m_1 g$.

Model

Solve the inequality for $m_3$.

Derivation

This gives $m_3 \le \mu_s m_1(m_1+m_2)/(m_2 - \mu_s m_1)$.

Result

Correct answer: (B) option (b).

Trap

Option (d) ignores the $m_2$ difference; anyone forgetting the carrier weight falls here.

Check

The denominator must be positive: the condition $m_2 > \mu_s m_1$ agrees with the given data.

Denominator condition. Source: 2016-03-19 Question 19.

H3 · Question 16-03 20
On a $53^{\circ}$ ramp with $\mu_k = 0.3$, a $2\ \text{kg}$ body is thrown uphill at $10\ \text{m/s}$. What is the work of friction up to point A, $2\ \text{m}$ away? ($\cos53^{\circ} = 0.6$, $\sin53^{\circ} = 0.8$, $g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$)

N and fk first. Source: 2016-03-19 Question 20.

H3 · Question 16-03 20 · Solution
Setup

$N = mg\cos\theta = 12\ \text{N}$; $f_k = 0.3 \cdot 12 = 3.6\ \text{N}$ opposes the motion.

Model

Set up the work model $W_f = -f_k d$.

Derivation

This gives $W_f = -3.6 \cdot 2 = -7.2\ \text{J}$.

Result

Correct answer: (D) $-7.2\ \text{J}$.

Trap

Option (e) takes the sign positive; anyone forgetting the opposition falls here.

Check

$|W_f|/(f_k) = 2\ \text{m}$ gives back the distance.

Sign discipline. Source: 2016-03-19 Question 20.

H3 · Question 16-03 22
For the same body, what is the work of the net force up to point A?

Sum the works. Source: 2016-03-19 Question 22.

H3 · Question 16-03 22 · Solution
Setup

Gravity work $-mg\sin\theta \cdot d = -32\ \text{J}$; friction $-7.2\ \text{J}$.

Model

Sum for the net work.

Derivation

The total is $-39.2\ \text{J}$.

Result

Correct answer: (C) $-39.2\ \text{J}$.

Trap

Option (b) flips the sign; anyone thinking work is positive on the way up falls here.

Check

Cross-check with energy: $\frac{1}{2}m(v_A^2 - 100) = -39.2$.

Cross-check with energy. Source: 2016-03-19 Question 22.

H3 · Question 16-03 24
Approximately how far can the body travel up the incline?

Take the net force. Source: 2016-03-19 Question 24.

H3 · Question 16-03 24 · Solution
Setup

Net retarding force $16 + 3.6 = 19.6\ \text{N}$, so $a = 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Model

Set up the model $d = v_0^2/(2a)$.

Derivation

This gives $d = 100/19.6 \approx 5.1\ \text{m}$.

Result

Correct answer: (C) $5.1\ \text{m}$.

Trap

Option (a) skips friction; anyone stopping it with $g\sin\theta$ alone falls here.

Check

Consistency holds with the speed at $2\ \text{m}$.

Consistency with the midpoint. Source: 2016-03-19 Question 24.

H3 · Question 16-03 25
If the body returns to its launch point, what is its speed approximately?

Downhill force differs. Source: 2016-03-19 Question 25.

H3 · Question 16-03 25 · Solution
Setup

Downhill the net force is $16 - 3.6 = 12.4\ \text{N}$; over $d \approx 5.102\ \text{m}$ the work is $\approx 63.3\ \text{J}$.

Model

Write $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = 63.3$.

Derivation

This gives $v^2 \approx 63.3$.

Result

Correct answer: (E) $\sqrt{63.3}\ \text{m/s}$.

Trap

Option (c) assumes a lossless return; anyone forgetting the friction loss falls here.

Check

The return speed must be smaller than the launch speed; it is.

Loss intuition. Source: 2016-03-19 Question 25.

H3 · Question 16-07 6
A rock released from rest falls into a fluid. Which statement about the motion is correct?

Read the initial condition. Source: 2016-07-23 Question 6.

H3 · Question 16-07 6 · Solution
Setup

A body released from rest speeds up; drag grows with speed, and the terminal speed is reached once the net force vanishes.

Model

Model: $ma = mg - f(v)$, with $f$ an increasing function.

Derivation

Speed rises monotonically while acceleration falls to zero; the terminal speed is approached from below.

Result

Correct answer: (B) (b) it will increase.

Trap

Option (a) assumes a high initial speed; anyone not reading the initial condition falls here.

Check

The $v$-$t$ curve levels off to a horizontal asymptote.

Draw the asymptote. Source: 2016-07-23 Question 6.

H3 · Question 16-07 7
A man in an elevator releases a bag and it does not fall to the floor. Which is possible? I. Free fall II. Descending at constant speed III. Accelerating downward at $g$ IV. Accelerating upward at $g$

Zero the effective g. Source: 2016-07-23 Question 7.

H3 · Question 16-07 7 · Solution
Setup

If the bag does not fall relative to the floor, the effective gravity is zero: the elevator accelerates downward at $g$.

Model

This is satisfied both by free fall (I) and by downward acceleration $g$ (III).

Derivation

I and III are jointly correct.

Result

Correct answer: (A) (a) I and III.

Trap

Option (c) mistakes upward acceleration for weightlessness; anyone mixing up the sign falls here.

Check

The relative acceleration is $g - g = 0$.

Write the relative acceleration. Source: 2016-07-23 Question 7.

H3 · Question 16-07 8
A $10000\ \text{N}$ car is pushed by four students with $500\ \text{N}$ in total. No friction, $g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$. What is the acceleration?

From weight to mass. Source: 2016-07-23 Question 8.

H3 · Question 16-07 8 · Solution
Setup

Convert $m = W/g = 1000\ \text{kg}$.

Model

Set up the model $a = F/m$.

Derivation

This gives $a = 500/1000 = 0.5\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Result

Correct answer: (B) $0.5\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Trap

Option (a) mistakes weight for mass; anyone confusing $W$ with $m$ falls here.

Check

$F/a = 1000\ \text{kg}$ should give back the mass.

Ratio check. Source: 2016-07-23 Question 8.

H3 · Question 16-07 17
Block $m_1 = 2.0\ \text{kg}$ sits on slab $m_2 = 4.0\ \text{kg}$. Force $F$ is applied to $m_1$ on the right. $\mu_s = 0.8$, $\mu_k = 0.6$, $g = 10.0\ \text{m/s}^2$. What is the maximum $F$ for them to move together without slipping?

Build the chain: f-a-F. Source: 2016-07-23 Question 17.

H3 · Question 16-07 17 · Solution
Setup

$f_{s,\max} = 0.8 \cdot 20 = 16\ \text{N}$; the largest acceleration of $m_2$ is $16/4 = 4\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Model

Write $F_{\max} = 6 \cdot 4 = 24\ \text{N}$.

Derivation

The result is $24\ \text{N}$.

Result

Correct answer: (A) $24\ \text{N}$.

Trap

Option (e) takes the maximum friction directly as $F$; anyone forgetting the carrier mass falls here.

Check

The $F = 18$ and $21$ questions stay below this threshold, consistently.

Consistency with below-threshold questions. Source: 2016-07-23 Question 17.

H3 · Question 16-07 18
If $F = 18.0\ \text{N}$, what are the accelerations of the masses?

Compare with the threshold. Source: 2016-07-23 Question 18.

H3 · Question 16-07 18 · Solution
Setup

Since $18 < 24$, there is no slipping; they move together.

Model

This gives $a = 18/6 = 3\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Derivation

Options (a) and (d) give the same value; both are correct, and (a) is the marked one.

Result

Correct answer: (A) (a) [$= 3$, equivalent to (d)].

Trap

Option (b) assumes the threshold acceleration for every $F$; anyone not setting up the proportion falls here.

Check

The required $f = 12 < 16$ keeps the statics consistent.

Twin-option note. Source: 2016-07-23 Question 18.

H3 · Question 16-07 19
If $F = 21.0\ \text{N}$, what is the friction between the blocks?

Compute the need. Source: 2016-07-23 Question 19.

H3 · Question 16-07 19 · Solution
Setup

$21 < 24$, no slipping: $a = 21/6 = 3.5\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Model

Write $f_s = m_2 a = 4 \cdot 3.5 = 14\ \text{N}$.

Derivation

This gives $14\ \text{N}$ ($< 16$, consistent).

Result

Correct answer: (E) $14\ \text{N}$.

Trap

Option (c) mistakes the maximum for the actual value; anyone missing the need-versus-capacity distinction falls here.

Check

$14 < 16$ confirms the regime.

Compare with the capacity. Source: 2016-07-23 Question 19.

H3 · Question 16-07 20
If $F = 18.0\ \text{N}$, what is the force that $m_1$ exerts on $m_2$?

Write the action first. Source: 2016-07-23 Question 20.

H3 · Question 16-07 20 · Solution
Setup

$a = 3$; the force of $m_2$ on $m_1$ is $-12\hat{i} + 20\hat{j}$ (friction backward, normal upward).

Model

Flip the signs by action-reaction.

Derivation

The reaction is $+12\hat{i} - 20\hat{j}\ \text{N}$.

Result

Correct answer: (E) option (e).

Trap

Option (d) writes $16$ for the normal; anyone taking the wrong weight falls here.

Check

The vertical component must give the $20\ \text{N}$ weight.

Convert to the reaction. Source: 2016-07-23 Question 20.

H3 · Question 16-07 21
If $F = 26.0\ \text{N}$, what is the acceleration of $m_1$ relative to $m_2$?

Switch to the sliding regime. Source: 2016-07-23 Question 21.

H3 · Question 16-07 21 · Solution
Setup

$26 > 24$, so there is slipping: $f_k = 0.6 \cdot 20 = 12\ \text{N}$.

Model

Compute $a_1 = (26-12)/2 = 7$ and $a_2 = 12/4 = 3$.

Derivation

The relative acceleration is $(7-3)\hat{i} = 4\hat{i}$.

Result

Correct answer: (B) $4\hat{i}\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Trap

Option (d) mistakes $a_1$ for the relative one; anyone not subtracting the carrier acceleration falls here.

Check

Since $a_1 > a_2$, it slips forward, consistently.

Take the difference. Source: 2016-07-23 Question 21.

H3 · Question 16-11 14
On a $30^{\circ}$ incline, blocks $m_A = 5$, $m_B = 2$, $m_C = 1\ \text{kg}$ sit stacked; $F$ is applied uphill to $m_A$. ($g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$, $\sin30^{\circ} = 0.5$) For the blocks to stay fixed, what should $F$ be?

Look at the total weight. Source: 2016-11-05 Question 14.

H3 · Question 16-11 14 · Solution
Setup

The total weight component $(5+2+1) \cdot 10 \cdot 0.5 = 40\ \text{N}$ pulls downhill.

Model

Equilibrium: $F$ balances this uphill.

Derivation

This gives $F = 40\ \text{N}$.

Result

Correct answer: (E) $40\ \text{N}$.

Trap

Option (b) uses $1$ instead of the sine; anyone forgetting the incline falls here.

Check

If $F$ is small the slip is downhill; if large, uphill.

Mark the direction. Source: 2016-11-05 Question 14.

H3 · Question 16-11 15
If $F = 36\ \text{N}$ is applied, what is the acceleration of the blocks? ($x$ positive uphill)

Divide the net by the total. Source: 2016-11-05 Question 15.

H3 · Question 16-11 15 · Solution
Setup

Write the net equation $36 - 40 = 8a$.

Model

The missing force produces downhill acceleration.

Derivation

This gives $a = -4/8 = -0.5\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Result

Correct answer: (B) $-0.5\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Trap

Option (a) takes a single block as the mass; anyone not dividing by the total mass falls here.

Check

$|a| \ll g$ is consistent with a small imbalance.

Sign convention. Source: 2016-11-05 Question 15.

H3 · Question 16-11 16
If $F = 36\ \text{N}$, what is the force that block B exerts on block A?

Cut block A. Source: 2016-11-05 Question 16.

H3 · Question 16-11 16 · Solution
Setup

For A: write $F - m_A g\sin30^{\circ} - N_{BA} = m_A a$.

Model

Substitute $36 - 25 - N = 5(-0.5)$.

Derivation

This gives $N = 13.5\ \text{N}$.

Result

Correct answer: (A) $13.5\ \text{N}$.

Trap

Option (b) assumes zero acceleration; anyone forgetting that contact changes with acceleration falls here.

Check

Cross-checking via B+C gives the same $N$.

Cross-check from the other side. Source: 2016-11-05 Question 16.

H3 · Question 16-11 17
A $7650\ \text{kg}$ helicopter lifts a $1250\ \text{kg}$ load with acceleration $1.20\ \text{m/s}^2$. ($g = 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$) What is the lift force?

Take the whole system. Source: 2016-11-05 Question 17.

H3 · Question 16-11 17 · Solution
Setup

Whole system: write $F_T - (7650+1250)g = 8900 \cdot 1.2$.

Model

Compute $F_T = 8900 \cdot (9.8+1.2) = 8900 \cdot 11$.

Derivation

This gives $F_T = 9.79 \cdot 10^4\ \text{N}$.

Result

Correct answer: (A) $9.79 \cdot 10^4\ \text{N}$.

Trap

Option (d) omits the acceleration; anyone mistaking weight for lift falls here.

Check

Check units and order of magnitude: it must be $10^4$.

Order-of-magnitude check. Source: 2016-11-05 Question 17.

H3 · Question 16-11 18
What is the tension in the cable? (Massless cable)

Cut the load. Source: 2016-11-05 Question 18.

H3 · Question 16-11 18 · Solution
Setup

Focus on the load: write $T - 1250g = 1250 \cdot 1.2$.

Model

Compute $T = 1250 \cdot 11$.

Derivation

This gives $T = 1.375 \cdot 10^4\ \text{N}$.

Result

Correct answer: (A) $1.375 \cdot 10^4\ \text{N}$.

Trap

Option (c) skips the acceleration; anyone assuming static tension falls here.

Check

$T <$ lift must hold; it does.

Compare with the lift. Source: 2016-11-05 Question 18.

H3 · Question 16-11 19
How much force does the cable exert on the helicopter, and in which direction?

Invoke the third law. Source: 2016-11-05 Question 19.

H3 · Question 16-11 19 · Solution
Setup

Newton's third law: the cable pulls the helicopter with the same magnitude in the opposite direction.

Model

The direction is downward.

Derivation

The magnitude is the previous $T$ value.

Result

Correct answer: (B) $1.375 \cdot 10^4\ \text{N}$ downward.

Trap

Option (e) flips the direction; anyone mixing up the action-reaction direction falls here.

Check

Writing this force downward in the helicopter equation balances it.

Substitute into the equation. Source: 2016-11-05 Question 19.

H3 · Question 16-11 20
Box B on a ramp with box A on top; $F$ pulls uphill on B while the velocity $v$ is constant downhill. ($m_A = 1$, $m_B = 9\ \text{kg}$, $\mu_k = 0.5$, $\mu_s = 0.9$, $g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$, $\cos30^{\circ} = 0.87$) For $\alpha = 30^{\circ}$, what is the kinetic friction?

Write the normal. Source: 2016-11-05 Question 20.

H3 · Question 16-11 20 · Solution
Setup

Write $f_k = \mu_k(m_A+m_B)g\cos\alpha$.

Model

Substitute $f_k = 0.5 \cdot 10 \cdot 10 \cdot 0.87$.

Derivation

This gives $f_k = 43.5\ \text{N}$.

Result

Correct answer: (A) $43.5\ \text{N}$.

Trap

Option (d) drops the cosine; anyone equating the normal with the weight falls here.

Check

Compare with the weight component $50\ \text{N}$.

Compare with the component. Source: 2016-11-05 Question 20.

H3 · Question 16-11 21
In the same setup, for $\alpha = 30^{\circ}$, what is the force $F$?

Set the net to zero. Source: 2016-11-05 Question 21.

H3 · Question 16-11 21 · Solution
Setup

Constant speed: write $(m_A+m_B)g\sin\alpha - f_k - F = 0$.

Model

Substitute $F = 50 - 43.5$.

Derivation

This gives $F = 6.5\ \text{N}$.

Result

Correct answer: (C) $6.5\ \text{N}$.

Trap

Option (e) assumes balance without friction and $F$; anyone failing to set the net to zero falls here.

Check

$F > 0$ comes out small and positive, consistently.

Sign check. Source: 2016-11-05 Question 21.

H3 · Newton's Laws (2/2) · Friction, inclined plane, pulley

Newton's Laws — second half: 58 questions

Friction equilibrium and the slip threshold, inclined planes, movable-pulley constraints, massive rope, wedge, elevator, rotating sphere. Each question: try first, then staged solution with → (Setup → Model → Derivation → Result → Trap → Check).

05 Nov 2016 (2 questions) · 25 Mar 2017 (9 questions) · 22 Jul 2017 (4 questions) · 21 Oct 2017 (5 questions) · 17 Mar 2018 (5 questions) · 14 Jul 2018 (7 questions) · 27 Oct 2018 (7 questions) · 16 Mar 2019 (6 questions) · 13 Jul 2019 (6 questions) · 26 Oct 2019 (7 questions)

H3b: 58 questions, 117 slides (this header + 116). The no-slip consistency check is emphasized in every solution.

H3 · 05 Nov 2016 · Question 22
Boxes A ($m_A = 1\ \text{kg}$) and B ($m_B = 9\ \text{kg}$) lie stacked on a ramp, sliding down together at constant speed. A force $F$ is applied to B up the slope. ($\mu_k = 0.5$, $\mu_s = 0.9$, $g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$, $\alpha = 30^{\circ}$) For $\alpha = 30^{\circ}$, what is the static friction force acting on A?

A is solved from its own free-body diagram alone; B's friction must not be mixed in.

H3 · 05 Nov 2016 · Question 22 · Solution
Setup

A is at rest relative to B and slides at constant speed; A's acceleration is zero. The forces on A are: the weight component $m_A g \sin\alpha$ (downward) and static friction $f_s$ (upward).

Model

Equilibrium along the slope for A: $m_A g \sin\alpha - f_s = 0$, i.e. $f_s = m_A g \sin\alpha$.

Derivation

$f_s = 1 \cdot 10 \cdot 0.5 = 5\ \text{N}$. Since the limiting value is $\mu_s N = 0.9 \cdot 1 \cdot 10 \cdot 0.87 = 7.8\ \text{N} > 5\ \text{N}$, no-slip holds.

Correct answer: (d) $5\ \text{N}$

Trap

(a) $43.5\ \text{N}$ is the kinetic friction between B and the ramp ($f_k = \mu_k (m_A+m_B) g \cos\alpha$) — it does not belong to A. (e) $45\ \text{N}$ likewise uses the wrong pair.

Check

$f_s = 5\ \text{N} < f_{s,\text{maks}} = 7.8\ \text{N}$ ✓ — the no-slip assumption confirms itself.

A is solved from its own free-body diagram alone; B's friction must not be mixed in.

H3 · 05 Nov 2016 · Question 23
In the same ramp setup, what is the maximum value the angle $\alpha$ can take for mass A not to move relative to B?

The no-slip threshold is always set up with the static coefficient; the kinetic coefficient is only good while slipping.

H3 · 05 Nov 2016 · Question 23 · Solution
Setup

The static friction needed to keep A from slipping must not exceed its maximum value: $f_s \le \mu_s N$. For A, $f_s = m_A g \sin\alpha$, $N = m_A g \cos\alpha$.

Model

No-slip condition: $m_A g \sin\alpha \le \mu_s m_A g \cos\alpha$, i.e. $\tan\alpha \le \mu_s$.

Derivation

At the threshold, $\tan\alpha_{\text{maks}} = \mu_s$; hence $\alpha_{\text{maks}} = \tan^{-1}(\mu_s)$.

Correct answer: (d) $\alpha_{\text{maks}} = \tan^{-1}(\mu_s)$

Trap

Options containing $\mu_k$ are distractors: the slip/no-slip boundary is written with the static coefficient only. The force $F$ does not change A's equilibrium.

Check

For $\mu_s = 0.9$, $\alpha_{\text{maks}} \approx 42^{\circ}$; since $30^{\circ} < 42^{\circ}$, this is consistent with the no-slip observation in Question 22 ✓.

The no-slip threshold is always set up with the static coefficient; the kinetic coefficient is only good while slipping.

H3 · 25 Mar 2017 · Question 3
A block of mass $m$ slides on a frictionless incline making an angle $\theta$ with the horizontal. What is the reaction force the surface exerts on the block?

The normal is always perpendicular to the surface; it is smaller than the weight; the downslope component is computed separately.

H3 · 25 Mar 2017 · Question 3 · Solution
Setup

There is no acceleration perpendicular to the surface; the perpendicular components balance. The perpendicular component of the weight is $mg\cos\theta$.

Model

Newton in the perpendicular direction: $N - mg\cos\theta = 0$.

Derivation

Hence $N = mg\cos\theta$.

Correct answer: (b) $mg\cos\theta$

Trap

(a) $mg$ is the horizontal-surface reflex; on a slope the normal is smaller. (d) $mg\sin\theta$ is the downslope component, not the normal.

Check

For $\theta = 0$, $N = mg$ (horizontal plane) ✓; for $\theta = 90^{\circ}$, $N = 0$ (free fall) ✓.

The normal is always perpendicular to the surface; it is smaller than the weight; the downslope component is computed separately.

H3 · 25 Mar 2017 · Question 12
A mass $m$ sits on a $2m$ block on a table; kinetic friction $\mu = 1$ on all surfaces. The masses are hitched to each other by a movable pulley; a hand pulls the pulley with $6mg$. What is the friction force between $m$ and $2m$?

First extract T from the pulley, then write $f_k = \mu N$ separately on each surface.

H3 · 25 Mar 2017 · Question 12 · Solution
Setup

The pulley is massless: $6mg = 2T$, so $T = 3mg$ in each strand. On the top block the normal is $N = mg$.

Model

Kinetic friction: $f_{k1} = \mu N = 1 \cdot mg$.

Derivation

$f_{k1} = mg$ follows directly.

Correct answer: (e) $mg$

Trap

(d) $3mg$ is the rope tension; friction is computed from the normal ($\mu N$), not from the tension.

Check

Since $f_{k1} = mg < T = 3mg$, the top block accelerates to the right; consistent with the motion assumption ✓.

First extract T from the pulley, then write $f_k = \mu N$ separately on each surface.

H3 · 25 Mar 2017 · Question 13
In the same setup (Question 12), what is the magnitude of the friction force between the table and the $2m$ mass?

Each contact surface's normal is found separately; the lower surface always carries the total weight.

H3 · 25 Mar 2017 · Question 13 · Solution
Setup

The normal on the lower surface carries the combined weight of both blocks: $N_2 = (m + 2m)g = 3mg$.

Model

$f_{k2} = \mu N_2 = 1 \cdot 3mg$.

Derivation

$f_{k2} = 3mg$ is found.

Correct answer: (b) $3mg$

Trap

(a) $mg$ counts only the top block; the lower surface carries the total load.

Check

Cross-check with the acceleration equations (Questions 14–15): $T - mg = m(2g)$ and $T + mg - 3mg = 2m(g/2)$ hold ✓.

Each contact surface's normal is found separately; the lower surface always carries the total weight.

H3 · 25 Mar 2017 · Question 14
In the same setup, what is the magnitude of the acceleration of the mass $m$? ($T = 3mg$, $f_{k1} = mg$)

A separate Newton equation for each block; tension along its pull, friction opposite the motion.

H3 · 25 Mar 2017 · Question 14 · Solution
Setup

What pulls the top block rightward is $T = 3mg$, what holds it leftward is $f_{k1} = mg$; the net force is rightward.

Model

Newton: $T - f_{k1} = m\,a_m$.

Derivation

$3mg - mg = m\,a_m$ gives $a_m = 2g$.

Correct answer: (e) $2g$

Trap

(d) $3g$ is the answer of those who forget to subtract friction.

Check

The rope constraint $2a_{el} = a_m + a_{2m} = 2g + g/2$ gives $a_{el} = 5g/4$; consistent with Question 16 ✓.

A separate Newton equation for each block; tension along its pull, friction opposite the motion.

H3 · 25 Mar 2017 · Question 15
In the same setup, what is the magnitude of the acceleration of the $2m$ mass?

When drawing the direction of the friction pair between the blocks, action–reaction must not be forgotten.

H3 · 25 Mar 2017 · Question 15 · Solution
Setup

What pulls the lower block rightward are $T$ and the friction from above $f_{k1}$ (to the right by action–reaction); what holds it leftward is $f_{k2} = 3mg$.

Model

Newton: $T + f_{k1} - f_{k2} = 2m\,a_{2m}$.

Derivation

$3mg + mg - 3mg = mg = 2m\,a_{2m}$ gives $a_{2m} = g/2$.

Correct answer: (a) $g/2$

Trap

The direction of the friction from the top block is often confused: it pushes the lower block forward (rightward), not backward.

Check

$a_m = 2g > a_{2m} = g/2$: the top block pulls ahead, consistent with the relative-slip assumption ✓.

When drawing the direction of the friction pair between the blocks, action–reaction must not be forgotten.

H3 · 25 Mar 2017 · Question 16
In the same setup, what is the magnitude of the acceleration of the hand pulling the pulley? ($a_m = 2g$, $a_{2m} = g/2$)

In the movable pulley, first the length constraint, then the acceleration relation; don't miss the factor of 2.

H3 · 25 Mar 2017 · Question 16 · Solution
Setup

The total rope length is constant: $L = (x_{el} - x_m) + (x_{el} - x_{2m})$; differentiate twice.

Model

Constraint: $2a_{el} = a_m + a_{2m}$.

Derivation

$2a_{el} = 2g + g/2 = 5g/2$ gives $a_{el} = 5g/4$.

Correct answer: (b) $(5/4)g$

Trap

(a) $(5/2)g$ is the answer of those who forget to divide by two; the constraint equation must always be written first.

Check

$a_{el} = 1.25g$, the average of the two blocks' accelerations $(2 + 0.5)/2 = 1.25$ ✓.

In the movable pulley, first the length constraint, then the acceleration relation; don't miss the factor of 2.

H3 · 25 Mar 2017 · Question 17
A $6.00\ \text{kg}$ block on top is pulled upward with $F = 200\ \text{N}$; between them a $4.00\ \text{kg}$ rope, below a $5.00\ \text{kg}$ block ($g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$). What is the tension at the midpoint of the rope?

In a massive rope the tension varies with position; isolate the mass below (or above) the desired point.

H3 · 25 Mar 2017 · Question 17 · Solution
Setup

The whole chain accelerates together. Total mass $15\ \text{kg}$; net force $200 - 150 = 50\ \text{N}$.

Model

First the system acceleration: $a = 50/15 = 10/3\ \text{m/s}^2$. Below the rope's midpoint there are $5 + 2 = 7\ \text{kg}$: $T - 70 = 7a$.

Derivation

$T = 70 + 70/3 = 280/3 \approx 93\ \text{N}$.

Correct answer: (c) $93\ \text{N}$

Trap

(a) $70\ \text{N}$ is only the lower weight; the acceleration term $7a$ must not be forgotten.

Check

Cross-check from above: for the upper $8\ \text{kg}$, $200 - T - 80 = 8a = 80/3$, again $T = 280/3$ ✓.

In a massive rope the tension varies with position; isolate the mass below (or above) the desired point.

H3 · 25 Mar 2017 · Question 18
A block B rests against the side surface of a cart accelerating rightward with acceleration $a$; the static friction between them is $\mu$. What must the smallest acceleration of the mass $m$ (the cart) be for the block not to fall?

In the accelerating reference frame, the normal comes from the acceleration and the friction condition from the weight.

H3 · 25 Mar 2017 · Question 18 · Solution
Setup

The normal pressing the block against the wall is $N = ma$; the holding friction is at most $\mu N$. Not falling requires $mg \le \mu N$.

Model

Condition: $mg \le \mu m a$.

Derivation

The $m$'s cancel: $a \ge g/\mu$; the smallest acceleration is $g/\mu$.

Correct answer: (a) $g/\mu$

Trap

(c) $g\mu$ is the answer of those who place $\mu$ on the wrong side; $\mu$ enters through the normal in the friction bound $\mu N$ — solve the inequality instead.

Check

As $\mu \to 0$, the required acceleration diverges (there is no surface to grip) ✓; as $\mu$ grows, less acceleration is needed ✓.

In the accelerating reference frame, the normal comes from the acceleration and the friction condition from the weight.

H3 · 25 Mar 2017 · Question 21
A force $\vec{F} = (2.0x)\,\hat{\imath} - (3.0y^2)\,\hat{\jmath}\ \text{N}$ acts on a $2\ \text{kg}$ object. What is the acceleration of the object at position $\vec{r} = 2.0\,\hat{\imath} + 1.0\,\hat{\jmath}$?

For a position-dependent force, first plug in the point, then find the magnitude, and last apply $F = ma$.

H3 · 25 Mar 2017 · Question 21 · Solution
Setup

The position-dependent force is first evaluated at the given point: $x = 2$, $y = 1$.

Model

$\vec{F} = 4\,\hat{\imath} - 3\,\hat{\jmath}\ \text{N}$; Newton: $\vec{a} = \vec{F}/m$.

Derivation

$|\vec{F}| = 5\ \text{N}$; $a = 5/2 = 2.5\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Correct answer: (d) $2.5\ \text{m/s}^2$

Trap

(c) $2.0$ is the answer of those who take only the $x$ component ($4/2$); (b) $1.5$, of those who take only the $y$ component.

Check

3-4-5 triangle: if the components are $4, 3$, the magnitude must be $5$ ✓.

For a position-dependent force, first plug in the point, then find the magnitude, and last apply $F = ma$.

H3 · 22 Jul 2017 · Question 11
A $m_1 = 2\ \text{kg}$ block sits on $m_2 = 4\ \text{kg}$; $\mu_k = 0.5$, $\mu_s = 0.7$ between them. No friction between $m_2$ and the table. $m_2$ is hitched by a pulley to a hanging $m_3 = 8\ \text{kg}$. Assuming joint motion, what is the friction force between the blocks?

First the system acceleration, then the top block's equation; last, check the no-slip consistency.

H3 · 22 Jul 2017 · Question 11 · Solution
Setup

The system acceleration is $a = m_3 g/(m_1+m_2+m_3)$. The only horizontal force accelerating $m_1$ is the friction between the blocks.

Model

$a = 80/14 = 40/7\ \text{m/s}^2$; $f = m_1 a$.

Derivation

$f = 2 \cdot 40/7 = 80/7\ \text{N} \approx 11.4\ \text{N}$, below the limit $0.7 \cdot 20 = 14\ \text{N}$; no-slip holds.

Correct answer: (a) $80/7\ \text{N}$

Trap

$14\ \text{N}$ (the limiting value) is not among the options; the question asks for the actual friction, not the maximum.

Check

$f = 80/7 < f_{s,\text{maks}} = 14$ ✓ — the move-together assumption confirms itself.

First the system acceleration, then the top block's equation; last, check the no-slip consistency.

H3 · 22 Jul 2017 · Question 12
In the same setup, what must the maximum value of $m_3$ be for $m_1$ to move together with $m_2$ without slipping on it?

In limit questions, first the threshold acceleration, then the system equation; the coefficient must be the static one.

H3 · 22 Jul 2017 · Question 12 · Solution
Setup

At the threshold, friction is at its limit: $f_{\text{maks}} = \mu_s m_1 g = 14\ \text{N} = m_1 a_{\text{maks}}$, hence $a_{\text{maks}} = 7\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Model

System: $m_3 g = (m_1+m_2+m_3)\,a_{\text{maks}}$.

Derivation

$10m_3 = 7(6+m_3)$ gives $3m_3 = 42$, $m_3 = 14\ \text{kg}$.

Correct answer: (d) $14\ \text{kg}$

Trap

Those who compute with the kinetic coefficient land on smaller values; the threshold is set up with the static coefficient.

Check

For $m_3 = 14$, $a = 140/20 = 7\ \text{m/s}^2 = a_{\text{maks}}$ ✓.

In limit questions, first the threshold acceleration, then the system equation; the coefficient must be the static one.

H3 · 22 Jul 2017 · Question 13
If $m_3 = 21\ \text{kg}$, what are the accelerations of $m_1$ and of $m_2+m_3$? ($a_1$: the acceleration of $m_1$; $a_2$: that of $m_2$ and $m_3$)

With a heavy hanging mass, first test the move-together assumption; if it fails, separate accelerations with kinetic friction.

H3 · 22 Jul 2017 · Question 13 · Solution
Setup

If they moved together, $a = 210/27 \approx 7.8$ and the required $f = 2 \cdot 7.8 = 15.6 > 14$: slipping occurs. Kinetic friction is $f_k = 0.5 \cdot 20 = 10\ \text{N}$.

Model

$a_1 = f_k/m_1$; $m_3 g - f_k = (m_2+m_3)\,a_2$.

Derivation

$a_1 = 10/2 = 5\ \text{m/s}^2$; $210 - 10 = 25a_2$ gives $a_2 = 8\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Correct answer: (c) $a_1 = 5\ \text{m/s}^2$, $a_2 = 8\ \text{m/s}^2$

Trap

Those who solve assuming joint motion get wrong accelerations; the no-slip consistency must be tested first.

Check

$a_1 = 5 < a_2 = 8$: the top block lags behind, consistent with the relative-slip direction ✓.

With a heavy hanging mass, first test the move-together assumption; if it fails, separate accelerations with kinetic friction.

H3 · 22 Jul 2017 · Question 17
A $m = 3\ \text{kg}$ block is on a $\theta = 53^{\circ}$ incline; $\mu_k = 0.6$, spring $k = 300\ \text{N/m}$. The block comes down with $v_0$ from $L = 70\ \text{cm}$ away, compresses the spring by $d = 30\ \text{cm}$, and stops. What is the minimum value of $\mu_s$ for the block to stay at rest when the spring is maximally compressed? ($\sin53 = 4/5$, $\cos53 = 3/5$, $g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$)

Force balance in the compressed position: spring up, weight down, friction covers the difference.

H3 · 22 Jul 2017 · Question 17 · Solution
Setup

In the compressed position the spring pushes up with $kd = 90\ \text{N}$; the weight component $mg\sin53 = 24\ \text{N}$ pulls down. Static friction must hold the difference.

Model

Condition: $\mu_s\,mg\cos53 \ge kd - mg\sin53$.

Derivation

$\mu_s \cdot 18 \ge 90 - 24 = 66$ gives $\mu_s \ge 11/3 \approx 3.67$.

Correct answer: (d) $11/3$

Trap

Those who take the normal as $mg$ ($30\ \text{N}$) head for the wrong threshold; on a slope the normal is $mg\cos\theta$.

Check

Getting $\mu_s > 1$ is not a physical obstacle (a very rough surface); the spring force $kd = 90$ is far above the weight component, so large friction is needed ✓.

Force balance in the compressed position: spring up, weight down, friction covers the difference.

H3 · 21 Oct 2017 · Question 11
A $m_1 = 4\ \text{kg}$ block sits on $m_2 = 6\ \text{kg}$; $\mu_s = 0.3$, $\mu_k = 0.2$ between them. No friction between $m_2$ and the floor. A horizontal force $F$ is applied to $m_1$ ($g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$). What is the maximum value of $F$ for joint motion?

In a system pushed from the top, the threshold acceleration comes from the lower mass, and $F$ from the total mass.

H3 · 21 Oct 2017 · Question 11 · Solution
Setup

At the threshold, $f_{\text{maks}} = \mu_s m_1 g = 12\ \text{N}$; this force accelerates $m_2$: $f = m_2 a$.

Model

$a_{\text{maks}} = 12/6 = 2\ \text{m/s}^2$; $F_{\text{maks}} = (m_1+m_2)\,a_{\text{maks}}$.

Derivation

$F_{\text{maks}} = 10 \cdot 2 = 20\ \text{N}$.

Correct answer: (c) $20\ \text{N}$

Trap

Taking $F = f_{\text{maks}} = 12$ is a common trap; $F$ accelerates both masses at once.

Check

For $F = 20$, $a = 2$; the required $f = 6 \cdot 2 = 12 = f_{\text{maks}}$ ✓.

In a system pushed from the top, the threshold acceleration comes from the lower mass, and $F$ from the total mass.

H3 · 21 Oct 2017 · Question 12
In the same setup, with $F = 16\ \text{N}$, what are the accelerations $a_1$ and $a_2$ of $m_1$ and $m_2$?

H3 · 21 Oct 2017 · Question 12 · Solution

Since $16\ \text{N} < F_{\text{maks}} = 20\ \text{N}$, the blocks move together.

Model

Like a single mass: $a = F/(m_1+m_2)$.

Derivation

$a = 16/10 = 1.6\ \text{m/s}^2$; $a_1 = a_2 = 1.6\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Correct answer: (a) $a_1 = a_2 = 1.6\ \text{m/s}^2$

Trap

Those who compute separate accelerations even though the limit is not exceeded switch to kinetic friction; compare with the threshold first.

Check

The required $f = 6 \cdot 1.6 = 9.6 < 12$ ✓ — the move-together assumption holds.

Below the threshold force the system behaves like a single mass; the check is $f < f_{s,\text{maks}}$.

H3 · 21 Oct 2017 · Question 13
In the same setup, with $F = 16\ \text{N}$, what is the magnitude of the static friction force?

H3 · 21 Oct 2017 · Question 13 · Solution
Setup

There is joint motion ($a = 1.6\ \text{m/s}^2$). The only horizontal force accelerating $m_2$ is the friction between the blocks.

Model

$f = m_2 a = 6 \cdot 1.6$.

Derivation

$f = 9.6 = 48/5\ \text{N}$.

Correct answer: (c) $48/5\ \text{N}$

Trap

(a) $16\ \text{N}$ is the answer of those who set friction equal to the applied force; that equality does not hold — the top block's equation is what counts.

Check

$48/5 = 9.6 < f_{s,\text{maks}} = 12$ ✓; the top block's equation holds too: $16 - 9.6 = 4 \cdot 1.6$ ✓.

The actual static friction comes out of the equation of motion; it must not be confused with the limiting value.

H3 · 21 Oct 2017 · Question 14
In the same setup, with $F = 24\ \text{N}$, what are the accelerations $a_1$ and $a_2$?

Past the threshold, two separate Newton equations are written with kinetic friction.

H3 · 21 Oct 2017 · Question 14 · Solution
Setup

Since $24 > 20$, slipping occurs. Kinetic friction is $f_k = \mu_k m_1 g = 8\ \text{N}$.

Model

$a_1 = (F - f_k)/m_1$; $a_2 = f_k/m_2$.

Derivation

$a_1 = (24-8)/4 = 4\ \text{m/s}^2$; $a_2 = 8/6 = 4/3\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Correct answer: (c) $a_1 = 4\ \text{m/s}^2$, $a_2 = 4/3\ \text{m/s}^2$

Trap

Those who solve assuming joint motion even though the threshold is exceeded land on options like (a).

Check

$a_1 > a_2$: the top block pulls ahead, consistent with the slip direction ✓.

Past the threshold, two separate Newton equations are written with kinetic friction.

H3 · 21 Oct 2017 · Question 15
A $280\ \text{kg}$ crate hangs from a rope of length $L = 15.0\ \text{m}$; it is pushed sideways by $d = 5.0\ \text{m}$ with a force $F$ and held at rest ($g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$, $\sqrt{2} = 1.4$). What is the magnitude of $F$ in the final position?

H3 · 21 Oct 2017 · Question 15 · Solution
Setup

In equilibrium the rope makes an angle $\theta$ with the vertical: $\sin\theta = d/L = 1/3$. Horizontally $F = T\sin\theta$, vertically $T\cos\theta = mg$.

Model

Dividing gives $F = mg\tan\theta$. $\cos\theta = \sqrt{8/9} = 2\sqrt{2}/3 \approx 2.8/3$; $\tan\theta = 1/2.8$.

Derivation

$F = 2800/2.8 = 1000\ \text{N}$.

Correct answer: (e) $1000\ \text{N}$

Trap

(a) $1200$ is the value from those who crudely adopt $\sin\theta \approx \tan\theta$ or misread the angle.

Check

$T = mg/\cos\theta \approx 3000\ \text{N}$; the horizontal component is $3000/3 = 1000$ ✓.

In hanging-equilibrium questions, first the geometry ($\sin\theta = d/L$), then $F = mg\tan\theta$.

$m_1 = 2\ \text{kg}$ on a horizontal plane ($\mu_k = 0.25$); the rope goes from a fixed pulley to $m_2 = 4\ \text{kg}$ riding a movable pulley, with the other end tied to the ceiling ($g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$). What is the relation between the magnitudes of the blocks' accelerations?

First the constraint equation, then the force equations; in the movable pulley the ratio is 2.

The total rope length is constant: $L = x_1 + 2y_2 + \text{sabit}$; differentiate twice.

Constraint: $a_1 = 2a_2$ (the horizontal block travels twice the hanging block's distance).

Derivation

Directly $a_1 = 2a_2$.

If the 1-to-2 ratio is written backwards in the movable pulley, you get (a); draw who takes up how much rope.

H3 · 17 Mar 2018 · Question 12 · Solution

Friction is $f_k = \mu_k m_1 g = 5\ \text{N}$. Equations: $T - f_k = m_1 a_1$ and $m_2 g - 2T = m_2 a_2$ ($2T$ pulls the rope down in the movable pulley).

$T = 5 + 2a_1 = 5 + 4a_2$; $40 - 2T = 4a_2$.

$40 - 10 - 8a_2 = 4a_2$ gives $30 = 12a_2$, $a_2 = 2.5$, $a_1 = 5\ \text{m/s}^2$.

If you forget that what acts on $m_2$ in the movable pulley is $2T$, not $T$, the result slips away.

Check

$T = 15\ \text{N}$ (Question 13); $15 - 5 = 2 \cdot 5$ ✓ and $40 - 30 = 4 \cdot 2.5$ ✓.

On the movable-pulley side the tension loads through both strands; $2T$ goes into the equation.

From Question 12, $a_2 = 2.5\ \text{m/s}^2$. The $m_1$ equation: $T - f_k = m_1 a_1$.

Model

$T = f_k + m_1 a_1 = 5 + 2 \cdot 5$.

Derivation

$T = 15\ \text{N}$.

Trap

Those who write $T$ instead of $2T$ in the $m_2$ equation end up at values like (e) $13$.

From the other side: $2T = 30 = 40 - 4 \cdot 2.5$ ✓ — both equations give the same $T$.

H3 · 14 Jul 2018 · Question 5

Giving (e) directly.

(a) is the inverse ratio; the figure shows the horizontal travel is double.

Check

The numerical solution of Question 14 ($a_1 = 16/3$, $a_2 = 8/3$) satisfies the ratio ✓.

A constraint question is solved from the rope length alone, without touching forces.

H3 · 14 Jul 2018 · Question 14
In the same setup, what is the tension in the rope attached to $m_1$? ($f_k = 2\ \text{N}$, $a_1 = 2a_2$)

Two equations + constraint close the three unknowns ($T$, $a_1$, $a_2$).

H3 · 14 Jul 2018 · Question 14 · Solution
Setup

Equations: $T - f_k = m_1 a_1$ and $m_2 g - 2T = m_2 a_2$; $f_k = 0.2 \cdot 10 = 2\ \text{N}$.

Model

$T = 2 + a_1 = 2 + 2a_2$; $20 - 2T = 2a_2$.

Derivation

$20 - 4 - 4a_2 = 2a_2$ gives $a_2 = 8/3$; $T = 2 + 16/3 = 22/3\ \text{N}$.

Correct answer: (a) $22/3\ \text{N}$

Trap

If you forget that $2T$, not $T$, loads $m_2$, the result goes astray.

Check

$m_2$: $20 - 44/3 = 16/3 = 2 \cdot 8/3$ ✓.

Two equations + constraint close the three unknowns ($T$, $a_1$, $a_2$).

H3 · 14 Jul 2018 · Question 18
A block of mass $m$ enters a rough region at $x = 0$ with speed $v_0$; there $\mu_k = bx$ ($b$ constant). What is the magnitude of the block's acceleration as a function of $x$?

With a position-dependent coefficient, acceleration is position-dependent too; constant-acceleration formulas do not apply.

H3 · 14 Jul 2018 · Question 18 · Solution
Setup

Position-dependent friction: $f_k(x) = \mu_k(x)\,mg = mgbx$; horizontally this is the only force.

Model

$|a| = f_k/m = \mu_k g$.

Derivation

$|a| = bgx$ is found.

Correct answer: (c) $bgx$

Trap

Those who forget $g$ and go for a dimensionless expression like (a) $3bx$ get caught by the unit check: acceleration must be in $\text{m/s}^2$.

Check

Units: $[b][g][x] = (1/\text{m})(\text{m/s}^2)(\text{m}) = \text{m/s}^2$ ✓ (Question 17: $[b] = \text{m}^{-1}$).

With a position-dependent coefficient, acceleration is position-dependent too; constant-acceleration formulas do not apply.

H3 · 27 Oct 2018 · Question 2
Air resistance is $D = bv^2$ ($b = 4.0\ \text{Ns}^2/\text{m}^2$). An $m = 10.0\ \text{kg}$ object falls under gravity ($g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$). What is the object's terminal (reached steady) speed?

At terminal speed the acceleration vanishes; the equilibrium equation directly gives the speed.

H3 · 27 Oct 2018 · Question 2 · Solution
Setup

At terminal speed the net force is zero: weight equals drag, $mg = bv^2$.

Model

$v = \sqrt{mg/b}$.

Derivation

$v = \sqrt{10 \cdot 10/4} = \sqrt{25} = 5.0\ \text{m/s}$.

Correct answer: (b) $5.0\ \text{m/s}$

Trap

Those who take drag to be linear in speed ($D = bv$) find a different limit; the exponent $2$ brings in a square root.

Check

Substituting: $4 \cdot 25 = 100 = 10 \cdot 10$ ✓.

At terminal speed the acceleration vanishes; the equilibrium equation directly gives the speed.

H3 · 27 Oct 2018 · Question 11
A $5\ \text{kg}$ object hangs by a rope from the ceiling of an elevator whose upward speed decreases by $2.0\ \text{m/s}$ every second ($g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$). What is the rope tension?

First the direction of the acceleration (velocity + change), then Newton; a slowing ascent lowers the tension.

H3 · 27 Oct 2018 · Question 11 · Solution
Setup

Since the elevator slows while moving up, the acceleration points downward: taking upward as positive, $a = -2\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Model

$T - mg = ma$, i.e. $T = m(g + a)$.

Derivation

$T = 5 \cdot (10 - 2) = 40\ \text{N}$.

Correct answer: (e) $40\ \text{N}$

Trap

(d) $50\ \text{N}$ is the answer of those who miss the direction of the acceleration and write down the weight; a slowing ascent lightens the load.

Check

A downward-accelerating elevator must give the same result: the acceleration is downward again ✓.

First the direction of the acceleration (velocity + change), then Newton; a slowing ascent lowers the tension.

H3 · 27 Oct 2018 · Question 13
A box of mass $m$ sits on a block $M$ on a frictionless floor; there is friction between them. A horizontal force $F$ is applied to the lower box. If there is enough friction for the blocks to move together, what is the acceleration of the system?

The move-together acceleration is always found with the total mass.

H3 · 27 Oct 2018 · Question 13 · Solution
Setup

A system moving together behaves like a single mass; the total mass is $m + M$.

Model

$a = F/(m+M)$.

Derivation

Giving (a) directly.

Correct answer: (a) $F/(m+M)$

Trap

(b) and (e) are the answers of those who count only one mass; the force acts on the whole system.

Check

For $m \to 0$, $a = F/M$ (single block) ✓.

The move-together acceleration is always found with the total mass.

H3 · 27 Oct 2018 · Question 14
In the same setup (Question 13), what is the smallest static friction coefficient that keeps the blocks moving together?

At the coefficient threshold, the numerator is the required friction and the denominator is the normal ($mg$).

H3 · 27 Oct 2018 · Question 14 · Solution
Setup

The force accelerating the top block is friction: $f = ma = mF/(m+M)$. The required condition is $\mu_s mg \ge f$.

Model

$\mu_s \ge f/(mg) = F/[g(m+M)]$.

Derivation

The smallest coefficient is $F/[g(m+M)]$.

Correct answer: (c) $F/[g(m+M)]$

Trap

Those who add $M$'s weight into the normal end up at options like (a); the normal belongs to the top block alone.

Check

Unit check: $[\text{N}]/([\text{m/s}^2][\text{kg}])$ is dimensionless ✓.

At the coefficient threshold, the numerator is the required friction and the denominator is the normal ($mg$).

H3 · 27 Oct 2018 · Question 15
Now suppose a vertical force $F_2$ also presses down on the top block. What is the smallest static friction coefficient for joint motion?

The vertical press increases the normal, lowering the threshold coefficient; the acceleration is unchanged.

H3 · 27 Oct 2018 · Question 15 · Solution
Setup

The acceleration is unchanged: $a = F/(m+M)$. The required friction is the same: $f = ma = mF/(m+M)$. But the normal grows: $N = mg + F_2$.

Model

Condition: $\mu_s(mg + F_2) \ge mF/(m+M)$.

Derivation

$\mu_s \ge mF/[(m+M)(mg+F_2)]$.

Correct answer: (a) $mF/[(m+M)(mg+F_2)]$

Trap

Those who think $F_2$ changes the acceleration end up at options with the wrong denominator; the horizontal acceleration stays the same.

Check

For $F_2 = 0$, the result of Question 14 is recovered ✓.

The vertical press increases the normal, lowering the threshold coefficient; the acceleration is unchanged.

H3 · 27 Oct 2018 · Question 19
A block of mass $m$ rests on a sphere of radius $R$ at a position making an angle $\varphi$ with the vertical. The static friction between the block and the surface is $\mu_s$. What is the smallest value $\mu_s$ can take (in terms of $R, m, \varphi, g, \mu_s$) for the block to stay put without slipping?

At that point the sphere's surface is an inclined plane: tangent = slope, normal = perpendicular.

H3 · 27 Oct 2018 · Question 19 · Solution
Setup

In the tangential direction, $mg\sin\varphi = f \le \mu_s N$; the normal is $N = mg\cos\varphi$.

Model

Condition: $mg\sin\varphi \le \mu_s mg\cos\varphi$.

Derivation

$\mu_s \ge \tan\varphi$; the smallest value is $\tan\varphi$.

Correct answer: (c) $\tan\varphi$

Trap

(a) $\cot\varphi$ is the answer of those who set up the $\sin/\cos$ ratio backwards.

Check

For $\varphi \to 0$ (the top), $\mu_s \to 0$ is needed ✓; the sphere acts like an inclined plane.

At that point the sphere's surface is an inclined plane: tangent = slope, normal = perpendicular.

H3 · 27 Oct 2018 · Question 20
The sphere rotates with constant angular speed $\omega$ ($v = \omega r$). What is the largest value $\omega$ can take for the block of mass $m$ to stay put?

On the rotating sphere, friction acts tilted upward; the two axis equations are divided.

H3 · 27 Oct 2018 · Question 20 · Solution
Setup

In the rotating system, vertical equilibrium is $N\cos\varphi + f\sin\varphi = mg$; horizontal (inward) equilibrium is $f\cos\varphi - N\sin\varphi = m\omega^2 R\sin\varphi$ (friction points toward the top, tilted upward). For the largest $\omega$, $f = \mu_s N$.

Model

$N(\mu_s\cos\varphi-\sin\varphi) = m\omega^2R\sin\varphi$ and $N(\cos\varphi+\mu_s\sin\varphi) = mg$.

Derivation

Dividing gives $\omega^2 = (g/R)(\mu_s\cos\varphi-\sin\varphi)/[\sin\varphi(\cos\varphi+\mu_s\sin\varphi)]$.

Correct answer: (c) $\omega = \sqrt{(g/R)((\mu_s\cos\varphi-\sin\varphi)/(\mu_s\sin^2\varphi+\cos\varphi\sin\varphi))}$

Trap

(d) is the answer of those who drop the $\cos\varphi\sin\varphi$ term in the denominator; the full denominator must be kept when dividing the two equations.

Check

In the $\omega \to 0$ limit the numerator vanishes: $\mu_s = \tan\varphi$ (Question 19) ✓ — the two questions agree with each other.

On the rotating sphere, friction acts tilted upward; the two axis equations are divided.

H3 · 16 Mar 2019 · Question 6
One of the forces acting on a $1\ \text{kg}$ particle is $\vec{F}(t) = 3t\,\hat{\imath} - 2\,\hat{\jmath}\ [\text{N}]$, and its position is $\vec{r}(t) = t/2\,\hat{\imath} - t^3\,\hat{\jmath}\ [\text{m}]$. What is the instantaneous power delivered to the particle by the forces other than $\vec{F}$ at the instant $t = 2\ \text{s}$?

First $\vec{v}$ and $\vec{F}_{\text{net}}$ from kinematics, then subtraction, and last the dot product.

H3 · 16 Mar 2019 · Question 6 · Solution
Setup

From the position, $\vec{v} = 0.5\,\hat{\imath} - 3t^2\,\hat{\jmath}$, $\vec{a} = -6t\,\hat{\jmath}$. At $t = 2$, $\vec{v} = 0.5\,\hat{\imath} - 12\,\hat{\jmath}$; the net force is $\vec{F}_{\text{net}} = m\vec{a} = -12\,\hat{\jmath}$.

Model

The given force is $\vec{F}(2) = 6\,\hat{\imath} - 2\,\hat{\jmath}$. The other forces are $\vec{F}_{\text{diger}} = \vec{F}_{\text{net}} - \vec{F} = -6\,\hat{\imath} - 10\,\hat{\jmath}$. Power is $P = \vec{F}_{\text{diger}} \cdot \vec{v}$.

Derivation

$P = (-6)(0.5) + (-10)(-12) = -3 + 120 = 117\ \text{W}$.

Correct answer: (d) $117\ \text{W}$

Trap

Those who find the power of the net force ($144\ \text{W}$) forget to subtract $\vec{F}$; the question asks about the other forces.

Check

Total power: $\vec{F} \cdot \vec{v} = 3 + 24 = 27$; $27 + 117 = 144 = \vec{F}_{\text{net}} \cdot \vec{v} = (-12)(-12)$ ✓.

First $\vec{v}$ and $\vec{F}_{\text{net}}$ from kinematics, then subtraction, and last the dot product.

H3 · 16 Mar 2019 · Question 8
A particle in linear motion has velocity $v(t) = (-t^2/2 + 3t + 3/2)$ ($\text{m/s}$, $t$ in seconds). At what instant does the force acting on the particle change direction?

The direction of the force is read off the acceleration; it suffices to find the instant $a = 0$.

H3 · 16 Mar 2019 · Question 8 · Solution
Setup

Force points in the same direction as acceleration via $F = ma$; the direction change happens at the instant the acceleration vanishes.

Model

$a = dv/dt = -t + 3$; we seek the $t$ that makes it zero.

Derivation

$-t + 3 = 0$ gives $t = 3\ \text{s}$.

Correct answer: (d) $3\ \text{s}$

Trap

Those who find the instant the velocity vanishes answer the wrong question; what changes direction is the force (the acceleration) going to zero — not the velocity.

Check

At $t = 3$, $v = -4.5 + 9 + 1.5 = 6\ \text{m/s} \ne 0$: while motion continues, the acceleration vanishes and the force changes direction ✓.

The direction of the force is read off the acceleration; it suffices to find the instant $a = 0$.

H3 · 16 Mar 2019 · Question 12
The velocity of body B relative to the ground is found to be $\vec{v}_{B} = (4t+2)\,\hat{\imath}$ ($\text{m/s}$), and its mass is $m_B = 5\ \text{kg}$. What is the magnitude of the total force acting on B?

From velocity to force in one step: differentiate, multiply by mass.

H3 · 16 Mar 2019 · Question 12 · Solution
Setup

The derivative of velocity gives acceleration: $\vec{a}_B = d\vec{v}_B/dt$.

Model

$\vec{a}_B = 4\,\hat{\imath}\ \text{m/s}^2$; Newton: $|\vec{F}| = m_B|\vec{a}_B| = 5 \cdot 4$.

Derivation

$|\vec{F}| = 20\ \text{N}$ (constant; not time-dependent).

Correct answer: (e) $20\ \text{N}$

Trap

(a) is the answer of those who multiply velocity by mass and forget to differentiate; first differentiate, then $F = ma$.

Check

Units: $\text{kg} \cdot \text{m/s}^2 = \text{N}$ ✓; (d) a magnitude cannot be negative.

From velocity to force in one step: differentiate, multiply by mass.

H3 · 16 Mar 2019 · Question 18
A $m_1 = 1\ \text{kg}$ block sits on a $m_2 = 2\ \text{kg}$ block on a frictionless floor; $\mu_s = 1/2$, $\mu_k = 1/4$ between them. A force $F$ is applied to $m_2$ at an angle $\theta$ below the horizontal ($\sin\theta = 4/5$, $\cos\theta = 3/5$, $g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$). Which value of $F$ keeps them moving together?

If the threshold value is not in the list, pick the one below it; the boundary condition is $\le$.

H3 · 16 Mar 2019 · Question 18 · Solution
Setup

The move-together acceleration is $a = F\cos\theta/(m_1+m_2)$. The top block's friction need is $f = m_1 a$; no-slip requires $f \le \mu_s m_1 g$.

Model

Condition: $F \le \mu_s g(m_1+m_2)/\cos\theta = 0.5 \cdot 10 \cdot 3/0.6 = 25\ \text{N}$.

Derivation

The limit is $25\ \text{N}$; of the options, only $22\ \text{N}$ lies below this limit.

Correct answer: (c) $22\ \text{N}$

Trap

The effect of the vertical component of $F$ on the normal does not touch $m_1$ in this question; the trap is to take the threshold to be $25$ and look for it in the list — $25$ is not there, so pick the value below it.

Check

For $F = 22$, $a = 22 \cdot 0.6/3 = 4.4$; the required $f = 4.4 < 5 = f_{s,\text{maks}}$ ✓.

If the threshold value is not in the list, pick the one below it; the boundary condition is $\le$.

H3 · 16 Mar 2019 · Question 19
In the same setup, with $F = 15\ \text{N}$, what are the accelerations of the blocks?

Below the threshold force there is a common acceleration; the check is again $f < f_{s,\text{maks}}$.

H3 · 16 Mar 2019 · Question 19 · Solution
Setup

Since $15\ \text{N} < 25\ \text{N}$ (the threshold), the blocks move together.

Model

$a = F\cos\theta/(m_1+m_2)$.

Derivation

$a = 15 \cdot 0.6/3 = 3\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Correct answer: (a) $3\ \text{m/s}^2$

Trap

Those who switch to kinetic friction without checking the threshold get wrong accelerations.

Check

The required $f = 1 \cdot 3 = 3 < 5$ ✓ — the move-together assumption holds.

Below the threshold force there is a common acceleration; the check is again $f < f_{s,\text{maks}}$.

H3 · 16 Mar 2019 · Question 20
In the same setup, with $F = 35\ \text{N}$, what are the accelerations $a_1$ and $a_2$ of $m_1$ and $m_2$?

In the angled push, first take the horizontal component, then write separate Newton equations.

H3 · 16 Mar 2019 · Question 20 · Solution
Setup

Since $35 > 25$, slipping occurs. Top block: $f_k = \mu_k m_1 g = 2.5\ \text{N}$.

Model

$a_1 = f_k/m_1$; $F\cos\theta - f_k = m_2 a_2$.

Derivation

$a_1 = 2.5 = 5/2\ \text{m/s}^2$; $21 - 2.5 = 2a_2$ gives $a_2 = 37/4\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Correct answer: (a) $a_1 = 5/2\ \text{m/s}^2$, $a_2 = 37/4\ \text{m/s}^2$

Trap

Mistaking all of $F$ for horizontal ($35$ instead of $21$) is the most common error; the horizontal component is $F\cos\theta$.

Check

$a_2 = 9.25 > a_1 = 2.5$: the lower block pulls ahead, consistent with the slip direction ✓.

In the angled push, first take the horizontal component, then write separate Newton equations.

H3 · 13 Jul 2019 · Question 1
A body of mass $m$ dropped into a fluid feels drag $F = kv$ ($v$ velocity) and buoyancy $f = A\rho g$ ($A$ volume, $\rho$ density). Taking downward $x$ as positive, which equation follows from Newton's second law?

Signs are written one by one according to the chosen axis; the sign of drag is opposite to velocity.

H3 · 13 Jul 2019 · Question 1 · Solution
Setup

Downward positive: weight $+mg$, buoyancy $-A\rho g$, drag opposite to velocity $-k\dot{x}$.

Model

$m\ddot{x} = mg - A\rho g - k\dot{x}$; each term is divided by $m$.

Derivation

$\ddot{x} = -(k/m)\dot{x} + g(1-\rho A/m)$.

Correct answer: (b) $d^2x/dt^2 = -(k/m)(dx/dt) + g(1-\rho A/m)$

Trap

Sign errors: drag is always opposite to velocity ($-k\dot{x}$); buoyancy reduces the weight ($1 - \rho A/m$), not increases it.

Check

For $k = 0$, $\rho = 0$, $\ddot{x} = g$ (free fall) ✓.

Signs are written one by one according to the chosen axis; the sign of drag is opposite to velocity.

H3 · 13 Jul 2019 · Question 6
$m_1 = 2.0\ \text{kg}$ on a horizontal plane ($\mu_k = 0.50$); a force $F = 20.0\ \text{N}$ is applied to $m_1$ pointing up and to the left at $30^{\circ}$ to the horizontal. The rope runs over a pulley down to $m_2 = 3.0\ \text{kg}$ ($\cos30 = 0.9$, $\sin30 = 0.5$, $g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$). What is the acceleration of $m_2$?

In the angled pull, first correct the normal, then add the two block equations.

H3 · 13 Jul 2019 · Question 6 · Solution
Setup

The angled pull reduces the normal: $N = m_1 g - F\sin30 = 20 - 10 = 10\ \text{N}$; friction is $f_k = 5\ \text{N}$. The horizontal component of $F$, $18\ \text{N}$, pulls to the right.

Model

$m_1$: $T - 18 - 5 = 2a$; $m_2$: $30 - T = 3a$.

Derivation

Adding gives $7 = 5a$, $a = 1.4\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Correct answer: (d) $1.4\ \text{m/s}^2$

Trap

Those who take the normal as $m_1 g = 20$ find friction $10$ and go for a small acceleration; the vertical component of the angled force feeds into the normal.

Check

$T = 25.8\ \text{N}$ (Question 7): $25.8 - 23 = 2 \cdot 1.4$ ✓.

In the angled pull, first correct the normal, then add the two block equations.

H3 · 13 Jul 2019 · Question 7
In the same setup, what is the tensile force in the rope?

One block suffices for the tension; the other block serves as a check.

H3 · 13 Jul 2019 · Question 7 · Solution
Setup

$a = 1.4\ \text{m/s}^2$. The $m_2$ equation is the shortest route: $30 - T = 3a$.

Model

$T = 30 - 3 \cdot 1.4$.

Derivation

$T = 30 - 4.2 = 25.8\ \text{N}$.

Correct answer: (a) $25.8\ \text{N}$

Trap

(e) $20.0$ is the answer of those who mistake the horizontal component of $F$ for the tension.

Check

From $m_1$: $T = 23 + 2 \cdot 1.4 = 25.8$ ✓ — both sides agree.

One block suffices for the tension; the other block serves as a check.

H3 · 13 Jul 2019 · Question 8
In the same setup, what is the magnitude of the friction force acting on $m_1$?

For kinetic friction, the normal is always taken from the current vertical equilibrium.

H3 · 13 Jul 2019 · Question 8 · Solution
Setup

Friction is $f_k = \mu_k N$; the angled pull had reduced the normal: $N = 10\ \text{N}$.

Model

$f_k = 0.5 \cdot 10$.

Derivation

$f_k = 5.0\ \text{N}$.

Correct answer: (e) $5.0\ \text{N}$

Trap

(a) $8.0$ is the answer of those who write $\mu_k m_1 g$ without correcting the normal.

Check

Net horizontal on $m_1$: $25.8 - 18 - 5 = 2.8 = 2 \cdot 1.4$ ✓.

For kinetic friction, the normal is always taken from the current vertical equilibrium.

H3 · 13 Jul 2019 · Question 9
In the same setup, what must the mass of $m_1$ be for the masses to move at constant speed?

A constant-speed question is an equilibrium question with $a = 0$; the unknown mass sits inside the normal.

H3 · 13 Jul 2019 · Question 9 · Solution
Setup

At constant speed, $a = 0$: $T = m_2 g = 30\ \text{N}$. Equilibrium of $m_1$: $T = F\cos30 + \mu_k(m_1 g - F\sin30)$.

Model

$30 = 18 + 0.5(10m_1 - 10)$.

Derivation

$12 = 5m_1 - 5$ gives $5m_1 = 17$, $m_1 = 3.4\ \text{kg}$.

Correct answer: (b) $3.4\ \text{kg}$

Trap

Those who assume zero friction go from $T = 18$ to an impossible result; friction is what maintains the equilibrium.

Check

Substituting: $0.5(34-10) = 12$; $18 + 12 = 30$ ✓.

A constant-speed question is an equilibrium question with $a = 0$; the unknown mass sits inside the normal.

H3 · 13 Jul 2019 · Question 18
A worker pushes a $20\ \text{kg}$ crate with $F = 20\ \text{N}$ over $1\ \text{m}$. The kinetic friction coefficient varies linearly with position: $0.15$ at the start of the stretch, $0.25$ at the end ($g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$). What is $\mu_k(x)$?

A line through two points: first the slope (difference/length), then the intercept.

H3 · 13 Jul 2019 · Question 18 · Solution
Setup

Linear increase: $\mu_k(0) = 0.15$, $\mu_k(1) = 0.25$. The slope is $(0.25-0.15)/1 = 0.10$ (units $1/\text{m}$).

Model

$\mu_k(x) = 0.15 + 0.10x$.

Derivation

Gives $0.25$ at $x = 1$ ✓; $0.15$ at $x = 0$ ✓.

Correct answer: (c) $\mu_k(x) = 0.15 + 0.10x$

Trap

(a) is the answer of those who mistake the final value for the slope; the slope is the difference divided by the length.

Check

In the integral of Question 19, the average coefficient $(0.15+0.25)/2 = 0.20$ is used; consistent with the linear model ✓.

A line through two points: first the slope (difference/length), then the intercept.

H3 · 26 Oct 2019 · Question 4
The acceleration of a $0.5\ \text{kg}$ object is $a(t) = 3t^2 - 1$ ($\text{m/s}^2$) with initial velocity $v(0) = 3\ \text{m/s}$. What is the magnitude of the average force acting over the $0$-$2\ \text{s}$ interval?

For the average force, first $\Delta v$, then divide, and last the mass; written with the avg subscript.

H3 · 26 Oct 2019 · Question 4 · Solution
Setup

Velocity: $v(t) = 3 + t^3 - t$. At $t = 2$, $v = 3 + 8 - 2 = 9\ \text{m/s}$. Average acceleration is $\vec{a}_{\text{avg}} = \Delta\vec{v}/\Delta t$.

Model

$\vec{F}_{\text{avg}} = m\,\vec{a}_{\text{avg}}$; $a_{\text{avg}} = (9-3)/2 = 3\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Derivation

$F_{\text{avg}} = 0.5 \cdot 3 = 1.5\ \text{N}$.

Correct answer: (a) $1.5\ \text{N}$

Trap

(b) $3$ is the answer of those who confuse acceleration with force; it must be multiplied by the mass.

Check

The instantaneous force is $F(2) = 0.5 \cdot 11 = 5.5\ \text{N}$ (in Question 5, $a(2) = 11$); the average may differ ✓.

For the average force, first $\Delta v$, then divide, and last the mass; written with the avg subscript.

H3 · 26 Oct 2019 · Question 13
A zero-natural-length spring of constant $k$ is attached to a wall; at its other end is a ring of mass $m$, threaded on a vertical rod at distance $l$ from the wall. The ring is released from the horizontal position. What is the normal force between the ring and the rod?

The horizontal component of a zero-natural-length spring does not depend on position; the geometry shows the cancellation.

H3 · 26 Oct 2019 · Question 13 · Solution
Setup

In a zero-natural-length spring, force is $k \times (\text{uzunluk})$. When the ring is $y$ below, the spring length is $\sqrt{l^2+y^2}$.

Model

Horizontal component of the spring force: $k\sqrt{l^2+y^2} \cdot l/\sqrt{l^2+y^2} = kl$ (constant!). The rod balances it.

Derivation

This gives $N = kl$.

Correct answer: (b) $kl$

Trap

One might think the horizontal component changes as the spring length changes; in a zero-natural-length spring the roots cancel and the component stays constant.

Check

Units: $[\text{N/m}][\text{m}] = \text{N}$ ✓; at $y = 0$ the spring is fully horizontal and the force is $kl$ ✓.

The horizontal component of a zero-natural-length spring does not depend on position; the geometry shows the cancellation.

H3 · 26 Oct 2019 · Question 15
In the same ring-and-rod setup (Question 13; $N = kl$), what is the largest value of $\mu$ for which the ring can start moving downward when released?

The starting condition is an instantaneous force balance — not energy.

H3 · 26 Oct 2019 · Question 15 · Solution
Setup

Initially the vertical component of the spring force is zero; $mg$ pushes down, and the largest static friction $\mu kl$ holds.

Model

For motion, $mg > \mu kl$.

Derivation

$\mu < mg/(kl)$; the largest value is $mg/(kl)$.

Correct answer: (b) $mg/(kl)$

Trap

Those who set up the inequality backwards go for a large coefficient; for motion, the pushing force must beat the holding one.

Check

The energy solution of Question 14 gives $Y = 2(mg/k - \mu l)$; at $\mu = mg/(kl)$, $Y = 0$ (motion never starts) ✓.

The starting condition is an instantaneous force balance — not energy.

H3 · 26 Oct 2019 · Question 16
In the same setup, what is the largest value of $\mu$ for which the ring can turn back upward from the lowest point it reaches?

At the turning point, the spring component and friction go into the same equation; $Y$ is taken from the previous question.

H3 · 26 Oct 2019 · Question 16 · Solution
Setup

At the lowest point ($Y = 2(mg-\mu kl)/k$), the upward component of the spring force is $kY$. Upward motion requires $kY > mg + \mu kl$.

Model

Substituting gives $2(mg-\mu kl) - mg = \mu kl$.

Derivation

$mg = 3\mu kl$ gives $\mu = mg/(3kl)$.

Correct answer: (c) $mg/(3kl)$

Trap

The answer (b) of Question 15 must not be carried over here; at the turning point the spring force and the friction direction are different.

Check

$mg/(3kl) < mg/(kl)$ ✓ — turning back is a stricter condition than starting off.

At the turning point, the spring component and friction go into the same equation; $Y$ is taken from the previous question.

H3 · 26 Oct 2019 · Question 17
Blocks $m$, $2m$, $3m$ stand side by side on a frictionless floor, pushed by a horizontal force $F$. If the normal between the left pair is $N_1$ and between the right pair is $N_2$, what are their values (in terms of $m$, $a$)?

A contact force is the mass to its right times $a$; it decreases from left to right.

H3 · 26 Oct 2019 · Question 17 · Solution
Setup

With common acceleration $a$, each contact force accelerates the mass to its right.

Model

$N_1 = (2m+3m)a$; $N_2 = 3ma$.

Derivation

$N_1 = 5ma$, $N_2 = 3ma$.

Correct answer: (c) $N_1 = 5ma$, $N_2 = 3ma$

Trap

(a) is the answer of those who assign the whole mass to every contact; each contact pushes only what is to its right.

Check

The difference $N_1 - N_2 = 2ma$: the middle block's equation is satisfied ✓.

A contact force is the mass to its right times $a$; it decreases from left to right.

H3 · 26 Oct 2019 · Question 19
A foot-pushed platform is attached to two identical stiff parallel springs. Pushing the springs in by $0.2\ \text{m}$ takes $80\ \text{J}$ of work. What is the spring constant of each spring?

In parallel springs the energy is doubled; $W = kx^2$ directly gives the constant.

H3 · 26 Oct 2019 · Question 19 · Solution
Setup

The energy stored in two parallel springs is $W = 2 \cdot \frac{1}{2}kx^2 = kx^2$.

Model

$k = W/x^2 = 80/0.04$.

Derivation

$k = 2000\ \text{N/m}$.

Correct answer: (e) $2000\ \text{N/m}$

Trap

Those who think it is a single spring find (b) $1000$; the parallel pair doubles the equivalent constant.

Check

In Question 20, at $0.4\ \text{m}$ the total work is $2000 \cdot 0.16 = 320\ \text{J}$; consistent with $320 - 80 = 240$ ✓.

In parallel springs the energy is doubled; $W = kx^2$ directly gives the constant.

H3 · 26 Oct 2019 · Question 20
If the same platform is pushed $0.2\ \text{m}$ farther (to $0.4\ \text{m}$ total), what are the extra work required and the maximum force?

Extra work = final energy $-$ initial energy; the force is largest at the very end.

H3 · 26 Oct 2019 · Question 20 · Solution
Setup

The total work is the energy at the final position: $W_{\text{top}} = k(0.4)^2$. The largest force is at the very end: $F = 2kx$.

Model

$W_{\text{top}} = 2000 \cdot 0.16 = 320\ \text{J}$; the extra is $320 - 80 = 240\ \text{J}$. $F_{\text{maks}} = 2 \cdot 2000 \cdot 0.4$.

Derivation

The extra work is $240\ \text{J}$ and the largest force is $1600\ \text{N}$.

Correct answer: (e) $240\ \text{J}$, $1600\ \text{N}$

Trap

Mistaking the extra work for $k(0.2)^2 = 80$ forgets that work depends on position quadratically, not linearly.

Check

Initially $F = 2 \cdot 2000 \cdot 0.2 = 800\ \text{N}$ (Question 19); twice that at the end ✓.

Extra work = final energy $-$ initial energy; the force is largest at the very end.

Circular Motion, Applications of Newton's Laws

36 questions, 72 slides. Topics: centripetal acceleration and force, conical pendulum, rotating rod and disk, vertical circle, friction limit, average velocity and acceleration.
