H4 · Question 2014-10-18 S8
If an astronaut inside a satellite in circular orbit around the Earth feels weightless, then the sum of all real forces acting on them is zero. What can be said about this statement?

Concept: felt weightlessness is free fall, not zero force.

H4 · Question 2014-10-18 S8 · Solution
Setup

The satellite and the astronaut orbit together; felt weightlessness and net force are different things.

Model

The only real force is gravity: $\vec{F}_{net} = m\vec{g}$.

Derivation

In a circular orbit $m\vec{g}$ provides the centripetal acceleration, $|\vec{g}| = v^2/r$; it is not zero.

Correct answer: (b) False.

Trap

Centrifugal force is mistaken for a real force; it is only an inertial effect seen in the rotating frame.

Check

If $\vec{F}_{net} = 0$, the satellite would go straight; there would be no circular orbit.

Concept: felt weightlessness is free fall, not zero force.

H4 · Question 2015-03-21 S1
A simple pendulum (a mass hanging from a string) swings from right to left. What can you say about the direction of the acceleration at the leftmost endpoint it can reach?

At the endpoint: velocity zero, acceleration maximum and tangential.

H4 · Question 2015-03-21 S1 · Solution
Setup

At the endpoint the velocity is instantaneously zero; the restoring force is at its maximum.

Model

$\vec{a} = \vec{a}_{t} + \vec{a}_{r}$ is resolved into components; when $|\vec{v}| = 0$, $|\vec{a}_{r}| = v^2/L = 0$.

Derivation

Only the tangential component remains: $|\vec{a}_{t}| = g\sin\theta$, toward the equilibrium position.

Correct answer: (a) Tangent to the path.

Trap

Option (b) belongs to the bottom point where the speed is greatest; the positions are being confused.

Check

If (c) were true, the pendulum would hang suspended at the endpoint; instead it turns back.

At the endpoint: velocity zero, acceleration maximum and tangential.

H4 · Question 2015-03-21 S3
If the speed of an object in uniform circular motion is tripled and its radius is halved, by what factor does its acceleration change?

Scaling: square on top, inverse at the bottom.

H4 · Question 2015-03-21 S3 · Solution
Setup

The magnitude of the centripetal acceleration $a = v^2/r$ is given by.

Model

New values: $v \to 3v$ ve $r \to r/2$.

Derivation

$a \to (3v)^2/(r/2) = 9 \cdot 2 \cdot v^2/r = 18\,v^2/r$.

Correct answer: (b) $18$.

Trap

(d) $36$; anyone who counts the radius effect twice falls for it.

Check

The ratio is dimensionless: $9 \times 2 = 18$.

Scaling: square on top, inverse at the bottom.

H4 · Question 2015-07-11 S9
Which of the following about uniform circular motion is false?

A constant vector also requires a constant direction.

H4 · Question 2015-07-11 S9 · Solution
Setup

In uniform circular motion the speed and $\omega$ are constant.

Model

The centripetal acceleration has the form $\vec{a} = -\omega^2\vec{r}$; its direction continuously turns toward the center.

Derivation

While the magnitude stays constant, the direction of the vector changes; it is not a constant vector.

Correct answer: (e) The acceleration vector is constant (the false one).

Trap

(d) None of them; it gets marked if the magnitude–direction distinction is missed.

Check

If the vector were constant, the trajectory would be a parabola.

A constant vector also requires a constant direction.

H4 · Question 2016-07-23 S3
What can be said about the velocity vector in uniform circular motion?

Velocity tangential, acceleration inward, 90-degree angle.

H4 · Question 2016-07-23 S3 · Solution
Setup

In uniform circular motion $\vec{v}$ is tangential, $\vec{a}$ is radial and points inward.

Model

The scalar product is $\vec{v} \cdot \vec{a} = 0$.

Derivation

This means that the two vectors are perpendicular to each other.

Correct answer: (c) Perpendicular to the acceleration vector.

Trap

(b) is marked if the roles of velocity and acceleration are confused.

Check

The tangent is perpendicular to the radius; geometry gives the same result.

Velocity tangential, acceleration inward, 90-degree angle.

H4 · Question 2016-11-05 S11
A particle of mass $m$ moves on a vertical circle of radius $R$ under an external force $F$ that keeps its speed at the constant value $v$ throughout the motion. When the particle completes one full revolution, what is the total (net) work done on the particle?

Net work is asked, not the work of a single force.

H4 · Question 2016-11-05 S11 · Solution
Setup

The speed remains $v$ throughout; the initial and final kinetic energies are the same.

Model

Work–energy theorem: $W_{net} = \Delta K$.

Derivation

Since $\Delta K = mv^2/2 - mv^2/2 = 0$, $W_{net} = 0$.

Correct answer: (a) $0$.

Trap

(c) does not ask for the work of the external force; gravity balances it, so the net work is zero.

Check

The energy has returned to the same value; the net work must be zero.

Net work is asked, not the work of a single force.

H4 · Question 2017-03-25 S5
What is the displacement vector of the particle between 20 s and 30 s?

Shared text: A particle of mass $m$ rotates at constant speed on a circle of radius $R = 5\ \mathrm{m}$; period $T = 40\ \mathrm{s}$. At $t = 0$ it passes through the origin. $\omega = 2\pi/T = 0.15\ \mathrm{rad/s}$, $R\omega = 3/4$. Position: $\vec{r}(t) = (R\sin\omega t)\hat{\imath} + (R - R\cos\omega t)\hat{\jmath}$. At $t = 20$ s, the top $(0, 10)$; at $t = 30$ s, $(-5, 5)$.

Displacement: final position minus initial.

H4 · Question 2017-03-25 S5 · Solution
Setup

Displacement is $\Delta\vec{r} = \vec{r}(30) - \vec{r}(20)$.

Model

Use the positions $\vec{r}(20) = (0, 10)$ and $\vec{r}(30) = (-5, 5)$.

Derivation

$\Delta\vec{r} = (-5 - 0)\hat{\imath} + (5 - 10)\hat{\jmath} = -5\hat{\imath} - 5\hat{\jmath}$.

Correct answer: (b) $(-5\hat{\imath} - 5\hat{\jmath})\ \mathrm{m}$.

Trap

In (a), if the direction is taken as initial-minus-final instead of final-minus-initial, the signs come out reversed.

Check

The components are of order meters; consistent with the $R = 5\ \mathrm{m}$ scale.

Displacement: final position minus initial.

H4 · Question 2017-03-25 S6
What is the average velocity of the particle between 20 s and 30 s?

Shared text: A particle of mass $m$ rotates at constant speed on a circle of radius $R = 5\ \mathrm{m}$; period $T = 40\ \mathrm{s}$. At $t = 0$ it passes through the origin. $\omega = 2\pi/T = 0.15\ \mathrm{rad/s}$, $R\omega = 3/4$. Position: $\vec{r}(t) = (R\sin\omega t)\hat{\imath} + (R - R\cos\omega t)\hat{\jmath}$. At $t = 20$ s, the top $(0, 10)$; at $t = 30$ s, $(-5, 5)$.

Average velocity: difference divided by time.

H4 · Question 2017-03-25 S6 · Solution
Setup

The average velocity is $\vec{v}_{avg} = \Delta\vec{r}/\Delta t$; $\Delta t = 10\ \mathrm{s}$.

Model

Take $\Delta\vec{r} = -5\hat{\imath} - 5\hat{\jmath}$ from the previous question.

Derivation

Dividing: $(-5\hat{\imath} - 5\hat{\jmath})/10 = -\frac{1}{2}(\hat{\imath} + \hat{\jmath})$.

Correct answer: (e) $-\frac{1}{2}(\hat{\imath} + \hat{\jmath})\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

Trap

Anyone who forgets to divide by the time marks the displacement option.

Check

Its magnitude is $\approx 0.7\ \mathrm{m/s}$; consistent with the instantaneous speed $0.75\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

Average velocity: difference divided by time.

H4 · Question 2017-03-25 S7
What is the average acceleration of the particle between 20 s and 30 s? (Take $\pi = 3$.)

Shared text: A particle of mass $m$ rotates at constant speed on a circle of radius $R = 5\ \mathrm{m}$; period $T = 40\ \mathrm{s}$. At $t = 0$ it passes through the origin. $\omega = 2\pi/T = 0.15\ \mathrm{rad/s}$, $R\omega = 3/4$. Position: $\vec{r}(t) = (R\sin\omega t)\hat{\imath} + (R - R\cos\omega t)\hat{\jmath}$. At $t = 20$ s, the top $(0, 10)$; at $t = 30$ s, $(-5, 5)$.

First the velocity difference, then divide by the time.

H4 · Question 2017-03-25 S7 · Solution
Setup

Average acceleration is $\vec{a}_{avg} = \Delta\vec{v}/\Delta t$; $\Delta t = 10\ \mathrm{s}$.

Model

Velocities: $\vec{v}(20) = (-3/4, 0)$, $\vec{v}(30) = (0, -3/4)$ (in $\mathrm{m/s}$).

Derivation

The difference is $(3/4, -3/4)$; dividing by the $10$ s interval gives $\frac{3}{40}(\hat{\imath} - \hat{\jmath})$.

Correct answer: (c) $\frac{3}{40}(\hat{\imath} - \hat{\jmath})\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.

Trap

(d) traps anyone who uses half the time instead of $\Delta t$.

Check

Its magnitude is $\approx 0.106\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$; the same order as the centripetal $0.1125$.

First the velocity difference, then divide by the time.

H4 · Question 2017-03-25 S8
Find the instantaneous acceleration of the particle at $t = 30\ \mathrm{s}$. (Take $\pi = 3$.)

Shared text: A particle of mass $m$ rotates at constant speed on a circle of radius $R = 5\ \mathrm{m}$; period $T = 40\ \mathrm{s}$. At $t = 0$ it passes through the origin. $\omega = 2\pi/T = 0.15\ \mathrm{rad/s}$, $R\omega = 3/4$. Position: $\vec{r}(t) = (R\sin\omega t)\hat{\imath} + (R - R\cos\omega t)\hat{\jmath}$. At $t = 20$ s, the top $(0, 10)$; at $t = 30$ s, $(-5, 5)$.

Instantaneous acceleration points toward the center.

H4 · Question 2017-03-25 S8 · Solution
Setup

At $t = 30$ s the particle is at $(-5, 5)$; the center $(0, 5)$ lies to the right.

Model

The instantaneous acceleration is centripetal: it points toward the center, i.e., in the $+x$ direction.

Derivation

Its magnitude is $v^2/R = 0.75^2/5 = 9/80$ (in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$).

Correct answer: (d) $\frac{9}{80}\hat{\imath}\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.

Trap

(c) traps anyone who confuses average with instantaneous acceleration.

Check

$\omega^2 R = 0.15^2 \cdot 5 = 0.1125 = 9/80$ gives the same result.

Instantaneous acceleration points toward the center.

H4 · Question 2017-03-25 S11
A $3\ \mathrm{kg}$ ball is whirled around a fixed point on a vertical circle by a $2\ \mathrm{m}$ string of negligible mass. Since the ball is fast enough, the string stays taut and perpendicular to the velocity of the ball. As the ball rises from the bottom to the top, which of the following is true? ($g = 10\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$)

A perpendicular force does no work.

H4 · Question 2017-03-25 S11 · Solution
Setup

The ball rises by $2R = 4\ \mathrm{m}$; the tension $\vec{T}$ is always perpendicular to the velocity.

Model

The work of gravity is $W_g = -mgh$; the work of tension is $W_T = 0$ because $\vec{T} \cdot \vec{v} = 0$.

Derivation

This gives $W_g = -3 \cdot 10 \cdot 4 = -120\ \mathrm{J}$.

Correct answer: (d) Gravity $-120\ \mathrm{J}$, tension zero.

Trap

(a) traps anyone who invents work for the tension to make the total zero.

Check

The energy loss is $120\ \mathrm{J}$; the kinetic energy decreases by that amount.

A perpendicular force does no work.

H4 · Question 2017-07-22 S18
Which of the following is the linear speed of the mass $m$?

Shared text: A block of mass $m$ is attached by a massless string of length $L = 1\ \mathrm{m}$ to a $r = 60\ \mathrm{cm}$ horizontal arm; the assembly rotates about a vertical rod with $\omega$. $g = 10\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, $\theta = 37^\circ$. The rotation radius is $R = r + L\sin37 = 1.2\ \mathrm{m}$.

Take the ratio; the tension cancels.

H4 · Question 2017-07-22 S18 · Solution
Setup

Conical pendulum: in the vertical direction $T\cos\theta = mg$, in the horizontal direction $T\sin\theta = mv^2/R$.

Model

Taking the ratio: $\tan\theta = v^2/(Rg)$.

Derivation

$v = \sqrt{Rg\tan37} = \sqrt{1.2 \cdot 10 \cdot 3/4} = \sqrt{9} = 3\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

Correct answer: (b) $v = 3\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

Trap

Anyone who uses the string length instead of the rotation radius reaches the wrong result.

Check

$\omega = v/R = 2.5\ \mathrm{rad/s}$ is also consistent (next question).

Take the ratio; the tension cancels.

H4 · Question 2017-07-22 S19
Which of the following is the angular speed of this system?

Shared text: A block of mass $m$ is attached by a massless string of length $L = 1\ \mathrm{m}$ to a $r = 60\ \mathrm{cm}$ horizontal arm; the assembly rotates about a vertical rod with $\omega$. $g = 10\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, $\theta = 37^\circ$. The rotation radius is $R = r + L\sin37 = 1.2\ \mathrm{m}$.

Angular speed: linear speed divided by radius.

H4 · Question 2017-07-22 S19 · Solution
Setup

In the previous question, the linear speed was found as $v = 3\ \mathrm{m/s}$ and the radius as $R = 1.2\ \mathrm{m}$.

Model

For rigid rotation the relation $v = \omega R$ holds.

Derivation

$\omega = v/R = 3/1.2 = 5/2\ \mathrm{rad/s}$.

Correct answer: (d) $\omega = 5/2\ \mathrm{rad/s}$.

Trap

Anyone who uses $L$ instead of $R$ gets result (a).

Check

The period $T = 2\pi/\omega \approx 2.4\ \mathrm{s}$ is in a reasonable range.

Angular speed: linear speed divided by radius.

H4 · Question 2017-07-22 S20
If $m = 2\ \mathrm{kg}$ and the maximum tension the string can withstand without breaking is $T_{max} = 64\ \mathrm{N}$, what is the largest value $\omega$ can take so that the system can rotate without the string breaking?

Shared text: A block of mass $m$ is attached by a massless string of length $L = 1\ \mathrm{m}$ to a $r = 60\ \mathrm{cm}$ horizontal arm; the assembly rotates about a vertical rod with $\omega$. $g = 10\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, $\theta = 37^\circ$. The rotation radius is $R = r + L\sin37 = 1.2\ \mathrm{m}$.

At the tension limit, use the horizontal equation.

H4 · Question 2017-07-22 S20 · Solution
Setup

The exam takes the geometry as fixed: $\theta = 37^\circ$, $R = 1.2\ \mathrm{m}$.

Model

Horizontal equation: $T\sin\theta = m\omega^2 R$.

Derivation

$\omega = \sqrt{T\sin\theta/(mR)} = \sqrt{64 \cdot 0.6/2.4} = 4\ \mathrm{rad/s}$.

Correct answer: (a) $\omega_{max} = 4\ \mathrm{rad/s}$.

Trap

Anyone forcing the vertical equation thinks $T = mg/\cos\theta$; the limit is in the horizontal equation.

Check

Note on the exam's approximation: in the exact solution the angle grows and the result comes out $\approx 4.4$; the options were prepared for fixed angle.

At the tension limit, use the horizontal equation.

H4 · Question 2017-10-21 S7
What is the tension in the lower string?

Shared text: A $1.5\ \mathrm{kg}$ ball is attached to a rotating vertical rod by two strings of length $L = 2.0\ \mathrm{m}$; the attachment points are $d = 2.0\ \mathrm{m}$ apart and the strings are taut. The upper-string tension is $35\ \mathrm{N}$. $g = 10\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. Each string makes $30^\circ$ with the horizontal.

Vertical equilibrium: upper minus lower minus weight.

H4 · Question 2017-10-21 S7 · Solution
Setup

There is equilibrium in the vertical direction: the upper string pulls upward, while the lower string and the weight pull downward.

Model

$T_{ust}\sin30 - T_{alt}\sin30 - mg = 0$.

Derivation

If $35 \cdot 0.5 - T_{alt} \cdot 0.5 - 15 = 0$, then $T_{alt} = 5.0\ \mathrm{N}$.

Correct answer: (d) $5.0\ \mathrm{N}$.

Trap

Anyone who forgets the weight finds $35\ \mathrm{N}$; not among the options.

Check

The upper string carries more than twice the weight; the lower string is close to going slack.

Vertical equilibrium: upper minus lower minus weight.

H4 · Question 2017-10-21 S8
What is the magnitude of the net force on the ball?

Shared text: A $1.5\ \mathrm{kg}$ ball is attached to a rotating vertical rod by two strings of length $L = 2.0\ \mathrm{m}$; the attachment points are $d = 2.0\ \mathrm{m}$ apart and the strings are taut. The upper-string tension is $35\ \mathrm{N}$. $g = 10\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. Each string makes $30^\circ$ with the horizontal.

Net force is the sum of the horizontal components.

H4 · Question 2017-10-21 S8 · Solution
Setup

The net force is horizontal; the horizontal components of the two strings add up.

Model

$F_{net} = (T_{ust} + T_{alt})\cos30$.

Derivation

$(35 + 5) \cdot 0.9 = 36.0\ \mathrm{N}$.

Correct answer: (b) $36.0\ \mathrm{N}$.

Trap

Anyone who also adds the vertical components finds a larger result; those are in equilibrium.

Check

All of this force is centripetal; the speed follows from it.

Net force is the sum of the horizontal components.

H4 · Question 2017-10-21 S9
What is the speed of the ball?

Shared text: A $1.5\ \mathrm{kg}$ ball is attached to a rotating vertical rod by two strings of length $L = 2.0\ \mathrm{m}$; the attachment points are $d = 2.0\ \mathrm{m}$ apart and the strings are taut. The upper-string tension is $35\ \mathrm{N}$. $g = 10\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. Each string makes $30^\circ$ with the horizontal.

Speed from the centripetal equation.

H4 · Question 2017-10-21 S9 · Solution
Setup

The centripetal equation $F_{net} = mv^2/r$ is used; $F_{net} = 36.0\ \mathrm{N}$.

Model

The radius is $r = (d/2)/\tan30 = 1/0.6 \approx 1.67\ \mathrm{m}$.

Derivation

$v^2 = 36 \cdot (1/0.6)/1.5 = 40.0$.

Correct answer: (b) $\sqrt{40.0}\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

Trap

Anyone who uses the string length instead of the radius goes to the wrong option.

Check

$v \approx 6.3\ \mathrm{m/s}$; consistent with a rotation rate of a few $\mathrm{rad/s}$.

Speed from the centripetal equation.

H4 · Question 2017-10-21 S10
What is the direction of the net force on the ball?

Shared text: A $1.5\ \mathrm{kg}$ ball is attached to a rotating vertical rod by two strings of length $L = 2.0\ \mathrm{m}$; the attachment points are $d = 2.0\ \mathrm{m}$ apart and the strings are taut. The upper-string tension is $35\ \mathrm{N}$. $g = 10\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. Each string makes $30^\circ$ with the horizontal.

Net force always toward the center.

H4 · Question 2017-10-21 S10 · Solution
Setup

In uniform circular motion the vertical components are in equilibrium.

Model

Only the horizontal, center-seeking component remains.

Derivation

The center is the rod axis; the net force is radial toward the rod.

Correct answer: (e) Radially toward the rod.

Trap

(c) is the option for anyone confusing centripetal with centrifugal.

Check

The direction is always toward the center; the magnitude stays $36.0\ \mathrm{N}$.

Net force always toward the center.

H4 · Question 2018-03-17 S17
What are the direction and magnitude of the friction force acting on the mass $m$?

Shared text: A disk of radius $R$ rotates with $\omega = 3\ \mathrm{rad/s}$; a $m = 500\ \mathrm{g}$ block sits at rest $r = 25\ \mathrm{cm}$ from the axis. $\mu_s = 0.7$, $\mu_k = 0.4$, $g = 10\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.

Friction meets the centripetal demand.

H4 · Question 2018-03-17 S17 · Solution
Setup

The block rotates together with the disk; the centripetal demand is $m\omega^2 r$.

Model

Demand: $0.5 \cdot 9 \cdot 0.25 = 9/8\ \mathrm{N}$; it must point toward the axis.

Derivation

The static-friction limit $\mu_s mg = 3.5\ \mathrm{N}$ is sufficient, so friction provides it.

Correct answer: (c) $9/8\ \mathrm{N}$, toward the axis.

Trap

The outward options belong to anyone mistaking centrifugal inertia for a real force.

Check

The limit is large; the block stays without slipping.

Friction meets the centripetal demand.

H4 · Question 2018-03-17 S18
What is the maximum possible value of the platform's angular speed, in $\mathrm{rad/s}$, for which the block can stay at rest?

Shared text: A disk of radius $R$ rotates with $\omega = 3\ \mathrm{rad/s}$; a $m = 500\ \mathrm{g}$ block sits at rest $r = 25\ \mathrm{cm}$ from the axis. $\mu_s = 0.7$, $\mu_k = 0.4$, $g = 10\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.

At the limit, friction is at maximum.

H4 · Question 2018-03-17 S18 · Solution
Setup

At the limit, static friction is at its maximum: $m\omega_{max}^2 r = \mu_s mg$.

Model

The mass cancels: $\omega_{max} = \sqrt{\mu_s g/r}$.

Derivation

$\omega_{max} = \sqrt{7/0.25} = \sqrt{28} = 2\sqrt{7}\ \mathrm{rad/s}$.

Correct answer: (d) $2\sqrt{7}\ \mathrm{rad/s}$.

Trap

Anyone who uses the kinetic coefficient finds a smaller result; the block is not slipping.

Check

The current $3\ \mathrm{rad/s}$ is below the limit; consistent.

At the limit, friction is at maximum.

H4 · Question 2018-03-17 S19
For this given situation, what is the acceleration of the mass $m$?

Shared text: A $m = 0.5\ \mathrm{kg}$ block rotates on a frictionless table $r = 50\ \mathrm{cm}$ from a hole; a string passes through the hole and suspends a mass $M$. The block makes $4$ revolutions per second while $M$ stays at the same height. $g = 10\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, $\pi \approx 3$.

Convert the frequency to angular speed first.

H4 · Question 2018-03-17 S19 · Solution
Setup

The block rotates with $f = 4\ \mathrm{Hz}$; its angular speed is $\omega = 2\pi f$.

Model

With $\pi \approx 3$, $\omega \approx 24\ \mathrm{rad/s}$.

Derivation

$a = \omega^2 r = 576 \cdot 0.5 = 288\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ (toward the center).

Correct answer: (b) $288\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.

Trap

Anyone mistaking the frequency for the angular speed (using $4$) finds a far smaller value.

Check

The string tension also comes from this acceleration (next question).

Convert the frequency to angular speed first.

H4 · Question 2018-03-17 S20
What is the value of the mass $M$?

Shared text: A $m = 0.5\ \mathrm{kg}$ block rotates on a frictionless table $r = 50\ \mathrm{cm}$ from a hole; a string passes through the hole and suspends a mass $M$. The block makes $4$ revolutions per second while $M$ stays at the same height. $g = 10\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, $\pi \approx 3$.

The tension links the two sides.

H4 · Question 2018-03-17 S20 · Solution
Setup

The string tension is the centripetal force: $T = ma = 0.5 \cdot 288 = 144\ \mathrm{N}$.

Model

Since $M$ is in equilibrium, $T = Mg$.

Derivation

$M = 144/10 = 14.4 = 72/5\ \mathrm{kg}$.

Correct answer: (a) $72/5\ \mathrm{kg}$.

Trap

Anyone who writes $g$ instead of the centripetal acceleration thinks $M = m$.

Check

$M \gg m$; naturally, it balances the large centripetal force.

The tension links the two sides.

H4 · Question 2018-07-14 S9
What is the magnitude of the normal force exerted on the car by the cylinder walls at point $B$?

Shared text: A $m = 500\ \mathrm{g}$ remote-controlled car travels at the constant speed $v = 6\ \mathrm{m/s}$ on a vertical circle of radius $R = 1.5\ \mathrm{m}$. At $t = 0$ the car is at point $A$ ($A$ on the right, $B$ at the top, $C$ on the left). $g = 10\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.

At the top, the weight helps.

H4 · Question 2018-07-14 S9 · Solution
Setup

$B$ is the top point; the center is below, and the centripetal demand $mv^2/R$ points downward.

Model

Demand: $0.5 \cdot 36/1.5 = 12\ \mathrm{N}$.

Derivation

From the equation $mg + N = 12$, $N = 12 - 5 = 7\ \mathrm{N}$.

Correct answer: (a) $7\ \mathrm{N}$.

Trap

Anyone who forgets to subtract the weight marks (d) $12\ \mathrm{N}$.

Check

If it were at the bottom, $N = 17\ \mathrm{N}$; shrinking at the top is natural.

At the top, the weight helps.

H4 · Question 2018-07-14 S10
What is the magnitude of the normal force exerted on the car by the cylinder walls at point $C$?

Shared text: A $m = 500\ \mathrm{g}$ remote-controlled car travels at the constant speed $v = 6\ \mathrm{m/s}$ on a vertical circle of radius $R = 1.5\ \mathrm{m}$. At $t = 0$ the car is at point $A$ ($A$ on the right, $B$ at the top, $C$ on the left). $g = 10\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.

On the side, the weight contributes nothing.

H4 · Question 2018-07-14 S10 · Solution
Setup

$C$ is on the side; the center is to the right, and the weight is perpendicular to the center direction.

Model

The centripetal demand $mv^2/R = 0.5 \cdot 36/1.5 = 12\ \mathrm{N}$.

Derivation

Weight has no component along this direction; $N$ provides it alone: $N = 12\ \mathrm{N}$.

Correct answer: (a) $12\ \mathrm{N}$.

Trap

(e) errs by copying the top-point equation and subtracting $mg$.

Check

On the side, the normal force is exactly the centripetal force.

On the side, the weight contributes nothing.

H4 · Question 2018-10-27 S5
The period of a body in uniform circular motion on a circle of radius $R$ is measured as $T$. What is the centripetal acceleration of the body?

Dimensional check eliminates options.

H4 · Question 2018-10-27 S5 · Solution
Setup

Speed is circumference over period: $v = 2\pi R/T$.

Model

Centripetal acceleration follows from $a_c = v^2/R$.

Derivation

$a_c = 4\pi^2 R/T^2$.

Correct answer: (d) $\dfrac{4\pi^2 R}{T^2}$.

Trap

(a) makes a dimensional error by writing $T$ without the square: acceleration needs $1/\mathrm{s}^2$.

Check

Dimensional check: $\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^2$ holds.

Dimensional check eliminates options.

H4 · Question 2018-10-27 S20
While the sphere rotates with constant angular speed $\omega$ as shown, what is the largest value $\omega$ can take for the block of mass $m$ to stay at rest? ($v = \omega r$)

Hardest question: ratio of two equations.

H4 · Question 2018-10-27 S20 · Solution
Setup

For the block rotating with the system, vertical equilibrium is $N\cos\varphi + f\sin\varphi = mg$.

Model

Horizontal inward equilibrium: $f\cos\varphi - N\sin\varphi = m\omega^2 R\sin\varphi$ (friction up the slope).

Derivation

For the largest $\omega$, set $f = \mu_s N$ and take the ratio.

Correct answer: (c) the expression with numerator $\mu_s\cos\varphi - \sin\varphi$.

Trap

A sign error gives options (d) and (e); the friction direction is critical.

Check

In the $\mu_s \to 0$ limit the numerator becomes negative: holding on without friction is impossible — consistent.

Hardest question: ratio of two equations.

H4 · Question 2019-03-16 S1
Which of the following is the force that keeps the car on the road in an unbanked (flat) curve?

With no slipping, the friction is static.

H4 · Question 2019-03-16 S1 · Solution
Setup

In a flat curve the centripetal force must be supplied in the horizontal plane.

Model

Since the tire does not slip, the contact is static, not kinetic.

Derivation

Static friction between tire and road takes on this job.

Correct answer: (c) Static friction force.

Trap

(b) marks kinetic with no slipping; as the name says, kinetic needs sliding.

Check

The moment the tires lock, the static limit is exceeded and the car skids.

With no slipping, the friction is static.

H4 · Question 2019-03-16 S2
For a moving object with constant $|\vec{v}|$, which of the following is always true?

Speed constant: tangential acceleration zero.

H4 · Question 2019-03-16 S2 · Solution
Setup

Tangential acceleration is the rate of change of speed: $a_{tan} = dv/dt$.

Model

Since the speed is constant, the derivative is zero.

Derivation

Radial acceleration can be nonzero (example: uniform circular motion).

Correct answer: (b) $a_{tan} = 0$.

Trap

(e) assumes the whole acceleration is zero; a change of direction is acceleration.

Check

In a uniform circle the speed is constant, but the acceleration $v^2/r$ persists.

Speed constant: tangential acceleration zero.

H4 · Question 2019-07-13 S10
What is the maximum frequency that keeps the block at rest relative to the rotating platform?

Shared text: A $m = 0.5\ \mathrm{kg}$ block sits $2.25\ \mathrm{m}$ from the center of a platform rotating with frequency $f$. $\mu_s = 0.9$, $g = 10\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, $\pi \approx 3$.

Convert from angular speed to frequency.

H4 · Question 2019-07-13 S10 · Solution
Setup

At the limit, write the equality $\mu_s mg = m(2\pi f)^2 r$.

Model

This gives $f = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\mu_s g/r}$.

Derivation

$f = \frac{1}{6}\sqrt{9/2.25} = 2/6 = 1/3\ \mathrm{Hz}$.

Correct answer: (d) $1/3\ \mathrm{Hz}$.

Trap

Anyone who writes $\pi$ instead of $2\pi$ finds twice the value.

Check

Below this frequency, friction meets the demand (next question).

Convert from angular speed to frequency.

H4 · Question 2019-07-13 S11
What is the magnitude of the friction force for $f = 0.25\ \mathrm{Hz}$?

Shared text: A $m = 0.5\ \mathrm{kg}$ block sits $2.25\ \mathrm{m}$ from the center of a platform rotating with frequency $f$. $\mu_s = 0.9$, $g = 10\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, $\pi \approx 3$.

Below the limit: only as much friction as needed.

H4 · Question 2019-07-13 S11 · Solution
Setup

Below the limit, friction is static and equals the centripetal force: $f_s = m(2\pi f)^2 r$.

Model

Substituting $2\pi f = 6 \cdot 0.25 = 1.5\ \mathrm{rad/s}$.

Derivation

$f_s = 0.5 \cdot 2.25 \cdot 2.25 = 81/32\ \mathrm{N} \approx 2.53\ \mathrm{N}$.

Correct answer: (d) $81/32\ \mathrm{N}$.

Trap

Anyone who writes maximum friction at every speed below the limit errs.

Check

The limit, $\mu_s mg = 4.5\ \mathrm{N}$, is higher; the block does not slip.

Below the limit: only as much friction as needed.

H4 · Question 2019-07-13 S12
What is the tension in the string at $t = 0$?

Shared text: A $m = 0.3\ \mathrm{kg}$ body on a circular path of radius $R = 1.5\ \mathrm{m}$; $\mu_k = 0.2$. At $t = 0$, $v_0 = 10\ \mathrm{m/s}$. $g = 10\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, $\pi \approx 3$.

Tension is the centripetal force.

H4 · Question 2019-07-13 S12 · Solution
Setup

In the horizontal plane, the string tension provides the centripetal force: $T = mv_0^2/R$.

Model

Inserting the numbers: $T = 0.3 \cdot 100/1.5$.

Derivation

$T = 20\ \mathrm{N}$ is found.

Correct answer: (b) $20\ \mathrm{N}$.

Trap

Anyone who also adds friction errs; friction is tangential, not radial.

Check

As the speed drops, the tension drops too (next question).

Tension is the centripetal force.

H4 · Question 2019-07-13 S13
What is the tension in the string after the body completes one full revolution?

Shared text: A $m = 0.3\ \mathrm{kg}$ body on a circular path of radius $R = 1.5\ \mathrm{m}$; $\mu_k = 0.2$. At $t = 0$, $v_0 = 10\ \mathrm{m/s}$. $g = 10\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, $\pi \approx 3$.

Lost work lowers the speed.

H4 · Question 2019-07-13 S13 · Solution
Setup

Work of friction: $W = -\mu_k mg(2\pi R) = -0.2 \cdot 0.3 \cdot 10 \cdot 9 = -5.4\ \mathrm{J}$.

Model

Since the initial kinetic energy is $15\ \mathrm{J}$, $9.6\ \mathrm{J}$ of kinetic energy remains; $v^2 = 64$.

Derivation

The new tension is $T = mv^2/R = 0.3 \cdot 64/1.5 = 12.8\ \mathrm{N}$.

Correct answer: (e) $12.8\ \mathrm{N}$.

Trap

Anyone who assumes constant speed and marks (b) ignores the work.

Check

The energy loss shows up in the speed, and the speed in the tension.

Lost work lowers the speed.

H4 · Question 2019-07-13 S15
What is the normal force acting on the marble at point $B$?

Shared text: A marble of mass $m$ released from rest at point $A$ of a frictionless circular surface of radius $R$. $A$ is at the center level; the bottom of the circle is $R$ below the center; $B$ is $R/3$ above the bottom.

First energy, then the centripetal equation.

H4 · Question 2019-07-13 S15 · Solution
Setup

$A$ is at the center level and $B$ is $2R/3$ below the center; the drop height is $h = 2R/3$.

Model

From energy, $v_B^2 = 2gh = 4gR/3$ is found.

Derivation

The center-directed equation $N - 2mg/3 = 4mg/3$ gives $N = 2mg$.

Correct answer: (c) $2mg$.

Trap

Anyone who skips the center-directed weight component finds $4mg/3$; not among the options.

Check

Energy before speed, then the force equation.

First energy, then the centripetal equation.

H4 · Question 2019-10-26 S6
What is the vertical component of the normal force exerted by the ring on the bead?

Shared text: A bead of mass $m$ slides without friction on a ring of radius $R$; the ring rotates about the vertical axis with constant angular speed. The bead keeps the position making the angle $\theta$ with the vertical; the orbit radius is $R\sin\theta$.

The vertical component balances the weight.

H4 · Question 2019-10-26 S6 · Solution
Setup

In frictionless contact the force is perpendicular to the ring; there is no other vertical force.

Model

Vertical equilibrium: $N_{dikey} - mg = 0$ is written.

Derivation

Hence $N_{dikey} = mg$ is found.

Correct answer: (d) $mg$.

Trap

Anyone who mistakes it for the full normal and adds angle factors errs.

Check

The vertical component counteracts the weight; the horizontal component points toward the center.

The vertical component balances the weight.

H4 · Question 2019-10-26 S7
What is the horizontal component of the normal force exerted by the ring on the bead?

Shared text: A bead of mass $m$ slides without friction on a ring of radius $R$; the ring rotates about the vertical axis with constant angular speed. The bead keeps the position making the angle $\theta$ with the vertical; the orbit radius is $R\sin\theta$.

The horizontal component is centripetal.

H4 · Question 2019-10-26 S7 · Solution
Setup

The normal points toward the center in the plane of the ring, with magnitude $N = mg/\cos\theta$.

Model

The horizontal component $N\sin\theta$ is taken as.

Derivation

Multiplying gives $mg\tan\theta$, which provides the centripetal force.

Correct answer: (d) $mg\tan\theta$.

Trap

Anyone swapping sine and cosine finds option (a).

Check

The horizontal component enters the speed equation (next question).

The horizontal component is centripetal.

H4 · Question 2019-10-26 S8
What is the square of the bead's speed, $v^2$?

Shared text: A bead of mass $m$ slides without friction on a ring of radius $R$; the ring rotates about the vertical axis with constant angular speed. The bead keeps the position making the angle $\theta$ with the vertical; the orbit radius is $R\sin\theta$.

Radius: the orbit, not the ring.

H4 · Question 2019-10-26 S8 · Solution
Setup

Horizontal equation: $mg\tan\theta = mv^2/(R\sin\theta)$ is written.

Model

The orbit radius is inserted as $R\sin\theta$.

Derivation

Solving gives $v^2 = gR\tan\theta\sin\theta$.

Correct answer: (d) $gR\tan\theta\sin\theta$.

Trap

Anyone writing the ring radius instead of the orbit radius finds option (b).

Check

In the $\theta \to 0$ limit the speed goes to zero; consistent.

Radius: the orbit, not the ring.
